caption:
Many SIDS have committed to 100% renewable energy in their power mix by 2030,, with a collective goal of adding 13 GW of new capacity. But achieving these targets requires more than infrastructure—it demands a whole-island ecosystem approach that integrates energy with food security, water management, marine industries, and economic resilience. 🏝️☀️🌊  
 
Learn how a whole-island approach to energy can drive economic opportunity and enhance community resilience in this new strategy document on Advancing a Just Energy Transition in SIDS 👉 go.undp.org/34Q
 
This approach translates into tangible solutions:  
 
🦀 Fisheries & Marine Economies – Ports account for up to 90% of SIDS' trade. Transforming ports into clean energy hubs can reduce costs and emissions across energy-intensive sectors
🌾 Agriculture & Water Security – 71% of SIDS face freshwater shortages. Solar irrigation systems can enhance agricultural productivity, while renewable-powered desalination and cold storage improve food and water security
☀️ Resilient Infrastructure – Decentralized microgrids, battery storage, and predictive climate tools can strengthen energy resilience, ensuring reliable power for critical services such as healthcare and disaster response
 
UNDP  is working with #SIDS to scale solutions that integrate energy with blue and green economies, making renewables a driver of long-term prosperity and self-reliance. 
 
Achieving this requires substantial international cooperation, with the true engine of change being the ingenuity and resilience of SIDS themselves.

With a focus on Sustainable Energy for Equity, Security and Prosperity, this year's Forum presents a critical opportunity to shape bold partnerships; mobilize investments; and advance policy solutions that put energy at the heart of sustainable and human development.

In 2025, it is critical that we move from intent to impactful action. Beyond traditional approaches, UNDP  is working with governments and partners to scale innovative financing - from blended finance to de-risking mechanisms - to ensure that capital flows where it is actually required.
 
I am looking forward to engaging with partners to discuss innovative and transformative sustainable energy solutions that are both effective and inclusive for everyone, everywhere.⚡️

Today, on International Women’s Day, we are reminded of the promises world leaders made 30 years ago in Beijing to deliver rights, equality and empowerment #ForAllWomenAndGirls
 
A key part of realizing these promises is ensuring a just and equitable energy transition. Sustainable energy and gender equality are deeply intertwined, yet key challenges persist in advancing both:
 
➡️ Energy poverty goes beyond being an infrastructure issue - it is a gendered crisis. On average, women and girls in Africa spend 50 hours a week collecting firewood, water and cooking – time that could be spent on education, improving livelihoods and health.🌐
 
➡️ Women are more than energy consumers – they are agents of change as energy producers, innovators and decision makers. 🙏
 
While the benefits of an inclusive and diverse workforce are clear, the gender divide in the energy sector persists. Women make up only 20% of the energy workforce, despite making up 40% of workers globally. Women-led startups receive less than 3% of energy investment capital.
 
Investing in women-led initiatives and empowering women as leaders in the energy sector can drive solutions for the just transition. ⚡️
 
2025 is a critical year for the gender-energy nexus. Milestones including CSW69 and COP30 present key moments for accelerated action. While #SDG7 is one of only six SDGs without gender-specific indicators, this should be no excuse not to scale up action towards achieving a gender-responsive just transition!
 
Now is the time to invest in women-led energy initiatives, advocate for gender-responsive energy policies, and support women’s leadership in the energy sector.

Not just on #IWD, but every day.
 
#SustainableEnergy #GenderEquality #IWD2025 #CSW69

caption:
How do we solve the energy access paradox? ⚡  
 
This week, leaders at the 2025 Sustainable Energy for All Global Forum tackle this pressing question.  
 
Over 658 million people still lack electricity — 571 million in Sub-Saharan Africa alone. The regional divide is growing. Yet sustainable energy is more than a commodity; it’s key to realizing development and human rights by powering education, health, livelihoods, food and water security and more.  
 
The opportunities are clear. Universal energy access in Sub-Saharan Africa could create 4 million jobs by 2030, while technological advances make sustainable electricity the most cost-effective solution. In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, sustainable energy offers a pathway to energy independence. 
 
We know the solutions. Closing the gap by 2030 requires $30 billion annually, with half of the investments needed in Sub-Saharan Africa. Driving large-scale electrification requires unlocking technological solutions and focusing on de-risking policy and finance to attract private capital. 
 
The world cannot afford to leave 658 million people in the dark. 
 
💡 Our latest Sustainable Energy Bulletin explores the path to bridging the gap, latest trends, and key opportunities ahead 👉 https://bit.ly/4bKL5Dj

I had the pleasure to participate in the “Small Islands, Big Solutions” roundtable discussion for SIDS at the #SEforALLForum.🇧🇧 
 The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS outlined the clear priority of placing sustainable energy at the center of development. With SIDS currently spending 5-10% of their GDP on fossil fuel imports, this Ministerial reminds us that: sustainable, reliable, and affordable energy must be the engine of resilience and economic growth in SIDS.🏝️

 With many SIDS already on track to achieve a 100% renewable energy power mix by 2030, this is not only about infrastructure; it’s about sovereignty and unlocking just development opportunities. Beyond ambition, we need concrete pathways to impact. 

 1️⃣ Unlock scaled and concessional finance: We need financing mechanisms that work for SIDS not against them, to reach the $5.9 billion needed annually to meet 2030 targets.

 2️⃣️ Scale SIDS-specific digital technologies: AI, smart grids, and geospatial tools can accelerate energy access & enhance resilience for SIDS. 

 3️⃣ Beyond technology and finance: We need to create enabling policy environments & strategic partnerships, especially through SIDS-SIDS cooperation. 

We are committed to driving a future where SIDS are not defined by vulnerability, but as leaders in clean, resilient, and digital societies. Let us rise up for SIDS in their sustainable energy revolution!🏝️⚡️  

To find out how @UNDP and and @AOSIS are advancing sustainable energy in SIDS for a for a resilient and equitable future, check the link in the comments below ➡️👇
 #EnergyForDevelopment #RisingUp4SIDS #SustainableEnergyRevolution   #JustTransition #ResilientFuture

caption:
Achieving Mission 300 requires a fundamental shift in how we approach Energy Access!⚡️ 

Yesterday, in a timely and critical session organized by The World Bank  and ESMAP - Energy Sector Management Assistance Program  - Energy Sector Management Assistance Program at the #SEforALLForum in Barbados, we discussed what it will take to scale distributed renewable energy and unlock financing to reach 300 million people by 2030: 

1️⃣ Distributed renewables must be embedded in national energy strategies: Clear interconnection policies are critical to ensuring mini-grids can complement, rather than compete with, national grids. When integrated effectively, they could provide up to 11% of new electricity connections. 

2️⃣ The cost of capital is a barrier to scaling clean energy: High borrowing costs and debt burdens are locking out investment. Policy and financial de-risking mechanisms, including debt-for-energyswaps and financial instruments, must be expanded. 

3️⃣ A whole-of-society approach is essential: Civil society, local leadership, and communities must be at the center of designing and scaling energy solutions, as seen in Guinea’s successful decentralized projects. 

Technology alone will not deliver M300. Policy and regulatory reforms, coupled with strategic financing, are needed to turn solutions into large-scale impact.🌐

UNDP  and United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)  are connecting policy, finance, and innovation to drive transformation. We are moving beyond business-as-usual approaches and rethinking financing clean energy to drive meaningful and lasting development impact. 

Through initiatives like the Africa Minigrids Program, Solar for Health, and financial de-risking instruments, we are committed to scale clean energy through collaboration!🤝⚡️
#EnergyForDevelopment #SEforALLForum #SustainableFinance #EnergyTransition

caption:
Powering the SDGs: From Connections to Consumption.💡

By 2050, the global population will grow by nearly 2 billion, driving electricity demand up by nearly 50%. While clean energy generation is on track to break new records over the 2025-2027 forecast period (with renewable capacity projected to triple by 2030) a critical question remains: how do people access energy? 

Yesterday at the at the #SEforALLForum, we gathered with an excellent group of experts -  Sarah Malm  (Gogla), Cassady Walters  (Rockefeller Foundation/GEAPP), Alexander Obiechina  Ltd), and Martijn Veen  (SNV) - to explore this pressing concern and discuss how finance, decentralized solutions, and innovation can unlock an inclusive, affordable, and productive energy future. 

Achieving universal electrification by 2030 requires $52 billion per year: but finance alone isn’t the answer. To close this gap, we must: 

➡️ Shift our focus from generating energy, to delivering it to people affordably, efficiently and securely. 

➡️ Link decentralized renewable energy solutions with productive uses that unlock a pathway to inclusive growth and improved livelihoods, creating a spiral of positive development outcomes. 

➡️ Increase energy storage capacity to accommodate new variable, context specific, renewable energy generation. 

➡️ Revolutionize our energy supply by harnessing AI to optimize energy storage systems. 

While we have made significant progress in energy generation, we are reminded that technology alone will not get us to our goals. With 685 million people still living without electricity, our work is far from over.  

We need innovative financial models, inclusive business strategies, and above all else, a commitment to leaving no one behind!☀️🤝⚡️
#EnergyForDevelopment  #EnergyAccess #RenewableEnergy #SustainableDevelopment

As small island digital states, SIDS are leveraging AI, IoT, and remote sensing to optimize energy planning, predict climate risks, and integrate energy with water, food, and transport systems:

🌊 Pacific SIDS are using open data platforms and digital assessments to enhance energy planning and financing transparency
☀️ Caribbean SIDS are integrating AI and IoT into energy systems to improve smart grid management
🏝️ AIS SIDS are upskilling and reskilling workforces needed for a resilient and inclusive energy transition that can empower women, youth and entrepreneurs through digital.

SIDS are also advancing the use of data through initiatives like the UNDP Data Platform for SIDS, leading data-driven policymaking. 💡👉 https://lnkd.in/ecnQjT_j

@‌UNDP is supporting SIDS in strengthening regulatory frameworks, unlocking financing, and building local technical capacity to harness digital innovation for accelerating their #EnergyRevolution. ⚡️

📌 Explore how digital innovation is shaping SIDS' energy future in this new policy paper on Advancing a Just Energy Transition in SIDS 👉 http://go.undp.org/34Q

caption:
Today, I joined fellow experts and practitioners at the Think7 Summit panel on "Energy Security and Climate", hosted by the Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI).
 
Climate change and energy security are deeply interlinked. While the global energy system fuels development, it also drives climate change, accounting for 75% of greenhouse gas emissions. As climate change intensifies, the links with energy security deepen. With conflicts, debt, and rising inequalities straining economies, the G7 has a strategic opportunity to support a just, inclusive energy transition that ensures no one is left behind:
 
➡️ Energy security is climate resilience. Despite record growth in renewables, climate disruptions in 2023 slashed wind energy output by up to 30% and hydropower by over 50% in some regions. Our energy systems must be designed for the climate of today - not the past.
 
➡️ Securing energy means rethinking how and where we invest. Over 90% of clean energy growth is in advanced economies and China, while SIDS face climate losses up to 9% of GDP and unsustainable debt. Through innovative tools like Debt Swaps for Energy, UNDP is helping unlock renewable investment - turning fiscal constraints into opportunities for resilience.
 
➡️ Digital, data, and AI are the new core of energy infrastructure. With electricity demand set to double by 2050, climate intelligence - from predictive models to smart grids - is essential to build resilient, investable, and future-ready energy systems.
 
Now is the time for the G7 to move from ambition to implementation. With 1.18 billion people still living in energy poverty, energy security must drive human development through partnerships, stronger Global South-North cooperation and targeted investment.
 
Thank you to CIGI and fellow panelists for a timely, forward-looking discussion.
 
#T7CIGI #T72025 #Think7CIGI #EnergyforDevelopment #EnergyTransition

Electric utopia or elite privilege? Rethinking e-mobility for the Global South🚗⚡
 
The future of mobility is electric - but is it truly global? In 2023, nearly one in five vehicles sold worldwide was electric, and by 2035 electric vehicles are projected to make up almost 50% of the global auto market. However, a staggering 95% of EV sales are concentrated in China, Europe, and the United States.
 
While the Global South remains largely on the sidelines, accounting for only a small fraction of these sales, the shift to e-mobility holds immense potential. It presents an opportunity to:
 
✅ Improve air quality and health outcomes, particularly in the Global South, where air pollution claims millions of lives, accounting for 89% of the 4.2 million premature deaths annually.
 
✅ Reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels, enhancing energy security and economic resilience.
 
✅ Electrify shared and public transport, ensuring affordable and inclusive mobility solutions, revitalizing a form of widely affordable transportation essential for last-mile connectivity.
 
✅ Create jobs and foster economic growth, as EV manufacturing alone is expected to create 1.5 million new jobs by 2030.
 
Despite solutions emerging, such as innovative financing models; digital technologies; and localized electrification strategies, the question remains: how can the Global South harness the e-mobility revolution to drive sustainable development and climate action?
 
I invite you all to explore these insights and the opportunities that lie ahead for the Global South to transition to e-mobility in my latest illuminem article: https://lnkd.in/dEQ62xiy

#EnergyForDevelopment #GlobalSouth #Emobility #JustTransition

Delighted to have joined the @YOUNGO Energy Working Group for a discussion on how youth can lead the sustainable energy revolution.
 
We discussed how to lift people out of energy poverty and ensure inclusive just transitions through exploring the potential of e-mobility; how AI solutions can drive energy access; and climate negotiations and energy policy.
 
Three key points stood out from the discussion:

1️⃣  Rethink the framing – we must ask ourselves, what can be done to leapfrog beyond the confines of the traditional renewable energy practices to deliver a sustainable energy revolution.

2️⃣  AI solutions need to put human development at front at centre – While AI can optimize energy systems, we must ensure it doesn’t exacerbate inequalities or divert resources from urgent priorities like universal energy access.

3️⃣  Inclusion and energy equality is non-negotiable – From youth, women to Indigenous communities, all voices must shape energy policies and negotiations to create equitable and lasting impact.
 
Thank you to YOUNGO Energy Working Group for pushing the boundaries to imagine an energy revolution to drive a net-zero future for all!💡
 
I invite you all to re-watch the session here: https://lnkd.in/etPxbKGv 

#EnergyForDevelopment #Youth4Energy #JustTransition

Delighted to have joined colleagues from @UNDP Bhutan on their webinar co-organized by @Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources to explore Bhutan’s green hydrogen potential.
 
In 2023, the world produced 97 million tons of hydrogen - but less than 1% came from low-emission sources. The momentum is growing, but the challenge is clear: how we choose to develop green hydrogen, and for whom, will define whether it delivers on its promise:

1️⃣ Green hydrogen must be a tool for development - not just decarbonization. With youth unemployment at 28.6% and 55% of the population living in rural areas, Bhutan needs growth that is inclusive and job-rich. Green hydrogen could support this, if linked to skills development, rural infrastructure, and the broader vision of Gross National Happiness.

2️⃣ Sustainability is not one-size-fits-all. While Bhutan has vast hydropower resources, green hydrogen production raises concerns about water use, land access, and biodiversity. It takes 9 litres of water to produce 1 kg of hydrogen. In a mountainous country, with seasonal water stress, these trade-offs matter. The goal must be to balance ambition with realism, scale with sustainability.

3️⃣ The transition must be just and equitable. That means ensuring benefits reach everyone. We should avoid extractive investment models and prioritize policies that keep value local, empower communities, and protect natural and cultural heritage.
 
@UNDP remains committed to supporting Bhutan's green hydrogen journey: not as champions of a single solution, but as partners dedicated to inclusive long-term impact.

⚡ Energy is a fundamental enabler of development — and nowhere is this more evident than in the health sector. It delivers one of the highest returns in climate adaptation, yet remains critically underfunded.

🔌 1 in 4 health facilities globally lacks electricity, and at least 25,000 in sub-Saharan Africa operate with no electricity access. Bridging this gap requires four strategic shifts:

✅ Integrating Sustainable Energy into Health Policies and Planning
Nearly 1 billion people rely on health facilities without reliable electricity. Energy must be integrated into health strategies and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) planning.

✅ Financing Sustainable Energy for Health Resilience
An estimated $4.9 billion is needed to electrify facilities in 63 low- and middle-income countries. Funding should prioritize decentralized renewable energy as core health infrastructure.

✅ Promoting Data-driven Decisionmaking
In 46 low- and middle-income countries, 60% of health facilities face unreliable power. Energy audits, monitoring, geospatial data, and AI-powered storage can improve reliability.

✅ Prioritizing Sustainable Energy in Fragile and Crisis-affected Settings
With 2 billion people in conflict-affected areas, solar mini-grids and Pay-As-You-Go models ensure care continues when the grid fails.

Investing in sustainable energy is not just about powering facilities — it’s about powering health systems that save lives.

#EnergyforHealth #UNDP #WorldHealthDay

“Tailoring electrification to local contexts and needs can both accelerate energy transitions and tackle last-mile mobility challenges, particularly in areas with inadequate public transport.”📣
 
In 2023, electric vehicles made up nearly one in five cars sold globally: yet 95% of these sales occurred in just three regions — China, Europe, and the United States. For many countries in the Global South, they are on the periphery of this transformation, despite facing the some of the most urgent pollution and energy security challenges.
 
But e-mobility isn’t just about cars: it’s about reimagining urban mobility systems as a catalyst for sustainable development.
 
Ultimately, the focus must be to create sustainable urban mobility systems centred around public transport that reflect the needs and asks of communities!

Closing Africa’s Energy Access Gap: Looking Beyond the Traditional Grid to a Decentralized Future.🌍⚡️
 
The global energy access gap is widening, and it is increasingly a challenge for countries in Sub-Saharan Africa. Of the 685 million people globally without electricity, 571 million live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
Grid expansion alone will not close Africa’s energy access gap.
 
Decentralized Renewable Energy (DRE) solutions, such as solar mini-grids and off-grid systems, are already offering a fast and cost-effective path to electrification. Not only could they provide 80% of new electricity connections in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, but they have already provided electricity access to 560 million people worldwide. These solutions go beyond access - they have become a catalyst for change in Africa:
 
➡️ Nigeria’s market-driven approach has enabled the deployment of +100 solar-powered mini-grids.
 
➡️ Easy Solar has brought power to +1M people in Sierra Leone and Liberia since 2016.
 
➡️ Retrofitting diesel-powered irrigation system with solar energy helped mango farmers boost yields by 185% per tree in Tanzania.
 
But to be successful, governments must be proactive in planning regulatory frameworks that enable mini-grids to complement national grids rather than compete with them; as without clear interconnection policies, these projects risk becoming stranded assets. Through leveraging digitalization, AI, and advanced grid technologies, smart decentralized systems can enhance efficiency, minimize energy losses and optimize renewable energy integration to power a sustainable and inclusive energy future.⚡️♻️
 
To find out why the future of energy in Africa lies beyond the traditional grid, I invite you to read this latest edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin here: 👉 https://bit.ly/4bKL5Dj
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #RenewableEnergy #EnergyAccess #Africa #MiniGrids

caption:
This Earth Day 2025, we take time to reflect on the importance of the circular energy revolution. The transition to sustainable energy is more important than ever: not only for the environment but for the global economy and society as a whole.
 
Historically, the production and consumption of energy has been responsible for >75% of greenhouse gas emissions - making it the primary driver of climate change and global warming. However, sustainable energy solutions, such solar and wind power, are becoming increasingly more accessible and cost-effective. In 2023, renewables accounted for 30% of global electricity supply. By 2030, electricity is projected to grow six times faster than energy demand driven by a surge in renewable energy adoption and the rise in electric vehicles. 
 
Yet as demand for electricity and battery storage & utilization increases, so too does the need for critical minerals. While less harmful than fossil fuels, we need to also ask ourselves:
 
➡️ With battery storage capacity currently at 3TWh, anticipated to triple by 2030, what will this mean for the battery sector on the whole? How and where will this impact on the demand for critical minerals?
 
 ➡️ Extracting minerals sustainably remains a challenge, with lithium production requiring 2.2 million liters of water per ton - an immense demand in regions with limited water access. How do we ensure that we are not exacerbating as opposed to enabling human development?
 
➡️ With 54% of critical mineral reserves sitting on Indigenous People’s land, how do we ensure these actors have a voice?
 
➡️ Although Africa currently holds over 50% of global reserves and production of cobalt and manganese, which are critical components for batteries, how do we ensure that these benefits are evenly distributed amongst all members of society? 
 
While renewable electricity continues to scale up - reshaping markets and accelerating innovation - we are reminded today on #EarthDay of the importance of proceeding with caution. A sustainable, circular energy revolution is critical to transforming lives and our global economies, reducing carbon emissions, improving air quality, and preserving our natural resources.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #EarthDay #SustainableEnergy #RenewableEnergy #ClimateAction #GoGreen

Delighted to have joined the opening panel of “Advancing a Just Energy Transition Through Multilateral Action”, hosted by New America  alongside Dr. Chola Milambo, Permanent Representative of Zambia to the United Nations, and moderated by Heela Rasool-Ayub.
 
At a time of rising tariffs, deepening debt burdens, and widening divides in global finance, we face a series of fundamental questions: who defines the energy transition, who benefits from it, and how do we deliver justice at scale?
 
Here are three key messages discussed:

1️⃣ A just energy transition is not a choice, it is a human right: Energy powers health, education, and livelihoods. Nearly 60% of healthcare facilities in 46 low- and middle-income countries face unreliable power. Access to energy is access to life-saving services.
 
2️⃣ Access is no longer just about electricity, it’s about security: Only 2% of global clean energy investment reaches Africa. We need systems that deliver fit-for-purpose finance, debt reform, and de-risking mechanisms that allow countries to drive transitions that advance social protection, gender equality, and local development.

Achieving universal electricity access by 2030 will cost USD 30 billion a year: But how do we get there?
 
While renewable energy investment in Africa grew 96% annually between 2010–2020 - outpacing global trends - the region still received just 2% of global renewable investment over two decades, with over 90% concentrated in a handful of countries. 
 
To close the energy access gap, it is estimated that Africa will require USD 25 billion annually. But public finance alone will not close the gap. Unlocking Africa’s energy future will require:
 ➡️ Deep sectoral reforms — with 58% of African utilities failing to recover operational costs, many remain financially unviable.
 ➡️ Cost-reflective tariffs and revenue certainty — essential to creating a stable investment climate.
 ➡️ Policy reforms — to allow private electricity providers to compete with state-run utilities.
 ➡️ Blended finance models — combining concessional capital with policy reform to de-risk and mobilize private investment at scale.
 
📌 Rwanda’s SEAP program is a strong example: backed by concessional loans, it extended 8,000+ km of power lines, connected 317,000+ new households, and trained 4,000 people — 30% of them women.
 
With the right policies, incentives, and blended finance, sustainable energy access in Africa is possible. The time to act is now - the world cannot afford to leave 685 million people in the dark. 💡
 
To find out more, I invite you to read the latest edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin:👉  https://bit.ly/4lxosH9
 
#EnergyForDevelopment  #Finance #EnergyRevolution

Recent trends such as AI-generated Studio Ghibli images and AI Doll action figures allow users to “cartoonize” their lives. However, these requests impose significant strain on data centres, often leading to infrastructure malfunctions caused by overheating or “melting” due to high demand.

Since OpenAI launched its extended image rendering capabilities in April 2025, over 700 million image generation requests have been made. Unlike “typical” ChatGPT text requests, which consume 2.9Wh, these image requests reportedly consume 3.25Wh. The additional 0.35Wh energy consumption has amounted to over 245 MWh - equivalent to the energy used to power 2,800 10W LED bulbs for a year.

Yet, while servers work overtime to render these trends, 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty, lacking access to air conditioning, heating, and lighting. This raises a critical question: While AI-generated images are increasing energy demand, how are digital technologies being used to close the access gap for those 1.18 billion energy-poor individuals?

Adopting digital technologies across the energy value chain can accelerate and economize the energy transition through:   
 
➡️ Enhancing efficiency and expanding access to renewable energy sources 
 
➡️ Identifying optimal investment opportunities and enabling informed based decision-making 
 
➡️ “Leapfrogging” traditional energy systems models by integrating more efficient and cost-effective energy solutions  

To learn more about how digital technologies are bridging this energy access divide, I invite you to read this previous edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin on Digital, Data, and AI here: 👉 https://lnkd.in/ey4__kbt     #EnergyForDevelopment #AI #EnergyAccess

caption:
Grateful to have joined the panel on “Solutions for Clean Cooking to Advance the SDG Agenda”, co-hosted with the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition (CEET). It was an important space to reaffirm what many of us in sustainable energy for development know well: clean cooking is not a side issue – it is a core pillar of a just and inclusive energy transition. 

Despite major gains in electrification and renewables, 2.1 billion people still rely on firewood, charcoal or dung to cook their meals. This is more than a technical challenge. It is a crisis of equity, health, gender justice, economic productivity and environmental sustainability. 

From the discussion, I emphasized three key action opportunities for scaling clean cooking access within sustainable energy systems: 

🔹 Integrate clean cooking into national electrification and energy access planning from the start. Clean cooking must be positioned as a core energy service – alongside lighting, refrigeration and productive uses – from the outset. This requires incorporating cooking energy demand into load forecasts, tariff design, appliance programmes, and rural mini-grid planning. When planning reflects the full needs of households, including cooking, the developmental impacts are significantly amplified. 

🔹 Scale blended finance and market-building instruments to unlock local market development. Despite offering an estimated $2.4 trillion in annual cost savings, clean cooking continues to receive < 1% of global energy investments. This imbalance reflects a broader failure to recognize clean cooking as a viable market. We must shift this narrative and mobilize coordinated public-private investment strategies. 

🔹 Leverage AI, geospatial tools, and smart technologies to enhance access, affordability, and targeting. The same technologies reshaping electricity access can revolutionize clean cooking. Digitalization offers a powerful opportunity to make clean cooking delivery more efficient, demand-responsive and inclusive. 

At UNDP’s Sustainable Energy Hub, we are supporting more than 80 projects across all regions, advancing clean cooking through technology, policy, and local enterprise development. The solutions exist. The time to act is now. 

To learn more about why clean cooking matters, what’s changing, and how we can scale solutions across the energy transition, I invite you to subscribe to the Sustainable Energy Hub’s bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eJGZ7XXq 

#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanCooking #SDG3 #SDG5 #SDG7 #SDG8 #SDG13

It was an important space to reaffirm what many of us in sustainable energy for development know well: clean cooking is not a side issue – it is a core pillar of a just and inclusive energy transition. 

Despite major gains in electrification and renewables, 2.1 billion people still rely on firewood, charcoal or dung to cook their meals. This is more than a technical challenge. It is a crisis of equity, health, gender justice, economic productivity and environmental sustainability. 

From the discussion, I emphasized three key action opportunities for scaling clean cooking access within sustainable energy systems: 

🔹 Integrate clean cooking into national electrification and energy access planning from the start. Clean cooking must be positioned as a core energy service – alongside lighting, refrigeration and productive uses – from the outset. This requires incorporating cooking energy demand into load forecasts, tariff design, appliance programmes, and rural mini-grid planning. When planning reflects the full needs of households, including cooking, the developmental impacts are significantly amplified. 

🔹 Scale blended finance and market-building instruments to unlock local market development. Despite offering an estimated $2.4 trillion in annual cost savings, clean cooking continues to receive < 1% of global energy investments. This imbalance reflects a broader failure to recognize clean cooking as a viable market. We must shift this narrative and mobilize coordinated public-private investment strategies. 

🔹 Leverage AI, geospatial tools, and smart technologies to enhance access, affordability, and targeting. The same technologies reshaping electricity access can revolutionize clean cooking. Digitalization offers a powerful opportunity to make clean cooking delivery more efficient, demand-responsive and inclusive. 

At UNDP’s Sustainable Energy Hub, we are supporting more than 80 projects across all regions, advancing clean cooking through technology, policy, and local enterprise development. The solutions exist. The time to act is now.

Clean cooking needs $8 billion a year to reach universal access – but we’re mobilizing barely a third of that. This isn’t just a funding gap. It’s a development failure.  

As I said early today: “We’re paying trillions of dollars to avoid spending billions." 

At what point do we stop calling this an “investment gap” when the cost of doing nothing is a thousand times higher? 

The numbers speak for themselves: 

➡️ $2.4 trillion – the estimated annual cost of dirty cooking in terms of healthcare, environmental degradation, and lost productivity. 

➡️ $2.5 billion - the total annual investment currently going into clean cooking solutions. That’s not even a third of what’s needed to achieve universal access by 2030. 

This is not an “investment gap.” It’s a missed opportunity to align climate, health, gender equity, and economic development goals through a single intervention. To change the trajectory, we need to shift the financing paradigm. Here are three catalytic approaches leading the way: 

1️⃣ Blended finance: Combining grants, guarantees, and concessional capital to de-risk private investment, reduce end-user costs, and help early-stage enterprises scale. 

2️⃣ Digital pay-as-you-go systems: Leveraging mobile payments and smart tech to improve affordability, enable real-time monitoring, and unlock access to carbon and impact finance. 

3️⃣ Outcome-based financing: Linking investor returns directly to measurable social and health results, shifting focus from inputs to verified impact. 

At UNDP, we’re advancing these models through Financial Innovation Labs, turning clean cooking from a development afterthought into core climate and infrastructure investment opportunities. Let’s de-risk, digitize, and diversify. Clean cooking is not a side issue; it's a frontline solution for sustainable development.  

#EnergyforDevelopment #CleanCooking

In 2024, 92.5% of all new power generation capacity came from renewable energy - a historic shift. AI is rapidly transforming energy systems, including lowering energy costs by around 10% through smart grids, enhancing grid stability, storage, and energy optimization. 

However, at the same time this last year of AI electricity usage was roughly 80TWh, set to double over the next 2-3 years. which could have equivalently provided basic energy access including lighting and some home appliances for over 200 million people, based on Tier 3 access at a minimum of 365KWh per person annually. 

How do you believe the future of AI and energy will both contribute to and challenge the pathways for countries? I appreciate all ideas shared in the comments, I really enjoy to hear your views.

It was a pleasure to join the webinar on clean cooking and to underscore a critical point: clean cooking is still too often viewed as a household issue, when in fact it reflects an entire value chain and a national development ecosystem. The scale of the challenge demands that we move beyond silos, bringing together data, finance, innovation, and policy to drive real impact, especially for women and marginalized communities.

At UNDP  we’re seeing the transformative power of this integrated approach from Tanzania, where geospatial data is aligning stove distribution with forest degradation trends and user feedback, to Kenya and Uganda, where dedicated eCooking tariffs are making electric cooking more affordable and accelerating the shift away from charcoal.

Together, we can scale these examples into systemic solutions, transforming what is possible and changing daily life for the 2 billion people who still lack access to clean cooking.

This conversation is just the beginning. I look forward to continuing our collaboration to place clean cooking at the heart of the global development and energy transition agenda. Thank you.

Clean cooking must be positioned as a core energy service – alongside lighting, refrigeration and productive uses – from the outset. This requires incorporating cooking energy demand into load forecasts, tariff design, appliance programmes, and rural mini-grid planning. When planning reflects the full needs of households, including cooking, the developmental impacts are significantly amplified.

Despite offering an estimated $2.4 trillion in annual cost savings, clean cooking continues to receive < 1% of global energy investments. This imbalance reflects a broader failure to recognize clean cooking as a viable market. We must shift this narrative and mobilize coordinated public-private investment strategies.

No one should have to risk their health to cook a meal. Everyday, over 2.1 billion people strain over open fires and inhale smoke just to feed their families. The energy conversation isn’t complete without clean cooking.
 
This is not just about energy, it is a development priority. It’s about health, gender equality, economic opportunity, and climate action.
 
In sub-Saharan Africa alone, nearly 1 billion people lack access to clean cooking - and 20 million more fall behind every year. In Ethiopia, studies show that a 40% subsidy is often needed just to make biogas affordable. Yet infrastructure barriers like limited grid access and LPG distribution make electric and gas stoves unfeasible for many rural and displaced communities. To scale these technologies meaningfully, it is estimated that we need need at least +$4.5 billion annually - compared to the $700 million currently received.
 
But there’s a way forward. Imagine embedding clean cooking into data-driven electrification planning, so that every new grid, mini-grid or appliance rollout simultaneously advances clean cooking:
 
➡️ In Eswatini, minigrids are supporting productive uses and energy-efficient appliances to boost project revenues.
 
➡️ In Zambia, policy roadmaps link electric cooking with productive uses like irrigation and refrigeration.
 
➡️ In Ghana, Haiti, Kenya, Nepal, and Tanzania, pilots show that integrating electric cooking early in minigrid planning improves business viability.
 
Together, we can move clean cooking from the sidelines to the center of global energy and development strategies. 
 
To find out more about this important interconnection, I invite you to read this UNDP policy brief that explores the pathway to universal clean cooking through integrated, data-powered energy transitions 👉 https://lnkd.in/enecbh7p 
 
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanCooking #DigitalTransformation #SDG7

Renewable energy is not just a climate imperative - it’s a precondition for digital economies and inclusive growth. 

By 2030, AI is projected to create nearly +170 million new jobs. However, with so many of these new roles yet to be formed, the question remains: how can we connect millions of job-seeking youth to this expanding sector? 

For countries with large youth populations, this isn’t a disruption; it’s an opportunity to build more equitable, future-ready economies. It all starts with energy. AI models and digital tools depend on reliable electricity, yet only 48% of people in Sub-Saharan Africa have access. With 70% of the region under 30yrs, the path forward is clear: renewable energy is the foundation for digital inclusion and youth-led innovation. The solutions are already here: 

➡️ Distributed solar power is enabling rural innovation hubs in Papua New Guinea, where youth and women are launching businesses and learning technical skills. 

➡️ In Indonesia, the Youth Co:Lab initiative supports youth-led enterprises delivering solar cold storage and clean cooking to last-mile communities. 

➡️In Uruguay, a public-private AI training program is scaling in public schools - preparing students for careers in energy, agriculture and logistics. 

➡️In the Dominican Republic, a national AI strategy is helping youth gain digital skills and launch small enterprises. 

Local innovation ecosystems must bridge the gap between energy, data, and jobs. Countries that invest in distributed renewable energy, open-source data platforms and localized AI training programs are better positioned to build domestic markets for AI-enabled services. 

This is not just a development challenge; it’s a strategic opportunity. With the right investment in energy, skills, and ecosystems, we can drive the AI and clean energy transitions from the ground up. To find out how, I invite you to explore the latest edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e28kqP-R 

#EnergyForDevelopment #EnergyRevolution #AIRevolution #JobsOfTheFuture #DigitalInclusion

Can #AI Learn from Nature—and Help Us Design a More Resilient Planet?

In 2024, AI consumed over 80 terawatt-hours of electricity—roughly equal to Belgium’s annual consumption. Within just three years, that could soar to 1,000 TWh—enough to power 125 million people, or the entire nation of Japan.

Meanwhile, 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty. That same energy could have powered basic needs—light, refrigeration, connectivity—for every one of them.

So, what kind of intelligence are we investing in?

Nature is not just a resource. It’s the original intelligence. With 3.8 billion years of R&D, nature has evolved systems that are efficient, adaptive, and regenerative.

That’s the promise of planetary design—a new development logic based on integration, not just innovation. As renewable energy systems expand, they are becoming more decentralized, complex, and interdependent—more like ecosystems. AI can serve as the operational brain: forecasting demand, managing complexity, and balancing flows.

At the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  Spring Festival, we reflected on a crucial question:
Will AI learn from nature—or help us forget it faster?

AI should help us see both the forest and the trees—managing trade-offs across water, energy, food, land, and health systems. Here’s how we can shape that future:

⸻

1️⃣ Build local value chains:
Indonesia, home to 21% of the world’s nickel reserves, is transforming mineral wealth into domestic battery and digital manufacturing capacity. UNDP  supports integrated strategies that align clean energy, digital infrastructure, and national development goals.

2️⃣ Invest in smart, distributed energy systems:
In India, AI-powered load forecasting and smart meters are cutting technical losses and outages. In states like Uttar Pradesh and Assam, digital energy management has reduced losses by up to 20% and improved billing for millions.

3️⃣ Develop sovereign, inclusive data ecosystems:
With 2.6 billion people still offline, entire communities remain invisible to AI systems shaping public services. Efforts like Africa’s Masakhane network—building AI in 40+ African languages—are paving the way toward more inclusive digital futures.

4️⃣ Govern AI like we govern ecosystems:
From optimizing illegal logging to deciding who gets access to food or healthcare, AI already impacts lives and global commons. Ethical, inclusive, and transparent AI governance isn’t optional—it’s essential.

⸻

AI should not only optimize—but integrate.
Not just mimic nature—but learn from its logic.

Because intelligence isn’t measured by how much we automate—but by how well we adapt, include, and sustain.

From artificial to planetary intelligence—the future is ours to shape.

#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalDevelopment #JustTransition #DataSovereignty #PlanetaryDesign #AIForGood #NatureBasedSolutions

Women and the $8.75B AI-in-Energy Opportunity: The Time to Act is Now

The global AI-in-energy market is already worth $8.75 billion and is projected to grow by over 30% annually—reaching an estimated $1.3 trillion by 2030. This transformation holds immense potential—not just for accelerating decarbonization, but for unlocking new pathways for women’s leadership, innovation, and economic participation.

And we’re already seeing results.

From Cameroon’s Green Girls Organization, which uses AI to bring off-grid solar and biogas solutions to rural communities, to the UAE’s AI-powered ZERO platform, which helps organizations track emissions and decarbonize, women are already leading the way with real-world examples of how inclusive AI can power inclusive energy transitions.

Yet today, women still represent only one-third of AI professionals and just 20% of the energy workforce—despite comprising 40% of the global labor force. In fast-growing fields like AI, demand surged eightfold in 2024, but only 28% of learners were women. And while 48% of STEM graduates in the Arab region are women, only 20% participate in the labor market. These gaps represent not a constraint—but a vast, untapped opportunity.

There is a clear path forward: 

1️⃣ Inclusive Education & Digital Access: Expanding AI- and energy-focused education—particularly for young women—is vital to building a diverse, future-ready workforce. With the AI-energy market projected to grow rapidly, targeted skilling programmes can address the gender gap in AI pathways and unlock underutilized talent. 

2️⃣ Inclusive Policy & Gender-Disaggregated Data: Gathering gender-specific data and using it to inform policymaking is essential to ensure women aren’t left behind in the AI-energy transition. Data-driven approaches can expose structural disparities, improve pay equity, and inform inclusive skilling and employment strategies—ensuring the transition mobilizes the full spectrum of available talent and leaves no one behind. 

3️⃣ Support for Women-Led Innovation: Fostering women’s participation in AI-energy entrepreneurship is not just about equity—it’s a strategy for accelerating the clean energy transition. As the AI-in-energy market moves toward a $1.3 trillion valuation by 2030, prioritizing investment and support for women-led innovation can drive clean energy adoption while aligning growth with gender equity and sustainable development goals. 

This is more than a moment—it’s a movement. It’s an opportunity to build inclusive AI-energy ecosystems from the ground up, ensuring that policymaking is no longer blind to the full scope of exclusion. The talent is out there; now we need the policies, investments, and support to make this vision a reality.

Africa stands at a pivotal juncture, where the energy transition and digital transformation are not just parallel trends; they are converging revolutions to unlock a new development paradigm.
 
Across Africa, more than 2,000 languages are spoken, with 75 of them having over a million speakers. Yet the AI systems already shaping markets, education, and public services are trained to recognize only a few. This is not just a technical gap; it’s a political one. When technology doesn’t speak your language, it can’t serve your future. That’s why localizing innovation - from data to design - is foundational.
 
Today, at the 2025 Oxford Africa Conference, I had the privilege to reflect on how AI and data technologies can become powerful enablers for a just and inclusive energy transition in Africa. The continent holds over 60% of global solar potential, 30% of the world’s critical mineral reserves, and a youth demographic poised to drive innovation and growth. Yet unlocking this potential requires more than ambition; it demands intentional design, inclusive architecture, and integrated systems:
 
1️⃣ Design for inclusion from the start: Across Africa, MSMEs make up 90% of businesses and 80% of employment. Yet they remain underserved by digital and energy infrastructure. AI systems must be built on local data, adapted to diverse operating contexts and geared toward inclusive growth. Digital tools, when intentionally designed, can extend services and financing to the last mile—turning technology into an equalizer, not a divider.
 
2️⃣ Co-develop digital and energy infrastructure: Energy and AI are not parallel tracks; they are co-dependent systems. We must invest in digital infrastructure powered by renewables and in energy systems optimized by AI. Africa currently accounts for just 1% of global data center capacity, but needs over 700 new centers by 2030. These should be clean-powered, locally managed, and embedded in national development strategies.
 
3️⃣ Move up the value chain in clean technologies: Despite holding 30% of the world’s critical minerals, the continent continues to export raw materials and re-import finished technologies at many times the cost. The future lies in integrated value chains: from mining and processing to battery manufacturing and renewable-powered digital infrastructure. The DRC–Zambia battery corridor offers a model for regionally coordinated value creation.
 
We have the innovation. We have the tools. Now we need to scale them and embed them into the heart of development strategies. The convergence of AI and clean energy isn’t just an opportunity; it’s a catalyst to redefine development outcomes across Africa.
 
The question is no longer whether Africa can lead, but how we ensure that leadership is equitable, sustainable, and strategically designed. 

 
#EnergyForDevelopment  #Digital  #OxfordAfrica2025 Oxford Africa Conference

caption:
In 2024, a power outage in the Maldives caused a 50-hour disruption of water. Not because of water scarcity, but because the electric pumps failed. Meanwhile, Roman aqueducts built +2,000 years ago were still functioning with no grid; no software; and no emissions.
 
So, we ought to ask ourselves: are today’s systems more advanced - or just more fragile?
 
Last week, at the TIDE Senior Advisors Retreat, I had the privilege to reflect on what really counts as innovation - and what happens when we optimize systems that leave people behind? Because the real question isn’t whether to innovate or optimize. It’s whether we are building energy systems that are resilient, inclusive, and future-ready. Here’s what we explored:
 
1️⃣ Innovation and optimization are interdependent. Solar PV costs fell 90% between 2008 and 2022. But innovation alone doesn’t decarbonize cities. Optimization, through smart meters, AI forecasting, and grid balancing, is what enables real-time impact.
 
2️⃣ Technology must deliver equity, not just efficiency. The top 10% of global energy users consume 20x more than the bottom 10%. Yet solutions are emerging: AI-powered tariffs from M-KOPA in Kenya, energy-efficient appliances in South Africa, mobile-enabled solar in Bangladesh.
 
3️⃣ Innovation must be guided by governance. AI can predict renewable variability with 90% accuracy. But without inclusive policy and regulation, it can also deprioritize vulnerable communities.
 
Optimization and innovation must go hand in hand with development. This is not just about technology. It is about justice and systems that serve everyone.
 So, the real question is: What are we optimizing for? Megawatts, or human wellbeing?
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalDevelopment #justtransition

caption:
Green hydrogen is booming. But is it truly driving a green revolution—or are we creating a global climate illusion?

Over 50 countries now have national hydrogen strategies, and by 2050, the global hydrogen trade could be worth $280 billion. Yet progress is uneven: 83% of current investments are concentrated in Europe and China, and fewer than 7% of announced projects have reached operation.

As momentum builds, it is crucial that local governments—especially in the Global South—have the tools, evidence, and agency to shape hydrogen pathways that reflect their development priorities. That’s why, together with Amir Lebdioui  and Pavel Bilek  I recently joined a conversation with Martin Lambert  Head of Hydrogen Research at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, to explore the findings of a new collaborative approach between UNDP  and TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  on green hydrogen.

As part of this work, we are developing practical guidelines to support local governments in navigating the development impacts of their hydrogen strategies—ensuring that national ambition translates into inclusive, context-specific outcomes on the ground. Hydrogen can be a powerful driver of inclusive and sustainable development if shaped deliberately and guided by the right evidence. Here’s how:

1️⃣ A Catalyst for Inclusive Growth
Green hydrogen can unlock significant economic opportunities. In South Africa, projections suggest a 3.6% increase in GDP and 370,000 new jobs by 2050. But realizing these benefits depends on building local value chains, investing in skills development, and designing policies that prioritize domestic gains—not just global supply.

2️⃣ A Climate Solution with Resource Realities
Hydrogen is key to decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. Yet it is resource-intensive: producing 1 kg of green hydrogen requires about 9 liters of purified water. Supporting countries to align hydrogen investments with local resource constraints—especially in water-stressed regions—is critical to long-term sustainability.

3️⃣ A Risk of Widening Inequality
Today, 83% of global electrolysis investments are concentrated in Europe and China. Without deliberate action, the hydrogen economy risks reinforcing global divides. But there’s also an opportunity: with the right strategies, countries can leapfrog legacy systems. In some contexts, direct electrification or alternative industrial pathways may be more viable.

The energy transition isn’t just about technology—it’s about people, priorities, and power. By asking the right questions and equipping local actors with the right tools, we can shape a hydrogen future that is just, inclusive, and grounded in real-world development goals.

#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustTransition #ClimateAction #FutureOfEnergy

In 2024, 92.5% of new power generation came from renewables. At the same time, AI is reshaping how we design, manage, and use energy, from smart grids to predictive maintenance. But these are not isolated shifts - they are twin engines of a new development era.

The renewable energy sector already supports 16.2 million jobs. By 2050, it could generate another 40 million. AI is also creating new roles - but it’s also consuming vast resources. In 2024, AI used more electricity than 150 countries individually, with projections set to double within a few years. That same energy could have powered basic access for ~1 billion people.

However the risks are not just environmental. Automation threatens jobs. Unequal access to energy, data, and digital skills threatens inclusion. 61% of people believe AI will support their work, yet many in low and medium HDI countries still lack the tools to participate in this future.

How do we build a just transition, not just a fast one?

1️⃣ Shift from extraction to local value creation: Build domestic supply chains for minerals, manufacturing, and services.

2️⃣ Close the digital divide: Expand digital and energy infrastructure so that everyone can access the future of work.

3️⃣ Align finance with inclusive transitions: Invest in national institutions, technical skills, and utility reform to empower countries to lead their own energy-AI pathways.

As we look to the G20, COP30, and the UN Financing for Development Summit, the imperative is clear: the energy transition must be smart, fast and fair. To find out more, I invite you to read this previous edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eY_FBqgp

The electric vehicle (EV) revolution is well underway, signaling a transformative shift in global transportation and energy systems. Just last year, EVs accounted for over 20% of all car sales globally, and nearly 1 in 2 new cars sold in China was electric.
 
However, as we move towards 2030, the growing demand for EVs also signals an imminent surge in battery demand, set to grow by 6–10X, posing a potential twin-challenge & opportunity for critical mineral use and extraction. Yet in this context, Solid-State Batteries (SSB) emerge as an enabling technology, offering up to five times the energy density of conventional lithium-ion batteries. Solid-state batteries offer significant advantages that align with global sustainable development priorities:
 
1️⃣Enhanced Performance and Safety:
SSBs provide higher energy density; faster charging times; and improved thermal stability, reducing risks associated with lithium-ion batteries. Their robustness across temperature ranges and extended lifespans also make them ideal for grid-scale energy storage, facilitating greater integration of renewable energy sources and enhancing grid resilience.
 
2️⃣Cross-sectoral Innovation:
The compact size and enhanced performance of SSBs present opportunities beyond EV applications including: electric aviation, shipping and even consumer electronics, enabling longer operational life and increased safety.
 
3️⃣Environmental Sustainability:
By minimizing reliance on flammable liquid electrolytes and reducing the demand for scarce minerals, SSBs contribute to lowering the environmental footprint of battery production and disposal, supporting circular economy principles.
 
The global push for solid-state battery innovation reflects a broader truth: clean energy transitions are no longer national ambitions, they are shared imperatives. Strategic investments from India, research partnerships between Brazil & Singapore, and cross-sector collaboration signal a growing recognition that technology must serve inclusive, sustainable development.
 
Solid-state batteries hold the promise not just of better performance, but of decarbonizing mobility, strengthening energy resilience, and accelerating progress toward SDG7. To find out more about this technology in greater detail, I invite you to read this previous collaborative blog on Deep Tech Series: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eXViZjKg
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #SolidStateBatteries #ElectricVehicles #CleanTech #SDG7

As urban heat intensifies, so does the demand for cooling - and with it, the urgency for inclusive, digital-first energy solutions.
 
Electricity generation from fossil fuels rose 1.4% from 2023 to 2024, driven largely by increased cooling demand in cities. Since the 1980s, the number of extreme heat days in urban centers has tripled - fueled by the twin problems of urban heat island effect & climate change.
 
By 2050, global installed cooling capacity is projected to nearly triple; from 22 TW in 2022 to 58 TW. But it’s not just about cooling homes and buildings. Data centers, the backbone of the AI revolution, consume over 40%+ of their energy for cooling alone, even more in warmer regions, to operate optimally.
 
This  isn’t just an energy and climate issue; it’s an opportunity to reshape how we govern and deliver smarter, more equitable, energy transitions:
 
🔹 AI for smarter governance:
Transparent, data-driven, tools make energy systems more transparent and accountable. They help optimize resources and support evidence-based infrastructure planning.
 
🔹 Equity through digital tools:
Kenya’s integration of digital tools like the Energy Access Explorer helped boost electricity access rates from 20% to 75% in under a decade; illustrating that data-led approaches can drive inclusive energy access.
 
🔹 A just digital transition:
Without inclusive policy frameworks, digital innovation risks deepening social inequalities. Equitable robust digital infrastructures and fair data governance are essential for climate justice
 
As global temperatures continue to break records, our policies, technologies, and infrastructure must keep pace of digital change. We need to ensure that cooling, connectivity and clean energy can reach everyone everywhere.

Decentralized Renewable Energy is more than a technology. It's a pathway to equity, resilience and economic transformation.

As we confront the urgency of climate action and global inequality, Decentralized Renewable Energy (DRE) emerges as one of the most transformative tools for sustainable development. At the intersection of technology, equity, and climate resilience, DRE offers an opportunity to radically rethink how energy is produced, distributed, and owned - especially in the Global South

Today, 685 million people still live without electricity and over 1.18 billion endure energy poverty; struggling to power irrigation for food security, digital tools for learning and/or essential equipment in health facilities. But as we accelerate toward universal energy access, how we achieve this goal is just as important as how fast we achieve it. 

The Global South has the opportunity to leapfrog fossil fuels and centralized grid models to design systems that prioritize justice, resilience, and local empowerment:

🔹 Empowering communities as energy "prosumers":
DRE allows households and communities to generate, use, and even sell electricity; breaking away from dependency on centralized grids and enabling more equitable energy participation. This shift not only democratizes energy production but also reduces energy access disparities.

🔹 Creating green jobs and building local capacity: 
From installation to maintenance, DRE systems generate employment and skills training for local populations. This strengthens community resilience while catalyzing long-term economic development.

🔹 Enhancing energy security and climate resilience: 
DRE systems can de-risk infrastructure vulnerabilities associated to centralized grid failures & imported fossil fuels; which is especially important in areas prone to conflict, natural disasters and/or slow infrastructure rollouts.

Decentralized energy is not just an infrastructure solution; it’s a catalyst for climate justice, gender equity, and economic inclusion. We need to prioritize enabling environments, financing mechanisms and policies that place communities at the center of the energy revolution. Find out how DRE can power and unlock more democratic and equitable energy futures: 👉 https://lnkd.in/edwEd7YE

🌊 As we mark #WorldOceansDay and the launch of the 2025 UN Ocean Conference in Nice, we have a pivotal opportunity: to align ocean health with the global energy transition.

The ocean is a foundation of life on Earth. It covers 75% of the planet; generates 50% of our oxygen; absorbs 30% of CO2 emissions; and supports +150 million jobs worldwide. It provides food, energy and critical resources to billions - yet remains under threat from rising temperatures, acidification, pollution, overexploitation and biodiversity loss.

If the ocean economy were a country, it would be the fifth largest economy in the world. That level of economic and environmental significance calls for bold, integrated responses. Here’s where development action can accelerate meaningful impact:

1️⃣ Decarbonize Maritime Transport as a Catalyst for Clean Energy Systems:
Maritime transport emits over 1GtCO2 annually (around 2.9% of global emissions) and is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize due to fossil fuel reliance and long asset lifecycles. To align with the Paris Agreement, zero-emission fuels need to make up 5% of international and 15% of domestic shipping by 2030. Transitioning to clean fuels can transform shipping from a major emitter into a catalyst for clean energy investment, innovation, and industrial demand, contributing directly to system-wide decarbonization and reducing global GHG emissions by 3-5% by 2030. 

2️⃣ Transform Ports into Clean Energy Hubs for a Just Transition:
Strategic clean fuel corridors can anchor renewable deployment, storage and grid upgrades at ports - especially in Small Island Developing States, where ocean-based exports account for 16% of GDP. Port electrification enhances climate resilience, connects maritime and energy planning, and ensures vulnerable economies benefit from the energy transition.

3️⃣ Integrate Maritime Decarbonization into Global Energy Finance:
Despite their potential, maritime and ocean-based clean energy solutions remain underfunded. In 2022, global clean energy investments reached  $2.1 trillion; yet < 1% was directed towards maritime energy developments. Offshore wind alone could grow from $39.6B in 2024 to $146B by 2031, powering up to 1.5B homes annually by 2050 and driving inclusive growth across coastal regions - especially in the Global South. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can unlock scalable pathways for maritime decarbonization and clean energy innovation at sea.

Decarbonization is critical, not only for SDG 13  and SDG 14, but for resilient, inclusive development. 

As we look toward this 2025 UN Ocean Conference, we must raise ambition; align public and private finance; and unlock innovation across the blue economy. A healthy ocean is not only vital for biodiversity. It is fundamental to a just energy transition

The ocean cannot wait - and neither can we.

 #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #MaritimeDecarbonization #SDG14

Offshore wind energy is more than a climate solution; it’s a strategic lever for national development, maritime decarbonization and long-term energy security. By 2030, global offshore wind capacity is projected to reach 212 GW, nearly quadrupling the 73 GW recorded in 2023. Annual additions are anticipated to grow from 9.5 GW in 2023 to over 45 GW by 2030, with China driving half the growth and Europe, the U.S., Japan and Korea emerging as key markets.

Yet, despite this momentum, offshore wind faces high capital costs; long lead times; and permitting barriers - especially in the Global South. These challenges have slowed momentum and shifted investor interest toward faster-moving solar PV projects.
 
Globally, if current commitments are realized, offshore wind could power +1.5 billion homes annually by 2050. But to make this a truly global solution - especially for emerging and climate-vulnerable economies - urgent action is needed across three key areas:

1️⃣ Integrate Offshore Wind into National Energy and Development Plans: Embedding offshore wind in long-term national energy strategies helps align permitting, grid infrastructure, and port development - making projects more investable. In 2023 alone, $33.75 billion was invested in offshore wind globally. With supportive policies, countries can attract a greater share of this capital while linking wind energy to jobs, exports, and green industrialization.


2️⃣ Scale Floating Wind to Unlock Untapped Resources: Traditional offshore wind turbines are fixed to the seabed in shallow waters, excluding many countries with deep coastal zones. Floating wind technology could allow for turbines to be installed further from shore, opening access to major wind resources in regions like Southeast Asia, West Africa and SIDS. As floating technology becomes more affordable, early investment and pilot projects can help bring these regions into the global offshore wind market. 


3️⃣ Use Public-Private Finance to De-risk and Attract Investment: At around $3,461/kW, offshore wind remains nearly three times as expensive as onshore alternatives. Such high upfront costs make it harder for new markets to compete. Targeted funding through green bonds, blended finance, and multilateral support can improve project economics and unlock long-term returns. With the right financial tools, offshore wind can scale  in regions where clean energy access is most needed.

Offshore wind isn’t just about clean electricity: it’s about building resilient economies, powering green industries, and creating a just transition.

The Global South holds vast offshore wind potential. With the right policies and partnerships, we can turn this into a catalyst for clean industrialization, energy security, and inclusive growth.

#EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #SaveOurOcean #OffshoreWind #MaritimeEnergy

What if the ocean isn’t just a climate risk, but a climate solution - and Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are already leading the way? SIDS may contribute <1% of global emissions, but their vast marine territories, abundant renewable resources and closely connected communities uniquely position them to pioneer solutions that are not only green, but also blue - integrating clean energy with ocean-based economies. From solar-chilled cold storage for fisheries in the Maldives to digital platforms in the Caribbean SIDS that use satellite data to guide sustainable marine planning, SIDS are showing that size is no barrier to impact.
 
@UNDP’s “Blue Economy for Green Islands” approach connects renewable energy with ocean-based industries to drive low-carbon, inclusive growth. By leveraging wind, solar, tidal, and ocean thermal energy, SIDS can diversify economies and decarbonize maritime sectors. Within this integrated framework, three transformative solutions stand out:
 
 
1️⃣ Whole-Island Renewable Ecosystems: Linking clean energy with ocean sectors like aquaculture, desalination, eco-tourism, and transport can cut emissions and boost livelihoods. Ocean industries already generate 16% of SIDS’ GDP. In Vanuatu and Cabo Verde, solar-powered fisheries and irrigation systems are strengthening food security, reduce emissions and expand local jobs. These systems also benefit women, who make up 52% of SIDS’ agricultural workforce, advancing gender equity and delivering gender-responsive benefits
 
 
2️⃣ Microgrids for Disaster Resilience: Decentralized systems like hybrid mini-grids are vital in SIDS, where disasters cause $1.6B in yearly losses. Vanuatu’s solar-hydro mini-grid powers schools, clinics, and markets for 50,000+ people. Such systems help close the SDG 7 access gap, which still affects 9% of SIDS’ populations, especially in rural areas.
 
 
3️⃣ Invest in #Ocean-Based Renewables: Offshore wind, tidal, and ocean thermal energy make up <2% of installed capacity in SIDS, despite vast potential. Scaling them can power ports, ferries, and aquaculture - creating low-carbon energy loops. Innovative finance tools like blue bonds, debt-for-energy swaps, and blended finance can de-risk investments and scale projects
 
The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS calls for placing sustainable energy at the heart of development, with many SIDS already leading the way towards 100% renewable energy in their power mix by 2030.
 
Find out how else SIDS are leading a new development path, where energy transitions are not just green, but inherently blue: 👉 go.undp.org/34Q  

#EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #SIDS #JustTransition #BlueEconomy

In 2024, the world added over 585 GW of renewables, and clean energy jobs surpassed 16 million. Solar is now the least expensive electricity source in history and global energy investments are expected to reach $3.3 trillion by 2025. This is more than a technology shift; it's a global economic transformation.
 
But one critical question remains: Are we making the energy transition work for everyone, everywhere?
 
In Mongolia, coal still dominates the energy system. In Ulaanbaatar, 1.6M people rely on raw coal for heat - driving pollution 27x over WHO limits, causing 7,000+ premature deaths and costing 10% of GDP.  Despite these challenges, Mongolia has committed to change - targeting 30% renewable energy by 2030.

1️⃣ Finance That Unlocks Scale:
By 2023, Mongolia attracted $533M across 12 utility-scale renewables. However renewables in Mongolia face high capital costs and limited de-risking. Green bonds, sovereign guarantees, and blended finance (like Paraguay’s $150M e-bus model from $20M in seed funding) can mobilize clean energy investment at scale.
 
2️⃣ Urban Energy That Protects Lives:
Coal-based systems drive both pollution and inequality. Ulaanbaatar’s air crisis is a public health emergency. A just transition must deliver clean heating, efficient housing, and e-mobility. UNDP pilots show solar + battery + insulation can cut emissions and protect over half the country’s population.
 
3️⃣ Digital Tools for Smart Equity:
Energy demand grew 4.7% per capita in one year. Mongolia’s vast geography needs digital planning. AI and geospatial tools - like smart meters in Chingeltei that track carbon savings -can guide clean energy to off-grid and low-income areas, just as UNDP is doing in Moldova.
 
4️⃣ Fossil Fuel Subsidy Reforms:
In Mongolia, fossil fuel subsidies reached $9B in 2023; a 120% increase since 2018. Yet by fully phasing them out, we could free up 3.6% of global GDP for reinvestment. With UNDP’s support, countries like Mongolia are designing reforms that reinvest from e-mobility to human capital and health systems.  
 
A just transition is about people, not just power. It’s about shaping a future where energy delivers jobs, health, resilience and dignity. Across Mongolia and Asia-Pacific, @UNDP is helping make that future a reality, ensuring no one is left behind.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #Mongolia #GreenFinance #DigitalForDevelopment

🌊⚡️What if the world’s smallest nations could lead the next big energy revolution?
 
At a marine testing site in Scotland, 20 Oyster wave energy converters have the potential to power 12,000 homes. Now imagine the transformative potential if Small Island Developing States (SIDS) - surrounded by ocean, rich in wave and tidal resources - could harness these innovations at scale?
 
Ocean-based energy technologies are fast becoming a practical solution to some of the world’s most pressing challenges: energy security, climate resilience and economic development. For SIDS, which face some of the highest energy costs globally, and are among the most vulnerable to climate change, these technologies offer a triple win; sustainable power, economic opportunity, and strengthened resilience.

With a combined global wave and tidal energy potential of over 55,000TWh/year, here’s how SIDS are already driving system-wide changes with how they manage & benefit from their blue economies:
 
🔹 Tonga is developing a 10-MW wave power park in Tongatapu - set to meet 50% of its energy needs and cut emissions by 20%.
 
🔹 Barbados is exploring Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), integrating it into a broader blue economy strategy supported by @UNDP and SIDS DOCK.
 
🔹 Seychelles is piloting the first floating solar PV project on lagoon waters, laying the groundwork for hybrid marine energy solutions through its marine spatial planning framework.
 
These are not isolated experiments. They are scalable, replicable and exemplify what’s possible when innovation meets local ambition and global support.
 
To see other success stores and find out how else SIDS are redefining development pathways, I  invite you to read this UNDP Policy Paper: 👉 go.undp.org/34Q  
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #UNOC3 #WaveEnergy #TidalEnergy  #SIDS #NetZeroIslands

The global shift to renewables is essential- but it must also be equitable. Cobalt and lithium are critical to clean technologies, yet their extraction often harms people and ecosystems. By 2050, the world will need 3x more cobalt and up to 40x lithium (compared to 2020 levels) driven by the needs of batteries, solar, wind, data centres and EVs .

In the DRC, which supplies over 70% of global cobalt, mining has polluted rivers, harmed crops and triggered human rights abuses -  including child labor. In Chile’s Atacama Desert, lithium operations have cut freshwater availability by 65%, threatening biodiversity and Indigenous livelihoods. 

This raises a critical question: how can we transition to a low-carbon future without deepening the nature and inequality crises? To ensure the clean energy transition is also a just transition, we must adopt integrated system-level solutions:

🔁 Closed-loop material systems can help reduce new extraction. Currently, only 1% of lithium and < 5% of cobalt is recycled from end-of-life batteries. Circular economy models - from battery reuse to advanced recycling - are essential to reduce demand for virgin mining.

🌍 Local value additions must be prioritized. Despite holding over half of global cobalt and manganese reserves,  Africa captures <5% of the global battery value chain. With battery demand set to triple by 2030, countries with an abundance of critical minerals should not be confined to raw extraction alone. By investing in local refining, battery production and and knowledge transfer, these countries can generate jobs, retain more economic value and reduce export dependency.

⚡ Smarter, greener grids are also important. Renewable energy sources are inherently variable. Next-generation energy efficient grids, such as AI-powered smart grids, can help balance supply and demand more effectively, reducing energy waste and integrating diverse power sources at scale.

The energy transition offers a once-in-a-generation opportunity to tackle climate change but only if it’s done in a way that is fair, inclusive and sustainable. To find out how mining can contribute to a just transition for both people and the planet, I invite you to read the Just Transition edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/ey8b-Dds
