Energy access is not just a technology challenge; it’s a matter of equity, regional cooperation, and economic opportunity.

Globally, 685 million people still lack access to electricity—80% of them in Sub-Saharan Africa. At the current pace, 660 million people could remain unelectrified by 2030, the vast majority in Africa. This is not merely a technical gap; it’s a development crisis that impacts health, education, livelihoods, and resilience.

But this is also a moment of unprecedented opportunity.

Africa holds extraordinary clean energy potential. Countries like Ethiopia and the DRC possess over 80 GW of hydropower potential, while the Sahel region enjoys some of the highest solar irradiance on Earth. Yet, between 2002 and 2020, Africa received less than 2% of the $2.8 trillion invested globally in renewable energy. Cross-border electricity trade remains limited, with just 10 GW of transmission capacity—compared to 127 GW in Europe.

This raises a critical question: how can we close the energy access gap without reinforcing inequality and fragmentation?
The answer lies in a just, integrated energy transition—where regional power trade becomes a catalyst for shared prosperity. And the solutions are within reach:

1️⃣ Invest in Cross-Border Infrastructure:
Regional power trading can reduce electricity supply costs by up to 30%, accelerating access in underserved areas. In the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), countries like Namibia and Botswana are already importing affordable hydropower from Zambia and Mozambique, enhancing both affordability and reliability.

2️⃣ Mobilize Inclusive Finance & Guarantees:
Bridging Africa’s $25 billion annual clean energy investment gap requires more than capital. Concessional finance, de-risking mechanisms, and technical assistance are critical to enabling LDCs to participate in regional markets and scale up electrification.

3️⃣ Leverage Regional Comparative Advantage:
Countries such as Ethiopia and the DRC generate more clean power than they consume, and the Sahel’s solar potential exceeds 2,200 kWh/m²/year. Regional trade allows these countries to monetize surplus energy, promote industrialization, and generate revenues that can support local development.

This is a defining moment. The energy access challenge is no longer just about generation—it’s about connection, cooperation, and coordination. With the right policies and targeted investments, Africa can shift from energy poverty to regional power prosperity, while advancing climate action and inclusive growth.

To learn how energy access and trade can transform economies and lives, I invite you to explore the latest insights here:  👉 https://lnkd.in/epaxVxyJ

public_card_text:
Energy access is not just a technology challenge; it’s a matter of equity, regional cooperation, and economic opportunity.

Globally, 685 million people still lack access to electricity—80% of them in Sub-Saharan Africa. At the current pace, 660 million people could remain unelectrified by 2030, the vast majority in Africa. This is not merely a technical gap; it’s a development crisis that impacts health, education, livelihoods, and resilience.

But this is also a moment of unprecedented opportunity.

Africa holds extraordinary clean energy potential. Countries like Ethiopia and the DRC possess over 80 GW of hydropower potential, while the Sahel region enjoys some of the highest solar irradiance on Earth. Yet, between 2002 and 2020, Africa received less than 2% of the $2.8 trillion invested globally in renewable energy. Cross-border electricity trade remains limited, with just 10 GW of transmission capacity—compared to 127 GW in Europe.

This raises a critical question: how can we close the energy access gap without reinforcing inequality and fragmentation?
The answer lies in a just, integrated energy transition—where regional power trade becomes a catalyst for shared prosperity. And the solutions are within reach:

1️⃣ Invest in Cross-Border Infrastructure:
Regional power trading can reduce electricity supply costs by up to 30%, accelerating access in underserved areas. In the Southern African Power Pool (SAPP), countries like Namibia and Botswana are already importing affordable hydropower from Zambia and Mozambique, enhancing both affordability and reliability.

2️⃣ Mobilize Inclusive Finance & Guarantees:
Bridging Africa’s $25 billion annual clean energy investment gap requires more than capital. Concessional finance, de-risking mechanisms, and technical assistance are critical to enabling LDCs to participate in regional markets and scale up electrification.

3️⃣ Leverage Regional Comparative Advantage:
Countries such as Ethiopia and the DRC generate more clean power than they consume, and the Sahel’s solar potential exceeds 2,200 kWh/m²/year. Regional trade allows these countries to monetize surplus energy, promote industrialization, and generate revenues that can support local development.

This is a defining moment. The energy access challenge is no longer just about generation—it’s about connection, cooperation, and coordination. With the right policies and targeted investments, Africa can shift from energy poverty to regional power prosperity, while advancing climate action and inclusive growth.

To learn how energy access and trade can transform economies and lives, I invite you to explore the latest insights here:  👉 https://lnkd.in/epaxVxyJ

caption:
Planning energy transitions without sufficient data is like trying to navigate in the dark.
 
Despite decades of progress, over 685 million people still lack access to electricity. Traditional data sources - household surveys, national censuses, static infrastructure maps - are too slow, too sparse, or too disconnected from on-the-ground realities to be able to accurately make investments and optimize projects.
 
To address this, UNDP  partnered with IBM  to co-develop two data-driven tools now featured in the International Energy Agency (IEA)  ’s new Energy & AI Observatory👉🏾 https://lnkd.in/e3yJs_Q4. 
These models represent a digital shift, as AI and open data enable a just energy transition through grounding data-driven actions in approaches that leave no one behind:
 
  1. Clean Energy Equity Index Developed with IBM and Stony Brook University, this tool generates an equity score at the subnational level across 53 African countries, combining data on education, income, emissions, and infrastructure. The index helps identify regions where clean energy investment will have the most equitable and transformative impact.
 
  2. Electricity Access Forecasting Model Built with IBM watsonx and trained on satellite imagery, infrastructure data, population growth, and land use dynamics, this model delivers hyper-granular (1 km²) forecasts to 2030 across 102 Global South countries. It enables governments to anticipate demand and prioritize underserved areas long before gaps become crises.
 
Both tools are now accessible through GeoHub, UNDP’s open data platform for geospatial intelligence. https://lnkd.in/erh3Qmny. Moving forward, the challenge will be how we can embed these tools into institutional decision-making, financing frameworks, and policy design.
 
#EnergyAccess #JustTransition #AIforDevelopment #GeospatialIntelligence #DigitalDevelopment #SDG7 #UNDP #IBM #IEA

🌿 Like Thailand’s Ratchaphruek tree, which blooms in synchrony under intense heat, Thailand’s energy transition is unfolding with resilience and purpose. Nature teaches us that thriving under pressure is possible — and Thailand is showing how to turn that lesson into inclusive, future-ready systems.

Grateful to join the Government of Thailand and national stakeholders in advancing a Just Energy Transition rooted in opportunity, equity, and long-term development. This is not just about megawatts — it’s about people, jobs, and systems that deliver for all.

🚀 Thailand is turning ambition into action across four key areas:

🔹 Aligning policies and scaling regional cooperation
To meet its 30% renewable electricity target by 2037, Thailand must deploy 32 GW of new capacity and mobilize $22B in investment. It is advancing integration across energy, climate, and industrial planning — while activating the ASEAN Power Grid and unlocking $1.3B via the ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility.

🔹 Deploying decentralized, people-first systems
With 20 GW rooftop solar potential and hydro-solar-battery pilots like Ubol Ratana, Thailand is cutting emissions and lowering rural electricity costs — currently up to 17% higher than in Bangkok — while boosting grid resilience.

🔹 Championing in cooling efficiency and digital growth
$2.7B in data center investments and surging cooling demand are driving clean innovation. From energy-efficient hospitals to green data hubs, Thailand is turning high energy use into climate-smart infrastructure.

🔹 Empowering SMEs and building green jobs
With 3.1M SMEs and over 230,000 EVs in 2024, Thailand is linking energy transition to entrepreneurship, regional value chains, and inclusive job creation. A just transition could generate over 172,000 renewable energy jobs by 2050, strengthening local economies.

At @UNDP, we are proud to support this journey — through policy, finance, and local capacity. Thailand is not just transitioning. It’s leading.

Let’s ensure Thailand’s energy future is not just greener, but fairer. Not just resilient, but just. ⚡🌏

Cleaner Air, Healthier Lives, Stronger Economies: Why We Need A Clean Energy Transition.
 
Every day, over 90% of the world’s population breathes unhealthy air, with air quality in many countries frequently exceeding dangerous thresholds (AQI >200); largely due to fossil fuel combustion. But the solutions are here, and the benefits are transformational.
 
Every breath of clean air is a right - not a privilege. Clean energy is a catalyst for climate action, human development and economic opportunity. Here’s how:
 
⚡️ Investing in renewables can bring substantial returns: Solar PV alone is now avoiding 1.4 Gt of CO₂ annually - proof that scaling renewables delivers fast impact. With continued investment in wind, e-mobility and heat pumps, we can slash both emissions and air pollution.
 
⚡️ Improved energy access means better health and cleaner skies: Achieving #SDG7 by 2030 could cut air pollution exposure by 75%, prevent 3.6 million premature deaths each year and unlock new jobs and opportunities; especially for the Global South.
 
⚡️ Resilient healthcare can be powered by clean energy: Clean power for hospitals will mean healthier people and fewer emissions. In regions like Sub-Saharan Africa, where 15% of health facilities lack electricity, clean energy can save lives and strengthen systems.
 
⚡️ Targeting methane and black carbon can improve air quality quickly: Cleaner cookstoves, smart methane regulation and support for transitions in fossil sectors can improve air quality quickly. In the continent of Africa alone, shifting to clean cooking fuels could save $66B/year and prevent 463,000 deaths annually - for just $8B a year.
 
⚡️ Digitalization and AI can be fueled by renewables: As data center electricity use is expected to double in the next year, powering them with renewables creates a new frontier: climate-smart digital infrastructure. A clean energy transition keeps us future-ready,  both economically and technologically.
 
At UNDP  we are proud to work alongside governments and communities to turn energy transitions into inclusive, clean-air development stories; from methane action in Turkmenistan to healthcare electrification in Africa.
 
The solutions are proven. The technologies are ready. The benefits  for health, jobs & the planet are substantial. Let’s build a world where clean energy means clean air for everyone, everywhere.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanEnergy #AirQuality #HealthAndEnergy

The latest Tracking SDG7 Progress Report reminds us that the global energy transition is not only a climate imperative but a development necessity.
 
Despite some progress, the world currently remains off track to meet #SDG7. As of 2023, 666 million people still lack access to electricity, and 2.1 billion rely on polluting fuels for cooking. These numbers are not just statistics: they represent lost opportunities for health, education, productivity and dignity. They provide us with both a reality check and a roadmap forward - which is where our focus must be:
 
🔋 Decentralized renewable energy (DRE) is already delivering results:
Between 2020 and 2022, DRE solutions accounted for +50% of new electricity connections in Sub-Saharan Africa. These technologies are affordable, resilient and ready to scale. With the right policy frameworks and investment flows, they can close the access gap in rural and underserved communities fast.
 
💰 Clean energy finance is growing - but it must be better targeted:
Global public finance for clean energy reached $21.6 billion in 2023, even amid economic and geopolitical instability. While incredibly promising, <10% reached EMDEs (excluding China). We need more concessional capital, blended finance models and de-risking tools to drive equitable investment where it’s needed most.
 
🍳 Clean cooking is rising on the agenda - and rightly so:
With only 7% of rural populations in Sub-Saharan Africa accessing clean fuels, now is the time to prioritize solutions that reduce health risks, empower women and support climate goals. Targeted investments in innovation and affordability can shift millions toward safer cooking practices.
 
At @UNDP, we see energy as a catalyst. Our integrated approach to sustainable energy is about more than about powering homes; it’s about unlocking futures. It’s about delivering health systems, schools, jobs, clean air, gender equality and climate resilience.
 
When we invest in energy for development, we multiply impact across the SDGs. What’s missing isn’t technology or resources: it’s urgency  and the willingness to act.  If we rise to the challenge and prioritize a just and inclusive energy transition, we can shape a future for people and planet where no one is left behind.

With over 230,000 EVs on the road, $1 billion in green bonds issued and world-leading solar manufacturing, Thailand is proving that clean energy transitions can be locally driven, nationally scaled & globally significant. And it's not stopping there.

This week, I had the privilege of presenting the just energy transition opportunities for Thailand at a multistakeholder dialogue co-hosted by the Government of Thailand and @UNDP. I unpacked how the country is already at the forefront of energy innovations, and what can be done to turn emerging challenges into bold opportunities:

1️⃣ Infrastructure That Works for People and Planet With 20 GW of untapped rooftop solar and a growing exposure to climate risks, Thailand can redesign its energy infrastructure toward decentralized, adaptive systems that boost both energy security and resilience.

2️⃣ Finance That Reaches the Last Mile Thailand issued $1B in green bonds in 2023. But $22B is still needed for renewables by 2037. Financial Innovation Labs (like UNDP’s Financial Innovation Labs) and national transition funds could unlock scaled, equitable investment - just as seen in Cuba and Brazil.

3️⃣ Data and Digital That Drive Equity Peer-to-peer solar trading in Bangkok already shows what's possible. With tools like the Clean Energy Equity Index, Thailand can harness AI and geospatial data to bring clean energy and channel investments to the communities that need it most.

4️⃣ Regional Leadership That Lifts All Boats Through ASEAN power trade, BRICS+ partnerships and the Indo-Pacific Clean Economy Agreement, Thailand is helping shape a new model of South-South cooperation. With Just Transition Innovation Zones, it’s ready to lead from the front.

As I said earlier this week: “Thailand is a leader for inclusive and sustainable growth. Not only in ASEAN, but globally.” The country’s energy ambitions are matched by its innovation and commitment to leave no one behind.

At @UNDP we’re proud to support Thailand in building an energy future that works for everyone. Because when Thailand advances a just energy transition, it doesn’t just transform its own future; it lights the way for the region and the world.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #Thailand #InclusiveGrowth

caption:
Is the clean energy revolution driving the Global South into a debt crisis?

With the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development Forum underway in Seville, we face a defining global challenge: an annual $4 trillion financing gap threatens progress on the SDGs and a just energy transition.

But this is also a turning point. While clean technologies are more affordable than ever (with 81% of new renewable energy additions more cost-competitive than fossil fuels) less than 15% of clean energy investment reached the Global South in 2023. At the same time, public debt is rising rapidly, threatening to derail both climate and development ambitions. This isn’t just a funding gap; it’s a systemic failure. Yet these signs point to a system on the brink of transformation.

The clean energy revolution is no longer optional; it’s essential. To ensure a fair and inclusive transition, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Reform fossil fuel subsidies: Globally, these reached $1.3 trillion in 2023. Redirecting even a portion of this toward clean energy, health and education could unlock massive development gains - especially where subsidies are untargeted and disproportionately benefit the wealthy.

2️⃣ Redesign public finance frameworks: Mobilizing private capital through blended finance, national development banks, and climate bonds can scale up investments while protecting fiscal space. These tools are key to de-risking investments and scaling renewables in places where markets alone won’t go.

3️⃣ Rebuild global cooperation: This goes beyond aid. We need debt-for-climate swaps, donor-backed guarantees and equitable financing frameworks tailored to the needs of the Global South. Efforts like Egypt’s €54M debt swap with Germany already show what’s possible.

At this FfD Forum, we face a choice: continue financing delay, or fund a just, resilient and sustainable future. The energy transition can either deepen inequality or drive inclusive development. The difference lies in how we choose to finance it.

What if the clean energy transition wasn’t just about cutting emissions - but about redesigning global finance to serve both climate and development?

As the world accelerates efforts to decarbonize, one critical challenge remains under-addressed: the growing tension between debt and decarbonization. Today, many countries in the Global South face a stark paradox - they can’t afford the transition, yet can’t afford to delay it.

With a global financing gap  +$4 trillion annually, the stakes are immense. Today, <15% of clean energy investment reaches the Global South. In Africa alone, the annual need for sustainable energy investment exceeds $200 billion, yet the continent receives just 2% of global clean energy flows.

But what if debt itself could be reimagined; not as a constraint, but as a catalyst for transformation? Here’s what a more equitable financing future could look like:

💡 Reform fossil fuel subsidies - worth $1 trillion in 2023, to free up vital public resources for clean energy, health, and education.

💡 Design smarter public financing frameworks - using tools like blended finance, green bonds, and sovereign wealth funds to mobilize private capital and reduce risk.

💡 Promote debt-for-energy swaps & donor-backed guarantees - aligning financial relief with climate action to unlock new flows of investment in high-need markets.

💡 Strengthen international cooperation - centering equity, supporting local policy design, and accelerating the deployment of clean technologies in underserved regions.

It is time to recognize that debt is not just an economic issue. It is a climate issue, a justice issue, a development issue and ultimately, a survival issue. Without bold, coordinated financial reform, the promise of a global clean energy transition risks remaining out of reach for those who need it most.

Rethinking Fossil Fuel Subsidies: A Lever for Transformative Change in Transport and Society

In Latin America and the Caribbean, fossil fuel subsidies consumed 0.6% - 1.3% of GDP between 2015 and 2021. While traditionally aimed to reduce energy costs for the population, they often fail to reach the most vulnerable and entrench high-emission transport systems.

It’s time to shift the narrative: Fossil fuel subsidy reform is not just a matter of fiscal discipline; it is a strategic development opportunity.

New analysis from UNDP  LAC Latin America and Caribbean  and UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub  outlines a three-step roadmap for governments to redirect subsidies toward low-emission public transport systems that are cleaner, more inclusive, and economically sustainable:

1️⃣ Build strong policy frameworks: Paraguay, Costa Rica, and Ecuador are embedding clean transport into national strategies through transparent fuel pricing and targeted reforms.

2️⃣ Invest in clean mobility: Uruguay’s MOVÉS initiative subsidizes electric buses up to $55K/year. Colombia provides tax incentives for low-emission vehicles. Paraguay links public subsidies to service quality standards.

3️⃣ Mobilize institutions and people: Cross-sector coordination and public engagement are making reforms more equitable, resilient and politically feasible.

Redirecting fossil fuel subsidies is about more than budget reform; it’s a catalyst for long-term social transformation. Sustainable transport systems can improve air quality, reduce inequality and create green jobs across the region.

Find out how @UNDP is supporting countries in delivering this transition: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBRWe5Rm 

#EnergyForDevelopment #FossilFuelReform #SustainableTransport #LatinAmerica #DevelopmentFinance

caption:
National Innovation Systems(NIS): A Strategic Lever for Inclusive Energy Transitions 

2024 was a milestone year: 17 million EVs were sold globally, making up more than 20% of all new car sales. The clean energy transition is accelerating, and National Innovation Systems (NIS) are ensuring that the Global South is is able to lead at the forefront.

NIS are policy-led frameworks that align government, research, industry and civil society to scale homegrown solutions, build local capacity & drive inclusive growth:

🔹 Bougainville (Pacific Islands): Innovation hubs, powered by Japan’s Pacific Green Transformation Project, deliver solar PV energy to IT labs, entrepreneurship incubators and women’s resource centers - supporting livelihoods and advancing climate goals.

🔹 India: “The Energy Transitions Innovation Challenge” has backed clean energy startups, scaled locally adapted solutions, de-risked investments and built long-term market capacity.

🔹 China: Public investment in brine-based lithium extraction in Qinghai is improving the sustainability and affordability of national battery supply chains. China already refines over 60% of the world’s lithium and leads global battery production.

National Innovation Systems are not just about research; they are tools for sovereign development, job creation and regional resilience. As energy systems become more digital and decentralized, context-specific innovation is essential - from AI solutions suited to tropical climates to technologies that serve Africa’s 3,000+ languages.

To learn how NIS can help the Global South become not just a consumer, but a co-creator of a cleaner, fairer energy future, explore the latest edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/ecsVJf4T

Regional interconnection is no longer a technical ambition; it’s a development priority. By integrating electricity markets and infrastructure, Regional Power Pools can reduce energy system costs by up to 23% while enabling near-100% renewable energy penetration.

As energy demand continues to increase - driven by digitalization, electrified transport and industrialization - regional grids offer the scale, flexibility and resilience that national systems cannot deliver alone. But what do these Regional Power Pools look like in practice?

⚡️ Cross-border electricity markets are scaling: In 2022, 9.8 TWh was traded through the Southern African Power Pool, while the West African Power Pool connected 14 of 15 ECOWAS countries under a unified market framework.

⚡️ Transport-energy corridors are being aligned with regional grids: Initiatives like Lobito and LAPSSET are electrifying mineral freight routes to anchor long-term renewable demand and reduce fossil fuel reliance.

⚡️ Structured energy trade between regions are advancing: The CASA-1000 project will enable the transfer of 1,300 MW of clean electricity from Central to South Asia, with commissioning expected in 2025.

⚡️ Collaborative green finance is underpinning integration: A partnership between the AfDB and AIIB is promoting co-financing, co-guarantees, and joint participation to accelerate green infrastructure development across Africa.

caption:
This year’s High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development takes place at a pivotal moment for the 2030 Agenda.
 
While energy is one of the most powerful enablers across the development agenda, 666 million people still lack access to electricity, and 2.1 billion rely on polluting fuels for cooking. These aren’t just energy issues; they're development emergencies

This week, as members of the SDG 7 Technical Advisory Group, we are launching a series of new Policy Briefs to support the HLPF discussions. They highlight just how central clean and inclusive energy is to unlocking progress across the development goals:

🌐 Zero Hunger: Energy powers irrigation, food storage and processing; critical to ending hunger and food insecurity.

🏥 Good Health and Well-being: Reliable energy keeps clinics running, vaccines cold, and clean air possible in homes and schools.

🧑‍🧒‍🧒 Gender Equality: Access to modern energy frees up time, reduces health risks and creates opportunities; especially for women and girls.

🛠️ Decent Work and Economic Growth: Energy access enables businesses to grow, jobs to be created and economies to thrive.

🏝️ Equity in LDCs, LLDCs, and SIDS: Clean energy drives local development, builds resilience and reduces dependency on volatile fuel imports.

The message is clear: energy action is development action. Without urgent investment and collaboration, we risk leaving millions behind. 

As #HLPF2025 discussions unfold, let’s turn these insights into action. Let’s scale up solutions that put energy at the heart of sustainable development for everyone, everywhere.

#EnergyForDevelopment #HLPF2025 #SDG7 #2030Agenda #LeaveNoOneBehind

With the right systems in place, Earth Observation (EO) - combining satellite data, sensors and machine learning - can become core digital infrastructure for climate-resilient energy development.

With over 15,000 satellites expected to launch this decade, governments across the Global South are starting to operationalize geospatial data for energy access, climate resilience and investment planning. With fewer than 20% of African countries integrating EO into national energy plans, there's a clear opportunity to transform decision-making - from pixels to policy:

🇪🇬 Egypt and 🇿🇦 South Africa are leveraging CBERS satellite imagery to identify optimal sites for renewable energy projects.

🌐 GeoSUR connects over 100 agencies across Latin America to co-manage geospatial infrastructure, accelerating regional coordination and planning.

🇧🇷 Brazil’s EO+AI platform combines satellite and climate data to map energy needs across five major biomes — driving smarter, climate-informed investment.

South–South initiatives like CBERS and GeoSUR are proving that  the Global South isn’t waiting; it’s already leading the digital revolution.

Explore the opportunities for energy and EO in our latest edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e7PmUFtw

caption:
“Over 90% of new renewables worldwide produced electricity for less than the cheapest new fossil fuel alternative. This is not just a shift in power. This is a shift in possibility... We have the tools to power the future for humanity. Let’s make the most of them. This is our moment of opportunity.” - António Guterres  
 
The clean energy future is no longer a promise, it’s a fact. The latest Unitednations secretarygeneral  synthesis report, Supercharging the New Energy Era - with contributions from UNDP  and partners - captures this global momentum and sets out what’s needed to turn it into lasting, inclusive progress. The full report is available here: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e_HHrGzg 
 
In 2024, renewables accounted for over 90% of new power capacity. Solar and wind are now the most affordable options in many markets. Battery storage has increased more than 40 times since 2015. Clean energy jobs now outnumber those in fossil fuels. These are not isolated achievements; they’re signs of growing global readiness to scale sustainable energy solutions that support the SDGs. 
 
Yet we face a dual challenge: “The energy transition is unstoppable. But the transition is not yet fast enough or fair enough.” Fossil fuels still dominate supply. Less than 20% of clean energy investment reaches the Global South - where it’s needed most. To turn momentum into inclusive, sustained progress, the report outlines six priority actions to keep the 1.5°C target within reach and ensure no one is left behind. 
 
1️⃣ Align policies: Ensure coherence, clarity, and certainty by integrating energy, climate, and economic policies to accelerate a just transition. 
  
2️⃣ Build infrastructure: Modernize grids, expand storage, and develop digital and physical systems to support a 21st century clean energy economy. 
  
3️⃣ Power growth with renewables: Meet rising electricity demand - especially from AI and data centers - with clean, affordable renewable energy. 
  
4️⃣ Center people and equity for a just transition: Put communities first by ensuring fair access, job creation and inclusive development in all transition efforts. 
  
5️⃣ Expand global cooperation: Strengthen trade, investment and innovation partnerships to supercharge deployment and reduce costs worldwide. 
  
6️⃣ Unlock finance for the Global South: Dismantle barriers to affordable capital and scale energy-transition investments to $1.4–1.9 trillion annually in EMDEs. 
 
This is not only an energy imperative - it’s a development opportunity. @UNDP stands ready to help scale solutions, unlock investment, and ensure the energy transition powers progress for everyone, everywhere. 
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #ClimateAction #DevelopmentFinance

" "
"1️⃣ Align policies: Ensure coherence, clarity, and certainty by integrating energy, climate, and economic policies to accelerate a just transition. "
"  "
"2️⃣ Build infrastructure: Modernize grids, expand storage, and develop digital and physical systems to support a 21st century clean energy economy. "
"  "
"3️⃣ Power growth with renewables: Meet rising electricity demand - especially from AI and data centers - with clean, affordable renewable energy. "
"  "

"  "

Too often, we treat the energy transition as something to be managed cautiously - especially when it comes to the role of young people. 
 
But the reality in the Global South tells a different story. In 2024, clean energy investments in electricity outpaced fossil fuels 7 to 1. This is not incremental progress; it’s a paradigm shift - one that youth are already helping to shape. 
 
As we accelerate into a future of electric vehicles, AI-integrated energy systems and smarter grids, we must reimagine, not just replicate, the systems we’ve inherited:

🔹 AI isn’t a silver bullet - its promise must not distract from the 1.18 billion people still living in energy poverty.
 🔹 EVs are only transformative if the benefits are shared - especially with communities in Africa, which holds over 50% of the world’s cobalt and manganese, yet often sees little value-added return.
 🔹 Energy is already central to climate action - cities use 78% of global energy and produce over 60% of emissions. The question isn’t whether to negotiate about energy, but how to ensure all voices are at the table.

Every day we should be working towards a sustainable energy revolution that addresses the needs and asks of people themselves. Young people are not simply  participants in this transition: they are already the dreamers, doers, and disruptors driving it forward. 

🎙 You can listen to my full reflections via the YOUNGO  Energy Podcast, available across all platforms: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eddJX87f

Let’s leap forward: not cautiously, but courageously. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #AIandDevelopment #YouthInEnergy #SystemsThinking

Many countries in the Global South are actively working to advance energy transitions - even in the context of tight fiscal constraints.  

In my latest illuminem  article, I unpack the conversation on debt and the energy transition; not as parallel issues, but as deeply interconnected challenges shaping development trajectories: 🔗📘  https://lnkd.in/euFEESVQ

Reallocating a portion of the $1 trillion in global fossil fuel subsidies could create the fiscal space needed to accelerate sustainable, inclusive energy systems where they are most needed. That is why we need a different model - one that: 

➡️ Redirects fossil fuel subsidies - freeing up public funds that can better serve people and planet. 

➡️ Unlocks blended and concessional finance - to channel more of the 85% of clean energy investment not yet reaching the Global South. 

➡️ Aligns debt relief with climate ambition - easing pressure for the 54 countries that spend +10% of government budgets on debt service. 

➡️ Invests in long-term resilience - so regions like Africa, needing $200B annually for clean energy, can tap into the resources that they need. 

Debt is no longer just a macroeconomic indicator; it is shaping what is possible in energy, in equity, and in development. 

Getting this right isn’t just urgent. It’s foundational. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #DebtAndDecarbonization #DevelopmentFinance

caption:
What if the world’s smallest island nations became the world's leaders in AI-powered clean energy? 🏝️⚡️ 
 
Small Island Developing States (SIDS) are redefining what it means to be energy-resilient, digital-first and development-driven. While facing some of the most acute climate and energy vulnerabilities, they are turning digitalization into a catalyst for just energy transitions. 
  
More than 60% of SIDS import over 90% of their fossil fuels, resulting in energy costs up to four times higher than those in continental regions. Despite these structural challenges, many SIDS are setting ambitious climate targets, including 100% renewable energy by 2030 and net-zero emissions by 2050 - a bold shift toward resilience, self-reliance, and economic transformation. 
  
Digital innovation is helping SIDS leapfrog traditional energy systems and transform access: 
 
🔋 Fiji, Palau, and Kiribati are pioneering smart energy management through the Smart Islands Project—boosting grid resilience and enabling remote, low-cost electrification. 
 
📊 Guyana is scaling digital connectivity with over 200 ICT hubs, empowering Indigenous communities with data access for local energy planning. 
 
📡 Kenya’s Energy Access Explorer is now being adapted to island contexts, using geospatial AI to guide investment and electrification strategies. 
 
By fusing digital intelligence with decentralized renewables, SIDS are unlocking new models of energy equity, resilience and sustainable development. With the right investments in open data, smart infrastructure, and local capacity, these “digital islands” can lead the way for the Global South.  
 
To see other success stores and find out how else SIDS are redefining development pathways, I  invite you to read this UNDP  Policy Paper: 👉 go.undp.org/34Q
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalForDevelopment #SIDS #CleanTechLeadership
#RisingUpForSIDS
Kanni Wignaraja Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS)

What if the path to 1.5°C runs through the innovation corridors of the Global South? 
 
As the impacts of climate change intensify, countries face a dual challenge: scale renewable energy and build inclusive, resilient economies.

The Global South is advancing on both fronts; not through incremental reform, but through cooperation, innovation and local value creation.

Modeling from UNDP  Charged for Change report shows that, with the right policies and investment, energy transitions could unlock universal access, reduce poverty by 193 million people and add $48 trillion to global GDP - all while staying within a 1.5°C pathway.

This transformation is not theoretical. It is already underway driven by a new development logic anchored in cooperation, innovation, and local value creation:
  
⚡ Under @ISA ’s Solar Initiative, over 570 clean energy scholars are advancing South-South R&D.
 
⚡ Indonesia has scaled mineral partnerships to grow nickel exports from $2B to $30B in just three years through value addition. 
 
⚡ DRC and Zambia are building a special economic zone to cut cathode precursor costs by 65%, while creating jobs and infrastructure.

⚡ Kenya is hosting geothermal-powered data centers, linking clean energy to digital development.

These are not one-off successes. They reflect a broader shift - where energy systems are being reimagined as engines of inclusion, productivity, and resilience.
 
The Global South is not waiting. It is redefining the future of energy.
 
🔗 Find out how the Global South is engineering a just transition through cooperation and innovation: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eWKQbMuC

On this #InternationalYouthDay, we celebrate the young people driving the energy transition - not in the future, but right now. 
 
With over a quarter of the world’s population under 30yrs, and nearly 90% living in the Global South, youth are already creating, innovating and delivering the solutions that will define our shared energy future. 

Globally, the green economy could create 8.4 million jobs for young people by 2030 - yet data shows that youth still face barriers in accessing these opportunities. Connecting skills training, innovation ecosystems and inclusive policies will be critical to unlock their full potential.

This year’s theme, Local Youth Actions for the SDGs and Beyond, reminds us that progress happens where global ambition meets community leadership. With over 65% of SDG targets linked to local governance, youth engagement is not a luxury; it’s essential.

When given the space to lead, young people bridge the worlds of technology, policy and sustainability - turning dialogue into design; ambition into implementation; and local innovation into global impact. Across the Global South, it is the young engineers, economists, policymakers and change-makers who are already connecting renewable energy to human development, making it affordable, inclusive and resilient. 
 
From building local energy community microgrids to shaping policy, designing AI-driven clean cooking solutions and mobilizing climate justice movements, young people are proving that the energy transition is not a distant promise; it’s a reality being forged in real time. Their digital fluency, fresh perspectives, and unwavering commitment to the sustainable energy transition are bridging the gap between innovation and implementation.  

On this #InternationalYouthDay, let’s commit to working together to expand opportunities for youth in the sustainable energy revolution, and recognize that the leadership we need for a just, inclusive energy future is already here - transforming local action into global change.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #YouthLed #InternationalYouthDay

What if integrating renewables wasn’t just about cutting carbon - but also saving lives? 
 
Every year, air pollution from energy systems causes 6.4 million premature deaths, with the greatest burden falling on women and children in low- and middle-income countries. Power generation, cooking, transport, and waste burning all contribute to a silent epidemic - with energy and related sectors together responsible for over 70% of global GHG emissions.  Yet digitally powered solutions are already helping make energy and transport systems more efficient; reducing both emissions and their health impacts: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eNH_Vefp
  
While 666 million people still live without electricity and 2.1 billion rely on polluting cooking fuels, the global energy-health crisis is also a moment of powerful opportunity. Across the Global South, countries are demonstrating that integrating renewables, powered by digital innovation, can simultaneously reduce emissions and deliver major health gains: 
 
🌱 Kenya is using geospatial tools like Energy Access Explorer to plan hybrid grid-extension and distributed renewables, improving rural access and air quality. 
 
🌱 India is optimizing microgrids with AI to better match demand with renewable supply - reducing fossil fuel use and energy waste. 
 
🌱 Trinidad and Tobago is pursuing wind energy and green hydrogen, shifting away from fossil-powered generation that fuels both pollution and illness. 
  
Digital technologies like IoT sensors, AI forecasting, and remote monitoring also help utilities manage grid stability and enhance energy efficiency – reducing energy use in buildings and transport by around 10–15% while accelerating a healthier energy transition in real time. 
 
This isn’t just energy action; it’s a pathway to cleaner air, stronger health systems and more resilient communities.

caption:
Grateful for the opportunity to join colleagues at @UNDPChina country office to to discuss how our new UNDP Strategic Plan 2026–2029 puts sustainable energy at the center of development; not just as an enabler, but as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve itself. 

China’s experience shows why this matters. With 47% of global wind & solar; 20M EVs (half the global fleet); and having already achieved its 2030 renewables target six years early, China is proving that transitions can be nationally transformative and globally catalytic. But ultimately, this is not only about megawatts; it is about people, communities and systems for shared prosperity. 

In our dialogue, I shared three priorities for deepening China’s leadership and expanding shared progress: 

🔹 South–South and triangular cooperation
With 25 regional projects totaling 12 GW of new capacity worth $5B under the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and partnerships across Africa, Asia and the Pacific, China is extending its leadership. The next step is moving from projects to scalable solutions grounded in governance, safeguards and inclusion. 

🔹 Digital, data & AI for energy systems
With grid investment projected at $100B annually and data center demand set to nearly double to 945 TWh by 2030, China is pioneering AI forecasting, digital twins and open data. Embedding these innovations into just transition frameworks is essential to ensure they deliver inclusive benefits 

🔹 Energy as a lever for human development 
As set out in the new Strategic Plan, success will not be measured only in megawatts, but in human outcomes: schools and clinics with reliable power; farmers with modern tools; households with clean cooking; and communities with greater resilience to crisis. 

At UNDP  we are proud to work alongside China and global partners to connect innovation with governance, finance, and inclusion. A just energy transition is not only a national achievement – it's a shared global responsibility. The real challenge is not how fast we expand renewables, but how effectively we connect them to the people who need them most. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #EnergyTransition #JustTransition #China

caption:
It was a real pleasure to meet with my friend Dr. Gloria Magombo, Permanent Secretary for Energy and Power Development in Zimbabwe, to reflect on how Zimbabwe can accelerate its energy transition in ways that put people, resilience, and prosperity at the center.
 
Our discussion touched on three priorities that are vital to unlocking this transformation:
 
🇿🇼 Supporting Zimbabwe’s National Clean Cooking Strategy With nearly 62% of the population still without access to clean cooking, and rural access below 10%, the new National Clean Cooking Strategy is more than an energy plan. It is a health plan, a gender equality plan, and an environmental plan. UNDP stands ready to support its implementation with policy expertise, innovative finance and local delivery models.
 
🇿🇼 Mission 300 Zimbabwe’s ambitious compact under Mission 300, targeting 100% electricity access by 2030 and raising clean cooking access to 70%, is a milestone moment. Building on our Solar for Health and mini-grid initiatives, UNDP  is committed to helping ensure these targets translate into real, reliable services for households, clinics, schools and enterprises.
 
🇿🇼 South–South cooperation and financial instruments Closing Zimbabwe’s annual energy gap - which currently costs the country 6.1% of GDP - requires innovative finance and regional collaboration. Instruments like the Renewable Energy Fund show how blended finance and South–South learning can unlock scale and inclusion.
 
Zimbabwe’s journey shows that energy is not only a national priority, it is a shared responsibility. By linking ambition with action, and innovation with inclusion, we can ensure the transition delivers for those who need it most.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #CleanCooking #Mission300 #SouthSouthCooperation #Zimbabwe

caption:
How can we unlock the financing needed for a just and inclusive energy transition that leaves no one behind?
 
Global clean energy investment reached a record USD 2.1 trillion in 2024, reflecting strong momentum for change. Yet less than 15% reached developing economies outside China, and only 2% flowed to Africa continent. How can innovative finance, risk-sharing tools, and new partnerships direct capital where it is needed most?
 
Join UNDP and GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference for a high-level dialogue on financing a just and inclusive energy transition - exploring how innovative financing mechanisms, de-risking approaches, and strategic cooperation can mobilize capital at scale and deliver lasting development impact for everyone, everywhere.
 
📅 Tuesday, 9 September 2025
🕓  16:00 - 17:30 (90 minutes)
📍 Beijing National Convention Center

caption:
Financing the global energy transition is no longer about if, but about how - and above all, for whom.
 
Later today, I am delighted to co-convene, with colleagues from GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  a high-level dialogue at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference in Beijing on financing a just and inclusive energy transition.
 
I will be joined by Beate Trankmann, Khaled, @wang yao, Pradeep Kurukulasuriya  Kurukulasuriya, @Yan Jing, and @Cheng Lin. Together, we will explore how investment can be de-risked in underserved markets, how financing can deliver not only megawatts but also lasting development impact, and how commitments made at #UNGA and #COP30 can be translated into bankable solutions for debt-distressed economies.
 
In 2024, the world invested over USD 2.1 trillion in clean energy. Yet <15% reached developing economies outside China, and only 2% flowed to the African continent - regions that hold some of the greatest potential and the greatest need. How can this imbalance be corrected? And what will it take to ensure that no country is left behind in the race to net zero?
 
📅 Tuesday, 9 September 
⏰ 16:00–17:30 (CST)
📍 Beijing National Convention Center

caption:
It was a pleasure to join colleagues and partners at the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition to reflect on how sustainable energy can be a true lever for human development.
 
At a time when cooperation is under strain, sustainable energy remains one of the most powerful levers for progress - creating jobs, powering schools and clinics, advancing gender equality, and building resilience. Because in the end, the energy transition is never only about megawatts; it is about people and communities. Yet with 666 million people still without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking, we must rethink where and how we act. That is why three priorities stand out:
 
⚡️ Clean cooking at scale - 2.1 billion people still cook with polluting fuels. Scaling clean cooking is not just about energy access, it is about saving lives, empowering women, and protecting the planet.
 
⚡️ Development assessment for a just transition - A just transition means linking energy to jobs, health, education, and resilience, so every investment delivers tangible benefits for people and communities.
 
⚡️ Harnessing digitalization & AI - Smart technologies can unlock grid capacity and optimize systems, but their true value lies in ensuring the transition is faster and fairer.
 
At @UNDP, our new Strategic Plan 2026–2029 positions energy as a strategic lever for shifting the development curve. With sustainable energy projects across 131 countries, we are already proving that the transition can be faster, fairer, and more transformative for people’s lives.
 
The technologies exist. The financing can be mobilized. The real challenge, and our shared responsibility, is ensuring no one is left behind.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableEnergy #CleanCooking #AIforDevelopment

caption:
The Future of the Energy–AI Nexus: How can AI accelerate a just energy transition by scaling finance and innovation?

Today at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference in Beijing, I will be hosting, alongside colleagues from @GEIDCO, a high-level dialogue on the future of the Energy–AI nexus. We’ll explore how AI can reshape sustainable energy – making projects more bankable, attracting finance and broadening access to clean power.

I will be joined by @Chen Ying, @Yuncheng Xu, @Peng Yijie, @Saifur Rahman, @Jerry Lou, and @Dennis She. Together, we will explore how AI can help turn ideas into bankable projects, attract private finance, and scale clean energy access in ways that drive equity and innovation.

By 2050, many emerging markets will face higher capital costs and limited technical capacity. The key question is: how can we take full advantage of the transformative opportunities of AI in the just energy transition, in order to scale up finance and innovation for impact where it is needed most?

📅 Wednesday, 10 September 2025
⏰ 09:00–10:30 (CST)
📍 Beijing National Convention Center

caption:
It was a real pleasure to deliver the keynote at the Capacity Building and Training Parallel Forum: Advancing Global Carbon Neutrality Goals through Capacity Building. 

The momentum is undeniable: in 2024, renewables accounted for 92.5% of all new power generation, global clean energy investment surpassed $2.1 trillion, (more than double fossil fuels), and the renewable energy sector now supports 16 million jobs worldwide — with the potential to reach 40 million by 2050.  

But to turn this momentum into lasting impact, we must close the gap in capacity - the systems, skills and institutions that transform ambition into action: 

1️⃣ Investing in institutions & people - Every dollar invested in governance and skills can unlock tenfold in climate and energy finance. From Zimbabwe’s lithium policy to India’s incentives creating nearly 1M jobs, capacity is what translates ambition into investment and livelihoods. 

2️⃣ Scaling South–South & regional cooperation - Cooperation multiplies results. The African Continental Free Trade Area could unlock $9B annually, while lithium alliances in Latin America and nickel policies in Asia show how shared standards and supply chains accelerate progress. 

3️⃣ Leveraging innovation responsibly - From AI making grids 30% more efficient to monitoring systems hundreds of times faster, innovation is reshaping our energy systems in real-time. But to close divides rather than widen them, it must remain inclusive, affordable and people-centered. 

Carbon neutrality is not only a technological challenge. It depends on institutions, skills, finance and cooperation — and embedding capacity building into every layer of the transition. The opportunities are immense, if we choose to seize them. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #CarbonNeutrality #CapacityBuilding #SouthSouthCooperation #Innovation

caption:
"Financing is not an end in itself; the real measure is the development it delivers." 

This was at the heart of the dialogue that I co-convened with GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  on “Bridging the Gap  Financing a Just and Inclusive Energy Transition.” 

We meet at a moment of paradox. Global clean energy investment will reach $2.2 trillion this year, yet less than 15% flows to developing economies outside China, and Africa, with its vast renewable potential, receives only 2% of that total. The challenge is not if the transition will be financed, but how - and whether it will be just, inclusive, and development-maximizing. From our panel session, three priorities came through strongly: 

🌏 Closing the financing gap through Southern leadership
From Africa’s green industrialization agenda to Asia-Pacific’s blended finance models, countries are already pioneering ambitious national strategies. The task now is to scale and aggregate pipelines to attract capital at the level required. 

🌏 De-risking & financial innovation as drivers of scale  
Sovereign green bonds in Indonesia, sukuk in the Middle East, and guarantee facilities in Africa show how innovative instruments can unlock billions. The next step is replication and mainstreaming. 

🌏 Maximizing development impact through energy investments  
Solarizing clinics in Zimbabwe, electrifying schools in Fiji, and powering farms in Bangladesh show how people-centered finance delivers. The task now is to scale these models so development outcomes define success. 

Grateful to Khaled Sharbatly , @Wang Yao, Pradeep Kurukulasuriya  Kurukulasuriya, @Yan Jing, and @Cheng Lin for their insights, and to @Beate Trankmann for reminding us that speed without fairness risks leaving people behind. 

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition will only succeed if it delivers for people first: lighting homes, powering schools and opening opportunities across the Global South.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableFinance #EnergyTransition

caption:
How can we navigate the green hydrogen pathways to drive energy resilience, industrial transformation, and inclusive growth across Asia-Pacific? And is this financially viable to deliver truly transformative change for our societies?
 
Today, I am delighted to co-convene, together with colleagues from @GEIDCO, a high-level dialogue at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference in Beijing. Our focus will be on how Asia-Pacific can lead the transition in ways that deliver inclusive growth, industrial transformation, and energy resilience.
 
I will be joined by @Yu Zhuoping, @Amir Lebdioui, @Zhu Yongsheng, @Wang Ju, and @Zhang Jinxuan. Together, we will explore how the region can advance the hydrogen transition; balancing domestic needs, export ambitions, and inclusive development.
 
By 2050, emerging and developing economies could account for up to 70% of global final energy demand - much of it in Asia. This places the region at the very center of the global energy transition. But the key question remains: will green hydrogen reinforce existing inequalities and export dependence, or can it accelerate a just and inclusive transition?
 
📅 Wednesday, 10 September 2025 ⏰ 13:30–15:00 (CST) 📍 Beijing National Convention Center

caption:
Delighted and an honor to deliver the keynote at the Opening Ceremony at the 2025 Global Energy Interconnection Conference in Beijing on behalf of UNDP - a gathering that comes at a pivotal moment for the global energy transition.

One message stood out clearly: clean energy is no longer tomorrow’s promise. It is today’s most powerful tool for jobs, growth and true energy security. In 2023, the sector employed 16 million people worldwide, with China alone accounting for 7.4 million - nearly half the global total. By 2030, clean energy and efficiency could generate 70 million new jobs, with each $1 million invested in renewables creating nearly three times more jobs than fossil fuels

The shift is already reshaping economies. In 2023, clean energy accounted for 10% of global GDP growth - rising to 20% in China and nearly one-third in the EU. The question now is not whether the transition is happening, but how fast we can scale it and how effectively we can ensure its benefits reach the people who need them most.

It was in this context that @UNDP and @GEIDCO announced a new MoU: a commitment to deepen collaboration on innovative finance, South–South cooperation and digital solutions that can accelerate a just and inclusive energy transition.

We stand at a moment of great possibility. Clean energy is not only about megawatts—it is about unlocking opportunities to create millions of new jobs and livelihoods. It is a driver of transformative change across our societies, reshaping how we live, produce, and connect. And with the power of digital tools, data, and AI, we can ensure energy security that is smarter, more resilient, and inclusive. Together, we can build an energy future that truly leaves no one behind.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SouthSouthCooperation #GEI2025

caption:
“Powering Inclusive Growth from Potential to Prosperity: Opportunities and Trade-offs in Green Hydrogen” 

Grateful to @Yu Zhuoping, Amir Lebdioui , @Zhu Yongsheng, @Wang Ju, and @Zhang Jinxuan, who joined me at our UNDP  and GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  high-level dialogue to explore how Asia-Pacific can ensure hydrogen drives inclusive growth, not just exports. 

But will incurred green hydrogen truly deliver for development? By 2050, green hydrogen could supply 12–22% of global energy demand, with Asia-Pacific at the center. The market, worth USD 8 billion today, could grow nearly eightfold by 2030. To get there, challenges around water (9 liters per kg), land (30,000 hectares of solar per million tonnes), and costs ($4.5–12/kg) must be managed, while scaling low-carbon hydrogen beyond today’s 1% share. And here, three priorities emerged from our discussion.

1️⃣ Align with development priorities: Green hydrogen must expand energy access, cut costs, and create jobs. If treated only as an export, communities risk being left behind. 

2️⃣ Embed safeguards: Large-scale hydrogen needs land, water, and minerals. Strong governance is vital to prevent water stress, land conflict, and inequality. 

3️⃣ Lead through cooperation: Regional partnerships on standards, infrastructure, and finance can amplify Asia-Pacific’s voice and build local value chains and skills. 

We explore these opportunities and trade-offs in more depth in our latest policy paper - Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: 🔗 https://lnkd.in/e7f_tvA9 

At @UNDP, we believe the real promise of green hydrogen lies not in the technology alone, but in the choices we make today to ensure it drives inclusive, sustainable development for all. 

#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustTransition #InclusiveGrowth

"AI and clean energy are no longer separate stories, but intertwined forces that are defining our collective future."

Together with distinguished colleagues - @Chen Ying, @Yuncheng Xu, @Peng Yijie, Saifur Rahman, @Jerry Lou, and Dennis She  I had the privilege to moderate “The Future of the Energy–AI Nexus: How can AI accelerate a just energy transition by scaling finance and innovation?” 

We meet at a moment of transformation. Clean energy is scaling at unprecedented speed; solar PV has grown more than 60x in a decade, and EVs now account for 1 in 5 new cars sold. In the same period, AI has reshaped entire industries. Their convergence creates not just opportunities, but new possibilities and a shared responsibility to direct them wisely. From our session, three priorities came through strongly:

🌐 AI as an enabler of access and affordability:
AI is already improving forecasts and grid management, potentially unlocking 175 GW of additional transmission capacity worldwide. The next step is ensuring these gains translate into reliable, affordable power for schools, hospitals, and communities, not just advanced markets 

🌐 Finance, trust, and inclusion as the bridge to scale:
Clean energy investment reached USD 2.2 trillion in 2025, but less than 15% flows to emerging economies beyond China. AI can reduce transaction costs and clarify risks, unlocking much-needed private capital. But safeguards and transparent data are vital to ensure inclusion 

🌐 Policy and innovation aligning for impact: 
AI is already accelerating breakthroughs; from new battery chemistries to efficiency gains that could cut energy use in light manufacturing by 8% by 2035. But technology alone is not enough. Policy must steer innovation toward human development - powering clinics, creating jobs and building resilience across the Global South. 

At UNDP  we believe the energy transition will only succeed if it is inclusive - creating jobs, powering clinics and schools, and building resilience across the Global South. The question is no longer if AI will shape energy, but how we choose to direct it. 

 #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableFinance #ArtificialIntelligence #GEI2025 #AI

{"@type": "WebPage", "author": {"name": "Amir Lebdioui", "image": {"url": "https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/D4E03AQFUdxYACPToaA/profile-displayphoto-shrink_400_400/profile-displayphoto-shrink_400_400/0/1716415657428?e=2147483647&v=beta&t=07NRO41oAg4j2qXAt9YG5kbVtQciUJqu0RZ5ZpZxRbg", "@type": "ImageObject"}, "url": "https://uk.linkedin.com/in/amir-lebdioui", "@type": "Person", "interactionStatistic": {"@type": "InteractionCounter", "interactionType": "http://schema.org/FollowAction", "userInteractionCount": 19791}}, "headline": "If you have been taught that Adam Smith is the 'Father' of economics, you have been misled.

Economic thought did not start in the 18th century with the European & Scottish Enlightenment, and several global south scholars wrote about economic theory long before. One of them was #IbnKhaldun, who conceptualised:
- the law of supply and demand (500 years before Smith‼️)
- the notion of a fiscal stimulus (no, it was not Keynes!)
- the inverted-U relationship between tax rates and the government's total tax revenue (what we call Laffer curve today, even if Arthur Laffer said he borrowed it from Khaldun)
- and a labour theory of value (what is considered as Marx's great original contribution). 

Why does it matter to restore his intellectual legacy, which has been erased from economics textbooks, even though he is widely known in sociology? 

It matters because depending on we come from, we experience and see the economy differently. To understand solutions to today's economic problems, we must therefore go beyond a eurocentric view of knowledge production. Recognising that great ideas have flourished and emerged in all places, not just Europe and the USA, is an important step to decolonise our learning and teaching. 

The TIDE Centre, University of Oxford’s new resource (and beautiful animated work by Econ Films) provides an introduction to Ibn Khaldun’s key ideas, and why that is still relevant. Should be compulsory to read for anyone interested in economics: https://lnkd.in/eZ-AZZSg"}

caption:
Green hydrogen has been hailed as the "fuel of the future", and since 2020 it has appeared in more than 60,000 media headlines, with 58 countries and regional blocs now having adopted hydrogen strategies - half of them in developing economies. The market, valued at USD 7.98 billion in 2024, could grow nearly eightfold by 2030.
 
But there are also central challenges yet to navigate. Land and water requirements are extremely demanding for reaching scale, and current costs remain high at USD 4.5–12 per kilogram, while dependence on critical minerals adds new risks. Without deliberate safeguards, the green hydrogen economy risks reinforcing historical extractive models, and exposing first mover nations to lost investments without the right guidance on technologies and pathways.
 
That’s why UNDP, together with the  TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, published 📄 Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework, which I had the chance to co-write with Dr. Amir Lebdioui  and Pavel Bilek,  🔗 https://lnkd.in/eEXrfn9t
 
The policy paper introduces a 3P Framework—People, Planet, Prosperity to ensure strategies deliver inclusive development:
🔹 People: Expand energy access, upskill the workforce, and support a just transition.
🔹 Planet: Safeguard land, water, biodiversity, and minerals through strong governance.
🔹 Prosperity: Integrate hydrogen into industrial policy, foster local value chains, and phase investments.
 
This report offers practical policy levers for countries to steer green hydrogen at the right speed, time, and direction. With transparent governance and context-specific strategies, it can become a driver of just transitions and shared prosperity.
 
#GreenHydrogen #EnergyTransition #JustTransition #UNDP #Oxford

caption:
As we head into New York Climate Week alongside UNGA80, the energy access challenge remains urgent: 2.1 billion people still lack clean cooking and 666 million live without electricity.
 
Closing these gaps isn’t just about finance and infrastructure - it’s also about having the right data to make smarter decisions.
 
That is why, in partnership with IBM  and Stony Brook University, UNDP  has co-developed two open, AI-driven tools now available on GeoHub: https://lnkd.in/epWZQYhA
 
⚡ Electricity Access Forecasting Model - projecting access to 2030 across 100+ countries to help identify underserved areas.
⚡ Clean Energy Equity Index - assessing equity across 53 African countries to guide just, inclusive energy transitions.
 
Already informing UNDP projects expected to benefit 600,000+ people, these tools demonstrate how AI and open data can transform energy planning - moving us from static surveys to predictive, real-time insights.
 
Ultimately, closing energy access gaps isn’t just about building infrastructure or mobilizing finance. It’s about ensuring that every clean energy investment is guided by the right data - making progress toward SDG7 more targeted, equitable and achievable.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #UNGA80 #AIforGood #CleanEnergy #ClimateWeekNYC

caption:
Mission 300 Development Partners Coordination Group: Aligning for Impact

Africa stands at an inflection point. Nearly 600 million people still live without electricity, yet the tools to close this gap—renewables, innovative finance, and new delivery models—are scaling faster than ever. The challenge is no longer just ambition, but delivery at pace and scale.

At today’s inaugural meeting of the Mission 300 Development Partners Coordination Group (DPCG), convened by the The World Bank Group  and the African Development Bank Group, I shared four key priorities that are essential to make Mission 300 a reality:

⚡ Joint forces for technical assistance and policy alignment: Coordinated support must go hand in hand with clear methodologies for measuring results, ensuring that productive energy use and clean cooking are fully embedded in national strategies.

⚡ Financial innovation and policy de-risking: Unlocking private capital at scale requires building bankable pipelines and sharing risk. UNDP  working with United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)  is advancing solutions to crowd in investment through guarantee schemes and blended finance mechanisms. Through the Africa Minigrid Programme, UNDP is supporting governments to create new regulatory frameworks and conduct Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI) analyses—a strategic complement to other initiatives such as AfDB’s Africa Mini-Grids Market Acceleration Programme (AMAP).

⚡ Compact Delivery and Monitoring Units (CDMUs): Turning commitments into impact requires strong local ownership. UNDP is supporting CDMUs in Congo, Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Mozambique through the Italy-supported Energy for Growth Initiative, helping accelerate delivery on the ground by identifying pipelines of bankable projects.

At @UNDP, our strength lies in country presence, convening power, and delivery capacity. By joining forces with partners, we can transform ambition into reality—accelerating Africa’s energy transition and ensuring no one is left behind.

#EnergyForDevelopment #Mission300 #AfricaEnergyTransition #UNGA80

caption:
Carbon-Free Energy: Keeping up momentum on corporate commitments

Corporate ambition for carbon-free energy is higher than ever. Over 40% of the world’s largest 2,000 companies have net-zero pledges, covering more than 90% of the global economy. The challenge is no longer ambition; but turning pledges into action that is inclusive, transformative and delivers real impact.

At today’s @SEforALL convening during New York Climate Week, I had the pleasure of opening the session with a keynote, where I highlighted three priorities to move corporate climate commitments from ambition to action:

1️⃣ Smarter integration of AI and clean energy: Globally, AI-enabled systems could reduce electricity demand by up to 10% by 2030. In India, smart meters are already cutting distribution losses by 20%, while Brazil is advancing clean power-shoring to relocate industries to renewable hubs and cut emissions by up to 40%.

2️⃣ Scaling clean energy investment in the Global South: Sovereign green bonds in Bolivia and Chile and corporate PPAs in India & Kenya are already showing what’s possible. Scaling these models across Africa and Asia could unlock tens of gigawatts of new renewable capacity.

3️⃣ Going beyond emissions reduction: Net-zero must deliver jobs, resilience and equity. From Paraguay’s e-bus fleets to Rwanda’s solar irrigation with electric cargo bikes - boosting crop yields by 25% - clean energy and e-mobility are already transforming communities.

At @UNDP, we believe net-zero will only succeed if it is also just. Corporate climate action must go beyond compliance checklists to strategies that build competitiveness, resilience, and equity.

#EnergyForDevelopment #CarbonFreeEnergy #ClimateAction #JustTransition

caption:
Accelerating the Energy Transition in the Global South: New Pathways for Action

It was a privilege to join experts from policy, business and academia at the high-level roundtable convened by Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW)  CSEP, and Columbia’s CGEP during #NYCClimateWeek.

I had the chance to share thoughts on electricity systems and networks: the backbone of any clean energy transition. Grids are not just wires; they are the backbone of the clean energy transition. Without resilient networks, renewables cannot reach homes and industries. That is why grid transformation is as critical as generation itself - and why AI’s ability to unlock 175 GW of capacity on existing lines, equal to Brazil’s entire power system, is a powerful opportunity.

The conversation also touched on the promise of digitalization, finance and the broader opportunities that modern energy systems can unlock. caption:
Can AI help power a Just Energy Future?

Today, we stand at a crossroads. ChatGPT now reaches over 400 million weekly users, yet 1.18 billion people still live without reliable energy access. This paradox highlights both the promise and the peril of AI: it can deepen divides, or it can help us build more efficient, resilient and equitable energy systems.

In this piece, co-written with my colleague Stefano Pistolese , we argue that a new paradigm, “planetary intelligence” is emerging. By learning from nature and managing systems holistically, AI has the potential to transform not just energy, but the interconnected challenges of water, land, biodiversity and culture. To seize this opportunity, we must act on three fronts:

1️⃣ Move from biomimicry to “machine ecology”: AI can shift from copying nature’s designs to managing energy like an ecosystem. Smart grids already cut losses by 20%, and predictive tools balance renewables in real time. At scale, this could cut emissions 10% by 2030 and expand access.

2️⃣ Scale ecosystem-level solutions: AI modeled on natural systems can manage trade-offs across water, land, and biodiversity, creating up to $1.3 trillion in value by 2030 while safeguarding planetary health.

3️⃣ Ground innovation in equity: Efforts like Masakhane’s 40 African language models show how planetary intelligence can reflect diverse cultures, widening who benefits from AI and ensuring inclusion in the energy transition.

The question is not if AI will reshape our energy future, but how - and whether it will do so in a way that serves all people, not just a few. With the right governance, AI can become a catalyst for just and sustainable development.

caption:
“SDG7 is not just one goal among many. It is the gateway to the entire 2030 Agenda.”

Together with distinguished colleagues – @Annika Blakstad Otterstedt, Rana Ghoneim , @Daniel Schroth, and @Fanny Missfeldt-Ringius – I had the privilege to moderate the session “Mobilizing a Final Push on SDG7 and Roadmap towards the 2026 HLPF Review.”

We met at a moment of paradox. Energy poverty is the single greatest constraint on development, yet 9 out of 10 dollars in clean energy still go to advanced economies and China. Meanwhile, 666 million people remain without electricity and 2.1 billion without clean cooking. This is not simply a financial imbalance, it is a developmental divide.

But it is also a moment of opportunity. Renewables, innovative finance, and new delivery models are scaling faster than ever – and the conversation is now evolving from compacts to implementation. Through initiatives like Mission 300, partners are joining forces to move from commitments to concrete action, accelerating delivery on the ground and ensuring energy access translates into better health, learning and opportunity

From our discussion, three imperatives came through strongly:

🙏 Reinvent cooperation With ODA falling by over 9% in 2024 and projected to decline further in 2025, traditional aid cannot close the gap. New coalitions and partnerships are needed to reach those left furthest behind.

⚡ Build resilient value chains Solar modules now cost just $0.10 per watt, but tariffs and fragmented supply chains risk eroding gains. Demand for lithium has quadrupled since 2015, yet Africa and Latin America still lack processing capacity - exporting resources while importing expensive technologies.

🌐 Leverage AI for inclusion Electricity demand from data centers and AI grew 20% in just two years, and could match the consumption of Canada and the UK by 2030. But AI can also optimize grids, cut losses of 20-25% in some countries, and unlock efficiency for universal access.

At @UNDP, we believe the energy transition must be measured not just in megawatts, but in lives transformed. 

#SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SustainableFinance #HLPF2026 #climateweeknyc

caption:
Clean Cooking: From overlooked issue to global priority

At today’s @UnitedNationsEnergy session on clean cooking, I was delighted to share why the clean cooking imperative must move from the margins of energy discussions to the center of sustainable development.

Every year, household air pollution from dirty cooking fuels causes 6.67 million deaths - more than malaria, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS combined. The economic costs exceed $2.4 trillion annually, yet clean cooking receives < 1% of global energy investment, far below the $8 billion needed each year to reach universal access by 2030. We’re paying trillions to avoid spending billions.

To reframe this we must:

1️⃣ Integrate clean cooking into electrification planning – as is already happening in Zambia, where e-cooking is part of mini-grid expansion strategies, making entire systems more viable while supporting productive uses like food processing and irrigation.

2️⃣ Unlock innovative finance and market development – as is already happening in Tanzania, where the UNCDF-backed CookFund uses concessional loans and results-based finance to reduce end-user costs by up to 60%, proving that public capital can de-risk private investment and build viable markets.

Africa holds 60% of the world’s best solar potential, a $190B clean energy opportunity.
 
At yesterday’s fireside chat on #Africa’s energy future, I argued that innovation here must mean access and industrialization first—not just decarbonization. Momentum is real, but what’s missing is bold finance, regional integration, and political will to make Africa not just a consumer, but a clean energy engine.
 
The paradox is clear: with 60% of solar potential and 30% of critical minerals, Africa still has 600M people without electricity—85% of the global deficit—while receiving just 2% of clean energy investment. Without action, we risk a green-tech divide.
 
Countries in Africa are closing the gap by: 
1️⃣ Deploying decentralized innovation at scale – as is already happening in Kenya’s EcoSafi stoves which halve cooking costs; and Nigeria’s containerized mini-grids which  power villages in a day. Together, such models could reach 380M people by 2030 at the lowest cost.
2️⃣ Leveraging #digital and #AI breakthroughs – from UNDP  & IBM ’s geospatial forecasting tool to M-KOPA’s AI-driven financing, digital innovation is the backbone of Africa’s industrial revolution.
3️⃣ Turning mineral wealth into local prosperity – instead of exporting bauxite at $65/ton and importing aluminum at $2,335/ton, Africa must process locally. With copper, cobalt, nickel, and lithium worth $16T over 25 years, Sub-Saharan Africa could capture $2T by building domestic industries.
 
The opportunity is historic: with $190B/year in clean energy investment by 2030, Africa can close its access gap, fuel industrialization, and drive global energy innovation.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #AfricaEnergyTransition #ClimateWeekNYC #Digitalization #SDG7
