Yesterday at a #UNGA80 side event on Data, Digital Transformation and the Resilience in the Energy Transition, I discussed a defining question for the AI era:
 
AI is already reshaping the #energy transition - but does it build resilience, or deepen fragility?
 
Last year, in Mexico’s drought-stricken Querétaro region, farmers rationed water and lost crops. Just a few kilometers away, billions were invested in new AI data centers requiring extensive water cooling systems. The paradox is striking.
 
By 2027, data centers are projected to consume nearly 900 TWh of electricity and 6.6 billion cubic meters of water annually, largely driven by AI. But at the same time, AI also holds promise: it can optimize renewable grids, enable faster climate forecasting, and unlock billions in private finance for clean energy in the Global South.
 
During the discussion, youth delegates asked powerful questions:
👉 Are we using #AI in a way that advances sustainable energy for all?
👉 How can we prevent AI from becoming another burden on already stressed systems, and instead ensure it can create real opportunities for development?
👉 Will we step up to govern our energy transitions, so they are not only resilient, but also just?
 
The answers will define whether AI accelerates the clean energy future - or becomes another burden on already fragile systems.
 
#UNGA #AI #EnergyTransition #Resilience #Sustainability

caption:
Planetary intelligence is the capacity for AI to steer global energy systems within ecological limits, integrating renewables, storage, critical-mineral supply chains, and demand management so that innovation drives resilience and inclusive access.
 
This paradigm calls for digital systems that are distributed, operate within real-world resource constraints, and anticipate long-term impacts on energy security and equity. AI must strengthen the foundations of a just, reliable, and affordable energy transition - rather than increase fragility.
 
Already, AI data centers consume more electricity than 150 individual countries and could demand 6.6 billion m³ of water annually by 2027. The minerals powering this growth - lithium, cobalt, rare earths - are extracted largely from the Global South while most of the value accrues elsewhere. Unless guided by principles aligned with the concept of planetary intelligence, the Energy-AI nexus risks deepening these inequities.
 
The question is no longer whether AI will shape the energy transition - it already is. The real question is how to steer it so that the benefits, resources, and risks are shared fairly.
 
Read more in here in this blog I co-authored with Stefano Pistolese 👉 https://lnkd.in/eNzYmY7U
 
#JustEnergyTransition #AI #PlanetaryIntelligence

caption:
Years of accelerating investments in renewables energy systems are paying off. Solar is now 41% cheaper than fossil fuels, and nearly 100 new climate commitments were announced last week at #UNGA80. Yet as geopolitical tensions and intensifying climate shocks threaten energy security, we must move beyond targets to build systems that are resilient by design.
 
🔗 Read more in the new Sustainable Energy Bulletin: The Era of Energy Security 👉 https://lnkd.in/exUQY3mf 
 
This priority of energy security was highlighted during a high-level dialogue during UNGA80 on Ukraine’s energy recovery which underlined that solidifying a green and decentralized energy system is an imperative for national security. Similarly, public and private actors reaffirmed their commitment to Mission 300 for accelerating energy access that is not only accessible but also affordable and reliable.
 
But the finance bottleneck for resilience persists: countries and companies have pledged $1.6 trillion by 2030 under Energy Compacts, yet less than 0.1% of global climate finance goes to adaptation in energy systems. We must make resilience bankable - turning protection of people and infrastructure into an investment case at scale. The future of energy security will also hinge on innovation and optimization - exactly where the triptych of digital, data, and AI is central. AI-driven risk modeling, paired with robust analytics and digital platforms, can help investors and policymakers optimize targeted financing where it is most effective.
 
As we head toward #COP30 in Brazil, progress will be measured not only by how quickly we transition to renewables but by how resilient and inclusive those systems are.

Yet as geopolitical tensions and intensifying climate shocks threaten energy security, we must move beyond targets to build systems that are resilient by design.
 
🔗 Read more in the new Sustainable Energy Bulletin: The Era of Energy Security 👉 https://lnkd.in/exUQY3mf 
 
This priority of energy security was highlighted during a high-level dialogue during UNGA80 on Ukraine’s energy recovery which underlined that solidifying a green and decentralized energy system is an imperative for national security. Similarly, public and private actors reaffirmed their commitment to Mission 300 for accelerating energy access that is not only accessible but also affordable and reliable.
 
But the finance bottleneck for resilience persists: countries and companies have pledged $1.6 trillion by 2030 under Energy Compacts, yet less than 0.1% of global climate finance goes to adaptation in energy systems. We must make resilience bankable - turning protection of people and infrastructure into an investment case at scale. The future of energy security will also hinge on innovation and optimization - exactly where the triptych of digital, data, and AI is central. AI-driven risk modeling, paired with robust analytics and digital platforms, can help investors and policymakers optimize targeted financing where it is most effective.
 
As we head toward #COP30 in Brazil, progress will be measured not only by how quickly we transition to renewables but by how resilient and inclusive those systems are.

We often discuss the role of #AI in energy through percentage gains - efficiency improvements, cost reductions, predictive accuracy. But the real impact is structural: AI is enabling new market dynamics that redefine how energy systems are governed and financed.
 
The foundation is the data infrastructure: smart meters, sensors, and digital grids generate continuous insight into how electricity is actually used. This demand-side visibility creates a national load profile that can enable transformative opportunities,
 
Once governments can see real demand and private sector can act on this #data, new dynamics  emerge:
	•	Auctions can be designed around measured needs, defining clearer requirements for renewables, storage, and flexibility
	•	Investors can leverage data to lower risk and improve project bankability
	•	Markets gain credibility as public data limits discretion and reduces risk of corruption
But the same visibility that empowers can also expose vulnerabilities. Without strong governance, data monopolies, surveillance risks, and algorithmic bias could distort markets rather than open them.
 
The #energy transition will not be powered by new technologies alone, but by the intelligence and integrity of the systems that govern them. Discover how in the newest Sustainable Energy Bulletin 👉  https://lnkd.in/eBAMvFDe
 
#AI #EnergyGovernance #EnergyMarkets #EnergyTransition

caption:
What if the future of AI wasn’t measured only in breakthroughs, but also in its true environmental cost?
 
Global data centers consume about 460 TWh of electricity annually - around 1.5 % of global demand. The portion of this demand from AI is growing rapidly and could reach 85–130 TWh by 2030. If this trajectory continues, AI could emit up to 1.6 Gt CO₂e by 2035 even as its deployment in energy, food, and mobility offers potential avoidance of 3.2–5.4 Gt CO₂e annually.
 
Because #AI operates on land, water, and kilowatt-hours, its footprint is real, and growing. Unchecked growth risks worsening energy inequities: many regions already grapple with power shortages, yet AI infrastructure is concentrated in the Global North.
 
By redesigning AI to align with planetary boundaries, we can mitigate its impact:
⚡ Transition data centers to 100 % renewable energy with transparent sourcing.
💧 Innovate in cooling systems to minimize water use and recycle heat for communities
📊 Promote efficiency standards and “green AI” benchmarks to guide responsible innovation
🌐 Ensure equitable access so the Global South benefits from AI advances, not just bears the costs
 
At the same time we can leverage its system benefits:
+⚡ AI optimization has already improved renewable-grid efficiency, raising wind power’s market value by up to ~20 %.
+💧 AI-based forecasting now prevents climate damages worth up to $50 billion annually through early-warning systems.
+📊 Optimization in logistics and manufacturing has already saved over 3 million metric tons of packaging material since 2015.
+🌐 Expanding sustainable AI infrastructure can accelerate investment in low-carbon technologies, projected to require $2.4 trillion annually by 2030 in emerging economies. 
 
To explore this further, I invite you to read my latest collaborative illuminem  article with my colleague Stefano Pistolese : 👉 https://lnkd.in/eRQ6mSsB 
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #DigitalForDevelopment #AIforGood

For decades, we’ve built energy grids around industry. But what if we did the opposite, and built industry and data centers around renewable energy sources?
 
This is the idea at the center of “powershoring”, which takes the approach of placing energy at the center of development literally, turning energy geography into economic strategy.
 
🇧🇷 Brazil is already positioned to apply this strategy. After years of expanding generation capacity faster than demand, Brazil holds an electricity surplus - a rare challenge in a world of energy scarcity. Under an agenda of green neoindustrialization, regions rich in wind power are attracting new investment in energy-intensive manufacturing, linking industrial growth directly to clean energy.
 
Learn how countries are turning their just energy transitions into a foundation for industrial growth in our latest Sustainable Energy Bulletin 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBAMvFDe
 
#Powershoring #IndustrialPolicy #EnergyTransition

caption:
Its promise is immense - to decarbonize heavy industry, enable green industrialization, create inclusive jobs, and strengthen energy security - yet its trajectory remains uncertain. How can green hydrogen truly become a development pathway?
 
The task for countries is to navigate this uncertainty wisely: aligning investments with national priorities that integrate hydrogen into energy and industrial strategies which build domestic value chains, expand energy access, develop skills and jobs, and protect land, water, and biodiversity - rather than locking into extractive models.
 
Green hydrogen must serve sustainable development, not just markets. People must be at the center, with local value chains that create jobs and new industries. A priority of needs of the Planet must guide the use and preservation of water and land for long-term resilience. And Prosperity should be shared - with green hydrogen fueling industrialization, enhancing energy security, and decarbonizing growth.
 
Our new policy paper by UNDP and  TIDE Centre, University of Oxford, Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework, introduces this 3P approach - People, Planet, and Prosperity - to help countries steer green hydrogen at the right speed, time, and direction 👉 bit.ly/Green-H2
 
#GreenHydrogen #JustTransition #EnergyForDevelopment

🔸First, that digital tools are changing how we can scale resilient energy systems. Geospatial mapping, digital twins, and AI-based risk models are transforming how we can mitigate vulnerability.

These efforts are already accelerating - from solarizing hospitals and clinics in Yemen, to restoring decentralized power in Ukraine, to bringing renewable energy to crisis-affected communities across Sudan, Somalia, and the Sahel. Read more in our new Sustainable Energy Bulletin on Crisis Settings 👉 https://lnkd.in/eBAMvFDe

Even as renewable investments surge globally, now exceeding USD 1.8 trillion annually and outpacing fossil fuels two-to-one, overall energy investment across Eurasia has fallen by nearly 30% since 2015.
 
Yet the region holds vast untapped potential. Regional cooperation is already reshaping its energy future, such as the recent MoU between Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan to advance the Caspian Green Energy Corridor, creating a new axis for renewable power trade, jobs, and local value chains.
 
This region will be the backdrop for this year’s 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, North Macedonia, where I joining dialogues o how too translate such initiatives from ambition to implementation - scaled through digital, financial, and human capital:
 
1️⃣ Digital Transformation

Now that the dust has <mostly> settled from #UNGA80, #ClimateWeekNYC and the whirlwind that was New York in September… I’ve finally stolen a moment to reflect - and, yes, to break my deliberate socials silence once again(!)

This year felt different.

Maybe it was because the UN turned 80, reminding us that while institutions age, ideas must stay young… Or maybe it was because the global conversations on AI, energy and inclusion finally began to feel more like collaboration than competition…🤷‍♂️

One thing that I am 100% certain on, is that I was very fortunate to join and host some truly powerful discussions - from the AI & Energy Justice panel at the SDG7 Action Forum (with Rana Ghoneim, Casey Weston, Dominique Souris, Ava Strasser and @Alankrita Dayal) to dialogues at Goals House, with IEEE Young Professionals & IEEE Power & Energy Society, and across Climate Week NYC.

Each space had its own rhythm - but one message echoed through them all:

The future of sustainable energy won’t just be engineered; it will be co-created.🌐

Our AI panel left a lasting mark. We talked about how artificial intelligence could unlock 175GW of hidden grid capacity - the equivalent of powering Brazil. But we also asked the harder questions: who benefits from those efficiencies… Who ACTUALLY gets left behind? If AI is to become the engines of the energy transition, it must also become an engine of justice.

But the real highlight wasn’t the stage time; it was the debates away from the spotlight. New ideas, innovations and shared purposes. Open, direct and (sometimes) cutting discussions that keeps our work relevant!

And that’s also what made Goals House special. Amid the chaos of New York, it offered something rare: space to think differently. To slow down enough to connect the dots between climate, innovation and equity - and to remember that progress happens not only on stages, but in the small, cross-sector moments of shared purpose.

Now, with #COP30 only weeks away, and the United Nations turning 80 today, it feels like the right moment to pause - to take stock of how far we’ve come and to think honestly about where we’re heading next.

So here’s to slowing down, asking better questions and keeping space for the quiet moments - because that’s where real progress often begins.

“Energy resilience” is not a uniform concept - it reflects distinct structural realities across regions and context.

🔵 In many crisis settings, it refers to continuity under disruption - distributed solar and storage systems keeping essential services operational amid physical and cyber risks.

🟠 In Central Asia, it implies interdependence - regional power pools projected to reduce generation costs by 8 percent through shared reserves and cross-border balancing.

🟢 In Sub-Saharan Africa, it denotes reliability - systems that can sustain demand growth and climate stress while extending access to those still excluded.

🔴 In Latin America and the Caribbean, it means protection - coastal grids redesigned with underground cabling and wind assets certified for category-five storms.

Yet, less than 1 percent of global adaptation finance is directed toward energy systems, despite investments in resilience returning multiples in gains in avoided losses and productivity.

Energy resilience binds infrastructure to governance, data to finance, and technology to social stability. In development terms, it is the capacity of an energy system to maintain function, equity, and trust when the environment around it changes.

Across Africa, the energy revolution is accelerating. Investments in renewables have nearly tripled since 2019, and solar is now the least-cost source of power in most African markets.

This transformation holds immense opportunity. Africa possesses around 60% of the world’s best solar resources, yet only 1% of installed solar capacity. Unlocking this potential could power homes and industries, create over 3 million new green jobs by 2030, and drive inclusive growth from the ground up. But for this revolution to deliver lasting development impact, it must be just - anchored in governance, innovation, and digital empowerment.

1️⃣ Strengthen Governance
Establish transparent, accountable institutions with continent-wide standards for procurement, land use, and revenue sharing to ensure renewable wealth translates into jobs, community benefits, and public trust.

2️⃣ Mobilize Innovative Finance
Move from isolated projects to bankable investment pipelines. Blended finance, risk guarantees, and local-currency mechanism can de-risk markets and crowd in private capital. By mobilizing the estimated $190 billion per year needed by 2030, African countries can power inclusive industrialization and deliver universal energy access.

3️⃣ Harness Digital, Data & AI
Leverage AI and digital tools to make systems smarter and more affordable. Predictive analytics can cut project costs by 15%, and generative AI - if locally embedded in value chains - could unlock over $100 billion in annual economic value.

Africa’s energy revolution is not a story of scarcity but one of sovereign opportunity. With the right governance, finance, and digital backbone, the continent can transform its renewable wealth into sustainable development and true energy independence.

#EnergyRevolution #JustEnergyTransition

caption:
The energy transition is about more than climate - it is about sustainable jobs, sovereignty, and inclusive economic growth. We need to refocus on human development at the center of energy.

Clean #energy now employs 35 million people worldwide, yet women represent only 32% of that workforce. Global investment has surpassed USD 2 trillion, outpacing fossil fuels—but translating this momentum into affordable, reliable, and inclusive energy remains the real challenge.

Smarter, decentralized systems can shift this balance. #Digital tools, #AI, and data-driven management can optimize demand, reduce losses, and improve reliability—helping every unit of energy power growth and resilience. Smarter grids alone could cut 1 gigaton of CO₂ annually and lower peak loads by 8–12% by 2050, while digitally enabled efficiency in public buildings can reduce energy use by up to 50%.

Yet energy and digital transitions are advancing faster than the systems that govern them and mitigate their risks. The priority now is pairing governance with institutional capacity and national innovation systems to make energy systems fairer, smarter, and more resilient.

This week in Skopje, I am pushing to advance these priorities during the 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development, focusing on scaling up action toward aligning innovation, governance, and human development for a just energy future.

#EnergyForDevelopment #DigitalTransition #UAEConsensus #IFESD

caption:
Globally, renewable-power capacity is projected to increase by around 4,600 GW between 2025 and 2030. The opportunity now is to ensure our digital, data, and human systems can absorb this growth—by strengthening coordination, governance, and skills to drive the structural change required for a just energy transition.

Today during Day 2 of the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I moderated a discussion centered on how digitalization, data, and AI can help overcome these limits—and the new vulnerabilities they create.

1️⃣ First, the main bottleneck for renewable adoption is now absorption capacity. Grids cannot integrate trillions of USD of investment in renewables without parallel investment in #digital coordination, data systems, and human expertise. If a solar panel lacks a sensor, it effectively doesn’t exist to the system.

2️⃣ Second, #AI must remain a decision-support system, not an autonomous agent. Human oversight and digital skills are essential—especially as clean-energy jobs now account for more than half of the world’s 67 million energy-sector jobs.

3️⃣ Third, a just energy transition requires algorithmic justice. Without inclusive data governance and intentional design, algorithms trained on developed grids will reinforce the very access gaps they could help close.

4️⃣ Fourth, flexibility remains the cheapest untapped resource. Yet, fragmented regulation still blocks dynamic tariffs and peer-to-peer trading. Digital tools can help realign incentives for consumers to use energy when renewables are abundant. Unreliable grids could otherwise cost developing economies $1.3 trillion in lost output by 2030.

Ultimately, the digital, #data, and AI revolution must serve human development. These tools are already creating new market dynamics that are redefining how energy systems are governed and financed, but we need to always be vigilant to preserve our focus on what actually matters: people.

#DigitalTransition #EnergyTransition #AIForEnergy #IFESD

caption:
Today during the third day of the International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, I joined young leaders for the “Youth in Energy” session to discuss their key role in shaping the revolution of energy, development, and digitalization — not as the generation of the future, but of the present. Some key actions that arose from the discussion included:

1️⃣ Invest in youth as the #digital natives of the energy transition
The world’s 1.8 billion young people are increasingly central as a creative power accelerating the energy revolution. In the Global South, entrepreneurs are three times more likely to start a business than peers in the Global North — yet over 90% of these ventures remain in informal markets. In Latin America, 36% of new entrepreneurs are under 34, but only 5% of youth-founded firms last beyond three years. Investing in reliable energy access, digital infrastructure, and early-stage finance can turn survival enterprises into scalable green innovators.

2️⃣ Build national innovation ecosystems that link ideas to markets
Youth have the creativity; what’s missing are the structures that connect their ideas to opportunity. Less than 1% of finance reaches youth-led solutions, and less than 1 in 8 young workers has formal training in green or digital skills. Governments must align education, finance, and entrepreneurship policies into national innovation ecosystems — frameworks of actors, institutions, and policies that generate, implement, and diffuse new technologies and knowledge.

3️⃣ Catalyze #youth entrepreneurship to become engines of jobs and inclusion
The task is not only to train youth but to enable them to create markets — through public procurement, incubators, and demand-driven programs. In Ghana, an agritech initiative is training 300,000 young people in AI, biotechnology, and green innovation to power modern value chains. Replicating such models can turn youth enterprises into digitally-enabled impact that can create inclusive jobs.

When young innovators can access finance and markets within larger innovation systems, they become true partners in accelerating the just energy transition.

#YouthInEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #IFESD

caption:
The energy transition is about acceleration, how quickly we can scale renewable integration. Digital, #data, and AI enable that speed — but we must not trade quickness for justice.

In Skopje this week during the 14th International Forum on Energy for Sustainable Development, I questioned, how can we shift the conversation from digital optimization to digital integrity?

#AI can now forecast grid conditions in near real time, anticipate renewable variability, and optimize power flows across billions of data points. Predictive analytics alone could unlock 175 GW of transmission capacity and cut peak loads by 12% — proof that digital systems can make grids both efficient and smarter.

But the faster we move, the less time we leave to verify the quality, origin, and bias of the data itself. In 2024, 4,875 cyber incidents were recorded across the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors — a sharp reminder that every new sensor and data link can also be an entry point for risk. And as 83 percent of urban residents are online compared with just 48 percent of rural populations, the same connectivity gaps that divide access also shape the data that train AI models.

Without open, interoperable, and verifiable systems, we risk building a transition that is more efficient — but not more equitable.

The technologies exist. What’s missing is sustained political will and coordination to ensure that data, AI, and markets work for people, not just performance. The #energy transition will not be powered by technology alone — but by the integrity of the systems and data it rests on.

#DigitalTransition #AIforEnergy #EnergyGovernance IFESD – 14 / 14th International Forum on Energy for sustainable development _14

🇬🇪 Georgia is harnessing renewable energy, digital systems, and cross-border connectivity to power new era of regional development.

During my discussion with Ms. Inga Pkhaladze , Deputy Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, we reflected on how Georgia is accelerating its energy transition with both speed and integrity.

Georgia is positioning itself as a renewable energy bridge to Europe. The Black Sea Submarine Cable, a ~1.3 GW high-voltage link between Georgia and Romania, will redefine regional energy trade, and Azerbaijan’s parallel plan for an additional 4 GW connection could transform the Black Sea into a new corridor of renewable exchange connecting the Caucasus, the EU, and Türkiye.

Beyond the grid, #Georgia’s ambitions stretch further — toward becoming a regional digital hub for #energy, expanding battery storage and recycling to build resilience, and oppportunities to explore green hydrogen for domestic use and export. Our discussion focused on the next phase: ensuring that new markets are cyber-secure, data-transparent, and ready for balancing, storage, and cross-border trade. 

Georgia is expanding off-grid solar solutions to bring electricity to remote communities, yet as solar panels arrive, the next challenge begins: ensuring local capacity to maintain them and to ensure they bring not only access but also build livelihood. harnessing data to identify data poverty and opportunities 

As the Deputy Minister put it, the question is not just how to generate more power — but how to generate more opportunity.

Douglas Webb Omar/Memo Tsereteli Ivana Zivkovic  

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #DigitalEnergy

caption:
⚡ Energy finance is about architecture — building systems that investors and citizens can both trust. In 2024, global renewable investment reached USD 624 billion, yet less than 15 percent reached developing economies outside China — and only 2–3 percent to Africa. 

The task ahead is not just to mobilize more capital, but to unlocking opportunities for clean energy where the need and potential are greatest. That requires financial and institutional systems capable of structuring, verifying, and absorbing investments at scale.

At the 14th International Forum on #Energy for Sustainable Development in Skopje, leaders from across regions agreed: capital follows credibility. A few ways they converged on we can do this:

1️⃣ Build national financing ecosystems, not fragmented projects, that can enable bankability of projects.
Energy-efficiency funds in Kosovo, Jordan, and Moldova show these financial mechanisms. The key for bankability starts with structuring projects with clear revenue models, transparent governance, and measurable performance to minimize investor risk.

2️⃣ Aggregate small projects to match investor logic.
Commercial lenders seek diversification. Aggregating small clean-energy projects — solar rooftops, retrofits, micro-grids — into verified portfolios lowers risk premiums and opens new credit lines for municipalities and SMEs. Inclusion also remains the ultimate de-risking strategy, as funds led by women in risk-management roles have proven on average lower default rates.

3️⃣ Embed data integrity into all financial instruments as the foundation of credibility.
Accurate baselines, open performance data, and auditability are now prerequisites for green finance. In Africa, the @AFREC Energy Information System is helping lenders quantify risk and track national progress with greater confidence. Digital monitoring and AI-driven analytics can accelerate access to finance — but ensuring the datasets they are built on are equitable remains central.

The real measure of progress will be how fast we can turn global liquidity into local legitimacy — through institutions capable of absorbing, managing, and sustaining capital.

#EnergyFinance #JustEnergyTransition #FinanceForDevelopment #EnergyForDevelopment #IFESD_14

Join me tomorrow the Global Sustainable Education & Leadership Conference 2025 in London, where I will be speaking on “From Renewable Wealth to Industrial Strength.”
 
Together, we’ll explore how partnerships, pipelines, and policies can turn ambition into action; driving innovation, sustainability and equity in energy access. caption:
Delighted to deliver remarks this morning at the Global Sustainable Education & Leadership (G-SEL) Conference 2025 on how we can turn ambition into action - and sunlight into shared prosperity.
 
Africa holds 60% of the world’s best solar potential, yet attracts  < 2% of global renewable investment. The issue isn’t resources; it’s the cost of capital and the confidence to invest. That’s why this conversation matters. Because unlocking Africa’s energy future isn’t just about power - it’s about people, production & partnerships:
 
1️⃣ Finance must be fair. Africa pays around $80 billion more annually in borrowing costs - not for poor performance, but for outdated perceptions of risk. Derisked finance is fair finance: built on trust, data and shared responsibility.
 
2️⃣ Energy must build industry. The continent holds 30% of the world’s critical mineral reserves but processes < 5% locally. Turning energy access into industrial strength means powering factories, not just homes.
 
3️⃣ Industry must create dignity. With 360 million young Africans entering the workforce in the next decade, inclusion is not a social goal - it’s an economic imperative. When women and youth lead, productivity and innovation rise together.
 
If the first industrial revolution was powered by coal, Africa’s will be powered by cooperation; between nations, investors, innovators and communities. Let’s move from potential to progress, and from progress to prosperity that endures.🌐🙏
 
#EnergyForDevelopment  #GSELC2025 #EnergyAccess #Sustainability

caption:
Last week, I had the opportunity to sit down with RASHID ABDALLAH, Executive Director of the African Energy Commission of the African Union  (AFREC), to discuss how data is reshaping Africa’s energy transition.

Data availability goes beyond merely monitoring progress; it plays a crucial role in de-risking investments and assisting governments and development partners in targeting projects and programs where they are most needed.

However, over 40 percent of African countries still depend on outdated or incomplete electricity data, which limits their ability to design effective policies or attract financing.

Since 2012, the African #Energy Information System, led by AFREC, has been enhancing the collection, validation, and dissemination of national energy data across the continent. Through capacity-building for national focal points, harmonization of data standards, and partnerships with regional and international organizations, AFREC is steadily improving the quality, credibility, and comparability of Africa’s energy data landscape.

In my discussion with Rashid, we explored how this initiative can align with UNDP ’s efforts to utilize geospatial analytics to move beyond binary indicators of energy access, aiming to understand how, where, and how effectively energy is used. After all, what does “access” mean if the energy is neither affordable nor reliable?

What innovations do you see as most promising for improving energy data availability? How can we ensure that #data-driven energy strategies translate into affordability, reliability, and equity? 

#JustEnergyTransition #DataForDevelopment #UNDP #AFREC #EnergyData Ahunna Eziakonwa Damilola Ogunbiyi Francesco La Camera Marcos Neto

🌍 As COP30 opens in Belém this week, the call to triple renewable energy capacity and accelerate just energy transitions has never been more urgent. AI and digital technologies are reshaping how energy is produced, traded, and managed. But as systems become more digitalized, the risks also increase, spanning data governance, algorithmic control, cybersecurity, and corruption in emerging value chains.

In 2024 alone, nearly 4,900 cyber incidents hit the energy and critical-infrastructure sectors. Addressing these risks is essential to ensuring that digital and AI-enabled energy systems expand equitable access rather than concentrate advantage. Today, we are pleased to share a new UNDP policy paper: 

 ⚡ Energy, Digital, and Anticorruption: Leveraging AI and Digital Innovation for Governance in the Just Energy Transition 👉 https://lnkd.in/eCM--xkt

It offers actionable pathways on how AI and digital innovation can power cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy systems:

1️⃣ Boost public-sector capacity. Bridging the AI gap between regulators and companies is key to fair and accountable energy markets, especially as global investment in the energy transition is projected to reach $4 trillion annually by 2030.
2️⃣ Increase transparency in markets and supply chains. India is using digital tools to boost transparency, reduce energy losses that once exceeded USD 16 billion annually, and attract new investment in the power sector.
3️⃣ Enable smarter energy planning. Combining AI and blockchain is optimizing energy demand, production, and distribution. In the UAE, Dubai’s state-owned utility DEWA uses AI-driven smart grids to predict electricity demand and manage supply more efficiently.
4️⃣ Mitigate corruption in critical minerals and decentralized energy. With demand for minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt projected to surge by up to 900% over the coming decades, responsible digital governance is vital to curb corruption and ensure sustainable access.

This policy paper offers practical pathways and examples from Brazil, Estonia, India, Ukraine, and others to illustrate how digital innovation and integrity systems can support cleaner, fairer, and more accountable energy transitions across countries.
 
#EnergyGovernance #AIandDigitalInnovation #JustEnergyTransition #UNDP COP30 Brazil

Its promise is immense - to decarbonize heavy industry, enable green industrialization, create inclusive jobs, and strengthen energy security - yet its trajectory remains uncertain. How can green hydrogen truly become a development pathway?
 
The task for countries is to navigate this uncertainty wisely: aligning investments with national priorities that integrate hydrogen into energy and industrial strategies which build domestic value chains, expand energy access, develop skills and jobs, and protect land, water, and biodiversity - rather than locking into extractive models.
 
Green hydrogen must serve sustainable development, not just markets. People must be at the center, with local value chains that create jobs and new industries. A priority of needs of the Planet must guide the use and preservation of water and land for long-term resilience. And Prosperity should be shared - with green hydrogen fueling industrialization, enhancing energy security, and decarbonizing growth.
 
Our new policy paper by UNDP  and TIDE Centre, University of Oxford , Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human Development-Centred Framework, introduces this 3P approach - People, Planet, and Prosperity - to help countries steer green hydrogen at the right speed, time, and direction 👉 bit.ly/Green-H2
COP30 Brazil

caption:
Green #hydrogen is projected to be able to reach 7-8% of final energy demand by 2050, more than double the needs of the entire shipping sector today.

But hydrogen must complement—never replace—development objectives.
 
At today’s #COP30 dialogue organized by the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition  and Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) , I steered the discussion to explore how to ensure green hydrogen supports national development priorities, protects ecosystems, and creates shared prosperity.

1️⃣ Align hydrogen with national development priorities:
When tied to national strategies, these investments can decarbonize hard-to-abate sectors and build local industry and energy security. Without this, they risk becoming extractive, with value exported and impacts retained.

2️⃣ Strengthen governance across the land–water–energy system
Hydrogen is not a standalone investment—it depends on water resources, land availability, and grid capacity. In Namibia, a 2-million-tonne project would require 18 million m³ of water annually, equivalent to the needs of more than 250,000 people. Countries need integrated planning, clear regulation, and national innovation systems.

3️⃣ Ensure hydrogen creates local prosperity, not only export pathways:
Not every country can or should pursue large-scale hydrogen. The right pathway depends on water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities.  Where hydrogen is viable, it must deliver domestic value: but in local jobs, resilient value chains, and equitable benefits.

These priorities underpin the UNDP –TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  report “Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen”, which introduces a People–Planet–Prosperity framework to help countries determine where hydrogen adds genuine value: 🔗📘 bit.ly/Green-H2
 
#GreenHydrogen #EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition #SDG7 #COP30 COP30 Brazil

caption:
At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat for a new-era partnerships, stronger national delivery capacity, and smart financing architectures.

The success of Africa’s energy transformation will not be measured by kilometres of cable laid, but by households switching on lights, health centres powering lifesaving equipment, and businesses growing with reliable, affordable electricity. Africa’s infrastructure is expanding fast—yet millions of connected households remain in the dark. Not only because the grid never reached them, but because they cannot afford to use it. 220 million Africans cannot afford basic electricity consumption, and 400 million cannot afford 500 kWh/year, barely a tenth of an average European household.

This affordability gap is one of the defining challenges for Africa’s economic future—but also a real opportunity to shape a new energy paradigm: one where investments are targeted, financing costs fall, and partnerships drive scalable, country-led solutions.

At the Africa Investment Forum’s Mission 300 Day in Rabat, I reaffirmed UNDP’s commitment to universal electrification in line with the UN-Energy Pledge. I had the pleasure to reflect with Aboubacar Said Anli, Minister of Energy, Water, and Hydrocarbons, #Comoros, Nialé Kaba, Minister of Minister of Planning and Development, #Côte d’Ivoire, Michael Franz , Team Leader, GET. Invest and moderated by Daniel Schroth Director at African Development Bank Group  , on how to ensure electricity is not only available but affordable, inclusive, and transformative:

1️⃣ Shift from counting connections to measuring development outcomes — in health, education, livelihoods, and productivity.
2️⃣ Reduce the cost of capital, which is 3–4 times higher in Africa; narrowing this gap can cut project costs by 15–25%.
3️⃣ Strengthen partnerships across governments, DFIs, development partners, and the private sector to align financing and delivery at scale.

This is where Mission 300 becomes catalytic. With coordinated compacts, unified delivery frameworks, and blended investment pipelines, #M300 shows how strategic partnerships can amplify impact, accelerate financing, and translate ambition into real improvements in people’s lives. UNDP stands with the The World Bank , AfDB, and all Mission 300 partners in transforming energy systems into engines of development, inclusion, and resilience.
Kevin KARIUKI The Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet

caption:
Join me virtually on 28th November at the Forum on Sustainable and Inclusive Energy Transitions in Seoul, where I’ll be speaking on “10th Anniversary of SDG 7: Making Energy Access A Reality.”
 
As we mark ten years of SDG 7, the need for accelerated action is clear. Around the world, 666 million people still lack electricity and 2.1 billion rely on traditional cooking fuels, not because solutions are absent, but because investment, inclusion and scalable delivery models have not yet reached the communities that need them most.
 
At the Forum, together we’ll explore how multi-stakeholder partnerships, impact-aligned investment and community-driven innovation can expand clean energy access and turn global ambition into concrete development outcomes. Ultimately, this discussion is about ensuring the energy transition delivers real benefits: powering livelihoods, strengthening essential services, and expanding opportunities of everyone, everywhere.
 
When inclusion sits at the center of the transition, clean energy becomes a catalyst for global social and economic progress - not just a climate goal.
 
If you’re in Seoul or joining remotely, be sure to join us. ⬇️
 
📆 28 November 2025
📍 Maple Hall, The Plaza Hotel
🕙 10:00 AM – 12:30 PM (GMT+9)
🔗 Register: https://lnkd.in/eTEvSJXW
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #InclusiveTransition #DCW2025

caption:
Energy took center stage during COP30 Brazil, but while the Belém Package moved negotiations forward, calls from 80+ countries to include phase-out language on fossil fuels didn’t make the final text. As SG Guterres warned — a 1.5°C overshoot is humanity’s red line.
 
Negotiations set the ambition, but implementation will define success. To meet UAE Consensus targets, the world needs 1,122 GW of new renewables every year from 2025 — a 16.6% annual growth rate — even as 90% of renewables were cheaper than fossil fuels in 2024. The challenge isn’t only speed, but who benefits and who carries the cost of this transition.
 
The Baku-to-Belém roadmap aims to scale climate finance to $1.3T annually by 2035, triple adaptation finance, and institutionalize a Just Transition Work Program. Yet efficiency gains remain slow with only 1% improvement in 2024.
 
This is where #digitalization and #AI can accelerate progress — if designed for people and planet. The new Technology Implementation Program, especially if linked to the idea of planetary intelligence, can offer a path to align clean energy, digital systems, and nature rather than trade between them.
 
Read more in The Energy Revolution: Beyond Humanity’s Red Line  👉 https://lnkd.in/eSZqrmks
 
#JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment

caption:
A just energy transition is not simply a technological shift. It is a development strategy. — it is social policy, industrial policy, climate policy, and a development priority all at once. 

This week, I’m with @UNDP colleagues in Dakar, Senegal, alongside 20+ country offices, energy experts, financiers and development practitioners to focus on what matters most: turning clean energy into development outcomes. 

Africa holds the world’s greatest renewable potential — including 60% of global high-quality solar and nearly 8,000 GW of solar capacity — and 30% of critical mineral reserves, positioning the continent to lead the green industrial economy.

How can we re-think Africa’s economic transformation through a just energy transition? 

Three opportunities will define its transition:
 
1️⃣ First, Africa is becoming central to the global clean-energy economy, building on green industry. Africa can go behind producing clean power — it can also industrialize it, from agro-processing to e-mobility to mineral value chains. A transformation that could save 3.7 million lives every year. 

2️⃣  Second, de-risking is essential to unlock finance at scale. Africa needs USD 190–200 billion annually for energy investment, yet risk is perceived at 2–3× reality. Blended finance, guarantees, and policy reform can flip this equation and turn pipelines into projects. 

3️⃣  Third, digitalization and AI make this transformation even more powerful, as scaling energy access is an economic imperative, which can reduce technical and commercial losses by up to 20-30%. Access must move from pilots to performance — especially for clean cooking and for deploying digital innovations that boost efficiency and productive use. 

#Digital and #AI tools can lower costs, improve planning, and support de-risking — but they are enablers, not substitutes. Community engagement, local capacity, and strong institutions remain the backbone of a just energy transition, especially where digital ecosystems are still emerging. 

Energy is ultimately about people, jobs, and dignity. This week in Dakar, with UNDP  colleagues and partners across Africa, we are working to turn the continent’s renewable wealth into universal access, green industries, and inclusive growth. 

#EnergyForDevelopment

3️⃣  Third, digitalization and AI make this transformation even more powerful, as scaling energy access is an economic imperative, which can reduce technical and commercial losses by up to 20-30%. Access must move from pilots to performance — especially for clean cooking and for deploying digital innovations that boost efficiency and productive use. 

#Digital and #AI tools can lower costs, improve planning, and support de-risking — but they are enablers, not substitutes. Community engagement, local capacity, and strong institutions remain the backbone of a just energy transition, especially where digital ecosystems are still emerging. 

Energy is ultimately about people, jobs, and dignity. This week in Dakar, with UNDP  colleagues and partners across Africa, we are working to turn the continent’s renewable wealth into universal access, green industries, and inclusive growth.

The 'Smart City' has been closely linked with #energy since the term was introduced. From smart energy meters, to the role of Big Data for energy and grid management. I've been getting more and more questions about what a 'smart' city looks like and wanted to re-share this article I co-authored with Calum Handforth  a while back. We argue that we need fewer 'smart' cities, and more 'smarter' cities. Smarter cities which:

* Put people at the heart of urban and technology planning and deployment. Not cities that try to retro-fit tech and energy projects and programmes around perceived citizen needs.
* Use a broad tech and innovation toolkit, and don’t just chase the latest innovation. For example, Big Data is important, but so too is the 'Thick Data' which helps us to learn more about energy consumers - or those that are energy-poor.
* Focus on outcomes, and not just the rollout of solutions - and, especially, we need ‘Smarter Cities’ which invest in the ‘connective tissue’ that creates meaningful urban spaces and places. We don’t want cities to just become ‘platforms’ of ‘use-cases’.

When writing this article, we were also inspired by the exciting and important opportunities for 'smart cities' in the Global North to learn from their counterparts in the Global South. 

And this is particularly relevant for energy, when so many innovations - including decentralised renewable energy, pay-as-you-go solar and other innovative business models, and frugal energy innovations - could be as relevant in New York as they are in New Delhi. 

Let me know your thoughts! https://lnkd.in/ghZnHY7g

This week, I very much look forward to joining global energy leaders in Abu Dhabi for the 16th Session of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly. It is an important opportunity to learn from, and connect with, Heads of State, Ministers, innovators and investors, and energy decision-makers.

This year, our focus will centre around the theme 'Powering Humanity: Renewable Energy for Shared Prosperity’ and there are three particularly important priorities that I want to share in these discussions:

1️⃣ Digitalization and AI: Ensuring that the energy–AI nexus accelerates a just energy transition by scaling finance, innovation, and future-ready clean energy jobs.

2️⃣ Finance and partnerships: Identifying opportunities to strengthen cooperation across governments, finance, and the private sector to mobilize capital and de-risk investment pathways for a just and inclusive transition.

3️⃣ Youth and inclusion: Creating platforms for young leaders from LDCs, SIDS, and developing countries to actively shape the future of sustainable energy through innovation and policy engagement.

At the start of a new year, we need now more than ever to turn global ambition into concrete development outcomes. And ensure that the energy transition delivers economic inclusion, equity, and human wellbeing.

📍 Abu Dhabi, UAE
📆 10–12 January 2026

#IRENA16A #EnergyForDevelopment

caption:
Digitalization and #AI are reshaping the clean energy transition, raising critical questions about skills, inclusion, and opportunity.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, I joined a series of sessions exploring how digitalization and AI can strengthen integrity and efficiency, empower youth, and shape the future of renewable energy jobs. I just wanted to re-share my three reflections: 

1️⃣ Innovation in #energy is not new
While digital and AI tools are accelerating change, innovation has long driven progress in the energy sector. We have fantastic innovation talent and heritage within and across the sector - and huge opportunities to amplify this. We need to explore and embrace new tech and new opportunities, but also build on our existing learning too. 

2️⃣ A broad and future-ready talent pipeline is essential
'#Digital', 'AI', and 'energy' are not discrete or homogenous jobs or sectors. They are wide-ranging and interlinked - and even inter-disciplinary. So, when we're talking about shaping the jobs of the future, we need to think broadly. There isn't a single 'energy' job, but a whole pipeline of different opportunities and entry-points. 

3️⃣ Energy talent is everywhere
All voices need to be represented and participate in energy policy, design, and delivery. Women are still under-represented in the sector, whilst the Global South is home to phenomenal talent building and deploying energy systems and solutions. We need to empower, platform, champion, and support this next generation of energy talent - wherever it's found. 


#IRENA16A #EnergyForDevelopment

caption:
Sustainable energy is not a nice-to-have. It is a catalyst for societies and economies, and a core driver of 21st-century industrial policy, growth, and development.

Since 2015, progress has been real. Energy transition investment reached a record USD 2.4 trillion in 2024, with renewables attracting nearly twice the funding of fossil fuels. Global electricity access rose from 87 to 92 percent between 2015 and 2023, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, ahead of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum, I reflected on where #SDG7 ⚡️stands today. Three priorities stood out.

1️⃣ A just energy transition is a people’s transition.
Renewables already support more than 16 million jobs and could more than double by 2030, but skills are not keeping pace. Without urgent investment in training and stronger South-South cooperation, workforce gaps risk becoming a binding constraint on long-term development.

2️⃣ Energy security must sit at the core of SDG7.
Diversified energy systems strengthen economic resilience, protect public finances, and reduce exposure to external shocks. In many fossil-fuel-producing countries, public revenues still depend heavily on oil, gas, or coal. Clean energy transitions can reduce import dependence, improve efficiency, and strengthen economic stability rather than create new vulnerabilities.

3️⃣ Leveraging #digitalization and #AI as enablers of the transition.
From smart grids to geospatial data, digital tools improve efficiency, reduce losses from unreliable grids, and lower investment risk. As AI becomes a growing energy consumer, its benefits will depend on alignment with clean power expansion, grid investment, and clear regulatory frameworks, especially where electricity systems are already constrained.

#IRENA16A #SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment

Sustainable energy is not a nice-to-have. It is a catalyst for societies and economies, and a core driver of 21st-century industrial policy, growth, and development.

Since 2015, progress has been real. Energy transition investment reached a record USD 2.4 trillion in 2024, with renewables attracting nearly twice the funding of fossil fuels. Global electricity access rose from 87 to 92 percent between 2015 and 2023, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, ahead of the 2026 High-Level Political Forum, I reflected on where #SDG7 ⚡️stands today. Three priorities stood out.

1️⃣ A just energy transition is a people’s transition.
Renewables already support more than 16 million jobs and could more than double by 2030, but skills are not keeping pace. Without urgent investment in training and stronger South-South cooperation, workforce gaps risk becoming a binding constraint on long-term development.

2️⃣ Energy security must sit at the core of SDG7.
Diversified energy systems strengthen economic resilience, protect public finances, and reduce exposure to external shocks. In many fossil-fuel-producing countries, public revenues still depend heavily on oil, gas, or coal. Clean energy transitions can reduce import dependence, improve efficiency, and strengthen economic stability rather than create new vulnerabilities.

3️⃣ Leveraging #digitalization and #AI as enablers of the transition.
From smart grids to geospatial data, digital tools improve efficiency, reduce losses from unreliable grids, and lower investment risk. As AI becomes a growing energy consumer, its benefits will depend on alignment with clean power expansion, grid investment, and clear regulatory frameworks, especially where electricity systems are already constrained.

#IRENA16A #SDG7 #EnergyForDevelopment

For Small Island Developing States 🏝️, the energy transition is not just about reforming energy systems. It is about economic stability, climate resilience, and national sovereignty. With renewables now cheaper than fossil fuels across most island grids, clean energy is no longer a cost—it is the smartest macro-economic choice.

Many #SIDS import the vast majority of their energy through fossil fuels. Around 60% import at least 90% of their energy, and in countries like the Maldives, fuel imports absorb more than 10% of GDP, reaching up to 16% across SIDS in some years. This dependence exposes economies to price volatility, supply disruptions, and extreme weather.

At the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly, I discussed how SIDS are not waiting to transition — they are already leading it. Out of necessity and innovation, they are building power systems designed for climate resilience, energy independence, and the water-energy-food nexus, from solar-powered desalination to resilient island microgrids.

The real bottleneck today is not technology — it is finance. What SIDS need are bankable investment pathways that combine concessional capital, guarantees, and risk-sharing instruments to crowd in private investors at scale. This is where digital# data and #AI become transformative: by improving demand forecasting, data transparency, grid management, and real-time performance tracking, they reduce uncertainty, lower the cost of capital, and turn small, fragmented projects into investable portfolios.

So the question is no longer whether SIDS should transition.
It is how fast we can align #finance, guarantees, and digital intelligence to unlock clean-energy investments that match their ambition — and their urgency.
#EnergyForDevelopment
#RisingUpForSIDS
#IRENA 16

caption:
The #AI era and the energy transition are advancing rapidly –– but unequally. 565 million people in Sub-Saharan Africa still lack electricity, and 900 million rely on biomass. Whilst annual data center spending to fuel the AI boom could require investments up to USD 7 trillion by 2030.

But improving the alignment of these 21st century trends could lead to important impact. 

When planned together, digital infrastructure and AI-enabled innovation can anchor new renewable generation, create reliable offtake, and catalyze local innovation ecosystems. 

What does AI mean for development if it does not change how people access energy, cook, or economic opportunities? During a Ministerial Address at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Assembly, I delved into what development-centered and meaningful AI-energy alignment looks like: 

1️⃣ AI is accelerating renewable deployment by turning planning into precision delivery: AI-enabled forecasting, digital twins, and grid analytics improve dispatch accuracy by 20-30% and cut curtailment by 10-12%, enabling faster integration of wind and solar at scale.

2️⃣ Digital systems are converting efficiency gains into fiscal space for access and inclusion: Energy inefficiency still drives nearly 60% of global energy losses, costing developing economies up to USD 1.3 trillion by 2030. Even a 10% efficiency gain, enabled by AI-based demand management and predictive maintenance, can unlock billions in savings.

3️⃣ Livelihood creation through productive use of energy: When energy and digital transitions converge, they create jobs, incomes, and development. And as clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for economic transformation.

With this emerging technology, we have the opportunity to revolutionize our energy systems, but only if AI is deliberately aligned with access, affordability, and resilience, rather than layered onto existing inequalities.

Join me tomorrow at the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)  Pavilion at the World Future Energy Summit where UNDP  alongside our convening partners will host the high-level side event “Bridging the Gap: Financing a Just and Inclusive Energy Transition.”

At a time when global clean energy investment has reached record highs, the distribution of capital tells a different story. Less than 15% of investment reaches developing economies outside China, and just 2% flows to Africa. Meanwhile, rising debt distress and constrained fiscal space are limiting the ability of many countries to invest in the very transition that could drive sustainable growth.

During this session, we’ll explore how innovative financing solutions - such as blended finance, de-risking instruments and debt-alleviation mechanisms - can help unlock capital at scale, while ensuring energy transition investments deliver real social, economic and environmental benefits. This conversation is about moving from ambition to action, and aligning climate goals with fiscal realities.

When finance is structured to work for vulnerable countries and communities, clean energy can become a powerful driver of resilience, opportunity and shared prosperity.

If you’re attending #WEFS, be sure to join us ⬇️

📆 15 January 2026
📍 IRENA Pavilion, ADNEC Centre Abu Dhabi

{"@type": "WebPage", "author": {"name": "Khaled Alazbe", "image": {"url": "https://media.licdn.com/dms/image/v2/D4D03AQHOnS93E7V7RQ/profile-displayphoto-shrink_400_400/profile-displayphoto-shrink_400_400/0/1701258421969?e=2147483647&v=beta&t=dOt92ruxLbDkKRUtW6KwuzbLe6RdOOz-rt9Doz6TUCo", "@type": "ImageObject"}, "url": "https://ae.linkedin.com/in/khaledalazbe", "@type": "Person", "interactionStatistic": {"@type": "InteractionCounter", "interactionType": "http://schema.org/FollowAction", "userInteractionCount": 3496}}, "headline": "Over the 8th and 9th of January, I participated in the 8th IRENA Youth Forum at MBZUAI (Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence), followed by the 16th International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) Assembly in Abu Dhabi. 

These two days were intense, practical, and formative, covering topics from policy and finance to digitalisation, AI, and energy access. I joined multiple panels, workshops, and technical sessions, and was grateful to contribute as a panellist in the discussion on the Ethics of AI in the Energy Sector, a crucial topic in planning, financing, and governing future energy systems.

The scale of the Assembly was remarkable. Being in the same rooms as ministers, heads of agencies, multilateral institutions, and private-sector leaders from around the world highlighted that energy transition is about more than just technology; it encompasses diplomacy, finance, and national development. I was honoured to represent Bahrain’s youth voice and to meet H.E. the Minister of Ministry of Electricity and Water Affairs of Bahrain during the Assembly.

The energy transition will not be driven by ambition alone—it will be shaped by whether we can turn global capital into real, investable clean-energy markets where energy demand, development needs, and climate goals intersect. 

In 2024, global investment in energy transition technologies reached a record $2.4 trillion, up 20% from 2023. Yet more than 90% of these flows went to China and advanced economies, even as fossil fuel subsidies remain at $1.1 trillion and external debt servicing reached $1.4 trillion, with 61 countries spending over 10% of public revenues just to cover interest payments.

At the UNDP  session today at the @IRENA Pavilion during #WFES2026, we focused on how to do exactly that, looking at the 3 financial solutions that unlock opportunity:

1️⃣ Strengthening local ownership and value chains is essential to turn renewable deployment into development. In regions such as North Africa, capacity is scaling rapidly, but external ownership and export-oriented models limit job creation, skills, and domestic value capture.

2️⃣ Using debt-smart and blended finance instruments can restore fiscal space for clean energy. In non-oil-producing MENA countries, debt-to-GDP ratios approaching 90% are crowding out public investment in energy, health, and education—making guarantees, concessional capital, and debt-linked climate finance critical.

3️⃣ De-risking and demand-anchoring mechanisms can lower the cost of capital. Today, renewable projects in high-risk markets face financing costs two to three times higher than in advanced economies, even though the technologies are the same.

These realities point to a simple truth: scaling clean energy without reforming financial systems will reproduce inequality. The future of a just transition lies in what we learn - and change - when capital is structured to reduce risk, retain value locally, and support inclusive investment, energy solutions become affordable, resilient, and scalable—making a just energy transition the engine for development pathways that are truly sustainable.

#EnergyForDevelopment #WFES2026 #DevelopmentFinance #Derisking

We are now in the #Zettabyte era - generating volumes of data never seen before in human history. With just one zettabyte equivalent to a trillion gigabytes, we often hear data being called the the new oil, gold, or currency. But data only creates value when it is translated into decisions. 

Data centres already consume 1.5–2% of global electricity, rising to 5–20% in major digital hubs, while putting growing pressure on power systems, water, and land. 

At the same time, when the just energy transition and the digital revolution are planned together, clean power and data reinforce each other. When clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for jobs, livelihoods, and sustainable development — not just electrons.

This is why, at UNDP , we are working closely with governments and energy partners to turn data into a development asset for the AI and energy transition. Earlier today, at #WFES2026 we reflected on what we are learning in practice. 
Three strategic insights stand out:

1️⃣Data, digital and AI are now a core asset for clean energy investment and delivery. High-quality energy data can de-risk projects and attract capital — but only if digital energy systems are cyber-secure. As grids become digital, cybersecurity becomes energy security, protecting hospitals, water systems, and local businesses. Geospatial and context-specific data can significantly improve energy planning, identify viable investments, and accelerate rollout.

2️⃣ Focus must shift from data systems to data ecosystems. Energy solutions increasingly generate data, but transformational impact depends on how these data flow across institutions, sectors and stakeholders. Building inclusive energy ecosystems requires systems-level approaches; linking data, energy priorities and development objectives, from national policy to local delivery.	

3️⃣ Data transparency and accountability can make energy systems inclusive. Our data shows 447 million “electrified” people do not actually use power. When energy data is transparent and well-governed, utilities and investors become accountable for who is served and who is left behind — turning energy systems into platforms for livelihoods and inclusive development, not just grid connections.

As we move deeper into the AI and energy transition, the real challenge is not generating more data - but using it effectively and governing it better, together. The future of the energy transition will be shaped not by how much data we generate, but on whether data systems reflect lived realities, enable better decisions, and align digital innovation with equitable energy outcomes

#EnergyForDevelopment #DataGovernance #WEFS #ThickData #BigData

caption:
Green hydrogen: fuel of the future, or risking another development divide?
 
Green hydrogen is a potential catalyst of sustainable development. Producing hydrogen through 100% renewable electricity could significantly reduce emissions, whilst also powering the sectors, industries, and opportunities that drive countries' growth and development. Green hydrogen could decarbonise heavy industry, support green industrialisation, create inclusive jobs, and strengthen energy security.
 
It has the potential to supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050.
 
But, how can we maximise its benefits - whilst avoiding creating, or entrenching, a new energy and technology divide?
 
1️⃣ Green hydrogen is not for everyone
As with other energy solutions, green hydrogen is one tool in the sustainable energy toolkit. Not every country is suited for large-scale hydrogen. Water availability, energy access needs, land use, and national development priorities must guide decisions. National leaders, and energy agencies, need to be supported and empowered to build the renewable energy portfolios that make sense for their local context.
 
2️⃣Take a holistic approach to energy planning, and don't undermine national climate priorities
Scaling hydrogen is resource-intensive, placing real pressure on land, water, and power systems. 2 million tonnes alone requires around 18 million cubic metres of water, making value creation highly sensitive to how projects are planned and governed. Hydrogen deployment needs to align with climate goals and with the responsible use of water and land. If these are in sync, the potential is considerable. .
 
3️⃣ Green hydrogen needs to deliver domestic value, and people need to come first
Jobs, skills, and local supply chains do not emerge by themselves. Domestic value capture needs to be built into project design from the outset - reaffirming the need to ensure green hydrogen is relevant to national contexts. Similarly, communities benefit only when institutions, regulation, and investment frameworks are aligned to protect resources and distribute gains fairly. Green energy needs to support people, and not just markets.
 
The potential of green hydrogen is immense. In South Africa alone, projections suggest a 3.6% increase in GDP and 370,000 new jobs by 2050. But these outcomes are not inevitable. Green hydrogen can be a powerful development accelerator. But only if it is designed intentionally to strengthen resilience, build local value, and support inclusive growth.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen

Energy has been centre stage at #Davos this week. And, amid all of this: AI. AI is not artificial. It has a long tail of energy-hungry physical data centres and GPU racks, critical mineral mining, and real-world inference demanding unprecedented power supplies.

So, how do we harness these two seemingly separate but, in reality, interconnected and intertwined revolutions - the energy transition, and the AI era? This is the focus of our new Bulletin, below, where we define the ‘digital energy stack’.

In the tech world, a ’stack’ is the collection of different technologies and components needed for a digital product or service to function. As you read this post, it sits on a ’stack’ of solutions: a web browser or LinkedIn application on your phone or other device. Internet and email protocols that (hopefully!) are displaying the below graphic and link correctly. And, layers of cloud hosting, connectivity, and - of course - energy, to make all of this happen.

We are applying this ‘stack’ approach to sustainable energy. We need a systems-level approach, and coherent and strategic efforts. There are seven elements in the ’digital energy stack’:

📊 𝐃𝐚𝐭𝐚 - the 'fuel' of the energy revolution. Big, Lean, and Thick Data.
📱 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐲 - including 3G and 4G, and IoT.
🖥️ 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐮𝐭𝐞 - the 'currency' of the 21st century.
🪪 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐏𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 - to amplify the impact of inclusive energy.
🔒 𝐂𝐲𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐲 - recognising energy's status as critical national infrastructure. 
🤖 𝐀𝐈 - with AI driving new energy solutions, but also creating new challenges.
🏛️ 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 - shaping the talent, culture, and  institutions of the energy transition.

Importantly, there is no single pathway for any of these seven components. Digital and energy innovation is occurring and emerging everywhere, from Silicon Valley to the Silicon Savannah. The Global South is not just an innovation taker - but a maker, and shaper.

Without intentional design, digital risks reinforcing and entrenching energy inequality rather than accelerating an inclusive and just energy transition. The question is no longer whether AI and energy will intersect. It is whether we design that intersection to deliver development, resilience, and equity at scale.

We invite partners, policymakers, and practitioners to help shape the digital energy stack with us 👉https://lnkd.in/eYRYQnmu

#EnergyForDevelopment #AI #DigitalEnergyStack

caption:
Clean Energy in the Age of Data and AI: How Data and AI Are Reshaping Clean Energy and Development?

26 January marks the International Day of Clean Energy, a moment to reflect on how we deliver equitable and sustainable energy transitions that leave no one behind and protect our planet.

For every generation, energy progress has never been just about technology—it has been about expanding what people and societies are able to do. Steam turned heat into motion and powered the first industrial surge. Electricity multiplied development, bringing light to homes, power to industry, and refrigeration that keeps food and vaccines safe. Today, clean energy is becoming the backbone of a new development era—one increasingly shaped not only by electrons, but by data and artificial intelligence.

AI-enabled forecasting and optimisation can unlock up to 175 GW of additional transmission capacity without building new lines, delivering power to millions of people. In practice, better forecasting has already increased wind power value by up to 20% and reduced outage duration by as much as half in some systems.

But this impact is not automatic. Without deliberate design and governance, data and AI can deepen strain on energy systems. When used intentionally, they can strengthen access, resilience, and fairness, and help deliver a just energy transition.

So how do we maximise these gains without creating or entrenching a new digital and energy divide?

1️⃣ Energy data must be treated as public infrastructure
Open, trusted data on demand, grid capacity, and system performance reduces uncertainty and unlocks investment at scale. When data is shared, the benefits of AI and digital tools can move from pilots to systems.

2️⃣ AI and energy must operate within land, water, and social limits
Efficiency gains matter only if they respect resource constraints and local realities. Digital optimisation cannot come at the expense of people or ecosystems.

3️⃣ Al needs to deliver for people
The growth of energy, digital, and AI should be judged by whether intelligence expands access, resilience, and livelihoods, not just system performance.
The opportunities are real. Data and AI can accelerate the energy transition in ways we have never seen before. 

But only if they are governed deliberately, aligned with development goals, and designed to serve people first.

#InternationalDayOfCleanEnergy #CleanEnergyDay #AI

Africa has made real progress on energy access over the past decade, with electrification in sub-Saharan Africa rising from around 51% in 2017 to over 61% in 2023. Yet nearly two out of every five people in Africa still lack electricity, as population growth continues to outpace connections. Progress is happening — but not yet at the speed or scale required.

The opportunity is immense. Africa holds 60% of the world’s best solar resources, more than 7,900 GW of solar potential, over 400 GW of hydropower, and vast wind and geothermal corridors. These resources position Africa to build clean, resilient energy systems that power development, jobs, and economic transformation.

As energy demand grows, the challenge is no longer only expanding access — but how to use data, digitalization, and AI to plan better, invest smarter, and deliver faster. Digital intelligence can help turn clean energy into a true platform for inclusion and growth.

Mobile networks, fibre, and IoT are not just digital infrastructure - they are also drivers of modern energy systems. They are key catalysts of energy access, and also drive energy planning and rollout at the largest scales. These synergies are only growing.

But the gaps are still huge. Around 2.2 billion people are not connected to the internet. Most of them in low- and middle-income countries. Synergies continue here, too. Many of the communities that most need energy access are also the least digitally connected. And, without reliable connectivity, digital tools for energy planning, monitoring, and payment simply cannot scale.

Connectivity anchors energy systems and amplifies their impact. And countries are leveraging this combined role through:

📡 Closer coordination between energy and connectivity providers, especially at the last mile
🛠️ ‘Dig Once’ and co-deployment approaches to roll out infrastructure faster and at lower cost
🌍 Exploring Community Networks in remote and underserved areas - bringing energy, connectivity, and local digital skills together

Connectivity is not a side issue in the energy transition. It is central to inclusion, resilience, and scale. Read more about the Digital Energy Stack here: https://lnkd.in/e7PebbrX

"We need smarter cities, not “smart cities”.

Technology can play a key role in improving #energy efficiency and access in cities. From smart meters to AI-enabled grid management. These are very familiar examples of “smart cities”. But cities are more than 5G and Big Data. They are drivers of opportunity, prosperity, and progress, generating 80% of global GDP. By 2050, 68% of the world’s population will live in cities, placing them on the front lines of climate change.

A focus on building “#SmartCities” risks turning cities into technology projects. We talk about “users” instead of people. And there can be a focus on discrete deployments of technology rather than the ‘connective tissue’ which makes cities the kinds of places where people want to live, work, and play. This risks constraining inclusive and sustainable urban development.

Truly smart cities recognize the ambiguity of lives and livelihoods. They use a broader innovation toolkit, where technology supports real needs, including energy systems, rather than defining the city itself.

Discover why truly smart cities are defined by people and connection, not just the deployment of technology, and what this means for energy innovation in cities.

Learn more : https://lnkd.in/ghZnHY7g

#EnergyForDevelopment"
