Across the Pacific, a different model of energy transition is rising 🌊
 
Not just a shift from diesel to renewables, but a whole-of-society transformation linking energy with mobility, food systems, digital infrastructure, and climate resilience.
 
In tourism-driven economies such as Fiji, Palau, Samoa, and Vanuatu, contributing 10% to 40% of GDP, renewable energy is already reducing operating costs and helping retain more value locally.
 
In French Polynesia, seawater air conditioning systems are cutting cooling electricity demand by up to 90%, showing how sustainable energy solutions can work with natural systems while improving efficiency.
 
At the 6th Pacific Regional Energy and Transport Ministers’ Meeting (PRETMM) in Port Moresby, I reflected on how this model is taking shape, not as a future vision, but as a system being built in real time.
 
🔹 Turning energy into a foundation for value chains: Electrification has increased from around 64% in 2009 to over 85% in 2022. The next frontier is what that energy enables. In Samoa, clean energy is expanding beyond electric vehicles to low-carbon outboard motors for fishing and sea transport, linking energy to livelihoods, markets, and mobility.
 
🔹 Building digital, data, and AI foundations: Energy systems need to be designed for both demand and risk. At UNDP, the SIDS Data Platform integrates over 4,000 indicators and 80+ geospatial datasets to support investment-ready, AI-enabled planning. In Tonga, a cable disruption in 2024 affected around one-third of the population for more than two weeks, highlighting the need for resilient, energy-backed digital systems. 
 
🔹 Shifting to distributed, resilient architectures: With urban centers growing at around 4% annually and geography limiting grid expansion, distributed systems are becoming central. In Papua New Guinea, where access remains around 20%, a 1 MW solar system in Bougainville is already delivering power to over 30,000 people, reducing costs by up to 50%. The new Off-Grid Regulation is now enabling these solutions to scale.
 
As the Pacific prepares to host pre-COP discussions ahead of COP31, there is a clear opportunity to bring this model to the global stage. 
 
Through Rising Up for SIDS and the SIDS Energy Offer, UNDP is working with partners to connect policy, finance, technology, and capacity into integrated systems that can scale.
 
If you are working in this space, we invite you to connect. We are ready to listen, partner, and support.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #RisingUpForSIDS

caption:
Who are new AI systems really being built for?

The global expansion of AI infrastructure is happening at extraordinary speed, but it is also opening a rare opportunity to rethink how energy, digital infrastructure, and development systems evolve together.

Right now, the world is adding roughly 255 GWh of new electricity demand every single day from the growth trajectory of AI and data centres, equivalent to connecting another medium-sized city to the grid daily.

At the 11th United Nations Forum on Science, Technology and Innovation during the side event co-organized with GEIDCO, I reflected on why this moment represents far more than a technological shift. It is increasingly becoming a restructuring of infrastructure, industrial systems, and energy demand itself.

Three opportunities stand out:

🔹 Turning AI demand into clean energy investment. In South Africa, solar wheeling models are already linking large-scale renewable generation to industrial and digital users through the national grid.

🔹 Turning energy systems into intelligent systems. In Brazil, AI-enabled monitoring is reducing transmission fault response times from hours to seconds across infrastructure carrying most of the country’s electricity.

🔹 Turning AI infrastructure into local capability and green industrial growth. Malaysia, for example, is positioning itself as a regional digital hub while linking digital expansion to broader industrial strategy.

The direction of this transition is not fixed. 

AI revolution could help countries accelerate cleaner infrastructure, strengthen sovereignty, and capture far greater value from the next wave of industrial transformation.

The difference will come down to how swiftly countries can turn this technological expansion into lasting economic and development opportunity.

#EnergyforDevelopment

caption:
Can the rapid expansion of AI and data centres become a driver of a just energy transition?

By 2030, electricity demand from data centres worldwide is projected to more than double to around 945 TWh, slightly more than Japan's entire annual electricity consumption. By 2027, AI alone could consume 4 to 6 billion cubic metres of water each year, equivalent to the annual water consumption of a country like Denmark.

Behind every AI model sits physical infrastructure, and the decisions made today on energy, grids, water, and data centres will either deepen inequality and infrastructure pressures or unlock investment, modernize systems, and expand development opportunities across the Global South. 
 
Three takeaways:

🔹 AI data centres must be embedded in national systems of innovation, not treated as isolated infrastructure. When digital and energy systems scale together, they build national innovation ecosystems. Without that integration, data centres risk serving external platforms while local capabilities remain underdeveloped.

🔹 AI infrastructure must strengthen resilience, not compete with it. In water-stressed and capacity-constrained settings, unmanaged AI growth can privilege data centres over households, health services, and small businesses, deepening inequality.

🔹 AI is becoming one of the largest new buyers of energy, and that buying power can shape entire energy systems. Without deliberate policy, grids risk being built to serve data centres at the expense of households, small businesses, and essential services. With the right frameworks, that same demand can accelerate renewable energy deployment and strengthen broader energy access.

The future of AI will depend not only on algorithms, but on how countries build the energy systems that power them.

#EnergyForDevelopment #AI #DataCenter #JustEnergyTransition

caption:
What does a just energy transition really look like in practice in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

In a school in Banja Luka, energy efficiency renovations have cut energy use by nearly half — making classrooms warmer, brighter, and easier to maintain for more than a thousand students and staff. Small changes like these signal a deeper transformation underway across the country.

In a new op-ed, "A Shared Just Energy Transition," I share why this transition is not only an energy shift, but one of the largest shared development opportunities for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Three priorities stand out:
🔹 Strengthen governance to unlock finance in renewables. Bosnia and Herzegovina's transition will require over $6 billion in investment, with the grid at the centre. With the Electricity Law and the National Energy and Climate Plan in their final stage of approval, the foundations are in place to mobilize bankable pipelines and innovative financing.

🔹 Transform coal regions into jobs, skills, and growth. Coal still employs 15,000 to 20,000 people directly and supports more than 150,000 jobs across related sectors. Repurposing mine land in Zenica, Banovići, and Kreka — with around 27 MWp of solar capacity planned — shows how existing infrastructure can be turned into productive economic assets when connected to a national innovation ecosystem.

🔹 Harness data, AI, and digital innovation to scale energy efficiency. Public buildings retrofitted through UNDP's Green Economic Development programme have already reduced energy use by 30 to 50 percent. With smart meter deployment already exceeding the 80% national target, accelerating their full use can unlock real-time data, dynamic tariffs, and stronger system resilience.

As UNDP , we stand ready to support this whole-of-system transformation by helping connect policy, finance, and technology to build resilience, create jobs, improve quality of life, and position Bosnia and Herzegovina at the forefront of the next generation of energy innovation.

🔗 More on UNDP's work in Bosnia and Herzegovina: https://lnkd.in/eSxRHd5B

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransition

With the Electricity Law and the National Energy and Climate Plan in their final stage of approval, the foundations are in place to mobilize bankable pipelines and innovative financing.

🔹 Transform coal regions into jobs, skills, and growth. Coal still employs 15,000 to 20,000 people directly and supports more than 150,000 jobs across related sectors. Repurposing mine land in Zenica, Banovići, and Kreka — with around 27 MWp of solar capacity planned — shows how existing infrastructure can be turned into productive economic assets when connected to a national innovation ecosystem.

🔹 Harness data, AI, and digital innovation to scale energy efficiency. Public buildings retrofitted through UNDP's Green Economic Development programme have already reduced energy use by 30 to 50 percent. With smart meter deployment already exceeding the 80% national target, accelerating their full use can unlock real-time data, dynamic tariffs, and stronger system resilience.

As UNDP , we stand ready to support this whole-of-system transformation by helping connect policy, finance, and technology to build resilience, create jobs, improve quality of life, and position Bosnia and Herzegovina at the forefront of the next generation of energy innovation.

I look forward to a rich discussion at the Oxford Department of International Development on the opportunities, risks and policy choices shaping the future of green hydrogen in the Global South.

By 2030, global electricity demand from data centres is projected to more than double to around 945 TWh, while electricity demand from AI-optimised data centres alone is expected to more than quadruple. AI is becoming an energy challenge as much as a digital one. 
 
At the same time, Advanced forecasting and AI-enabled grid management are already improving renewable integration by up to 20–30%, reducing curtailment and increasing system efficiency.
 
How will the rise of Artificial Intelligence reshape global energy systems and sustainable development?
 
On Friday, 15 May, I will be delivering a guest lecture at the University of Cambridge on Artificial Intelligence, Energy Systems, and Sustainable Development.
The session will explore how AI, energy transitions and sustainable development are becoming increasingly interconnected, and why this nexus is now central to industrial policy, geopolitical competition and development strategy. Drawing on a People, Planet and Prosperity approach, the lecture will examine whether AI-driven transformation can support inclusive growth and green industrialisation in the Global South, or whether it risks reproducing existing inequalities and dependencies.
 
I look forward to engaging discussions with students, researchers and practitioners on the governance, investment and policy choices shaping the future of AI and sustainable development.
 
Date: Friday, 15 May 2026
Time: 2:30 – 4:00 PM
Venue: LT2, Engineering Department, Trumpington Street, University of Cambridge
 
#ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyTransition #SustainableDevelopment #GreenIndustrialisation #GlobalSouth #UNDP

caption:
There is a lot of discussion about green hydrogen. But the real question is about development impact.
 
Green hydrogen has the potential to decarbonise hard-to-electrify sectors, support green industrialisation, create jobs, and strengthen energy security. Often described as the fuel of the future, it is projected to supply up to 12% of global energy demand by 2050.
 
But that future is not guaranteed.
 
Green hydrogen also places significant pressure on land, water, and energy systems. Producing 1 million tonnes of hydrogen requires around 30,000 hectares of solar panels, while nearly 70% of planned electrolyser capacity is located in water-stressed regions.
 
Three takeaways stand out:
🔹 Green hydrogen is not a one-size-fits-all solution. Countries must weigh water availability, land constraints, energy access needs, and industrial priorities.
 
🔹 Hydrogen must create domestic value. India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 500,000 jobs and 125 GW of renewable capacity by 2030, backed by $1.83 billion for domestic electrolyser manufacturing.
 
🔹 Inclusion must be designed from the start. By 2023, although 4.3 GW of green hydrogen capacity had been announced globally, only 0.3 GW, around 7%, had actually been built. The challenge is increasingly about planning, institutions, and governance.
 
Green hydrogen must serve sustainable development, not only markets. The opportunities are real, but only if local communities, institutions, and the private sector are included from day one.
 
I look forward to discussing these questions further at today’s panel discussion, Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human-Centred Framework, at the University of Oxford .
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustEnergyTransition TIDE Centre, University of Oxford

caption:
If green hydrogen is the future, who gets to own that future?

By 2050, hydrogen is projected to supply around 12% of global energy demand, with demand rising to over 430 million tonnes. Yet around 83% of global hydrogen investment remains concentrated in Europe and China, even as many of the world's most competitive low-cost production sites are likely to emerge across Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East.

This raises a bigger development question: will countries become producers of green hydrogen, or creators of the industries, jobs, and value chains built around it?

This was a central theme from today's discussion at the University of Oxford on the UNDP  -TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  report Navigating the Currents of Green Hydrogen: Towards a Human-Centred Framework.

While the opportunity is growing rapidly, delivery is still struggling to keep pace. By 2023, although 4.3 GW of global green hydrogen capacity had been announced, only 0.3 GW — around 7% — had actually been built. The constraint is no longer renewable potential alone. Increasingly, the barriers are governance, finance, infrastructure, and institutional readiness.

Three strategic priorities stand out:

🔹 From export commodities to integrated value chains. Hydrogen should be viewed not only as an export opportunity, but as an industrial strategy. The greatest development gains may come from local manufacturing, green fertilisers, and decarbonised industries — not raw hydrogen exports.

🔹 Jobs, skills, and national innovation systems. Chile aims to create over 100,000 jobs through its hydrogen strategy, while India targets around 500,000 jobs and 125 GW of renewable capacity by 2030. South Korea shows how coordinated ecosystems across research institutions, universities, and industry can transform hydrogen into a national innovation system.

🔹 Linking hydrogen finance and infrastructure with public value. The risk is that hydrogen projects become closed export enclaves — privately powered, externally financed, and weakly connected to domestic economies. South Africa's hydrogen strategy includes EU support for ports, railways, and pipeline infrastructure, while Brazil's Ceará Green Hydrogen Hub is anchoring around $7 billion in industrial and logistics investments.

The success of green hydrogen will not be measured by megawatts or export contracts alone. It will be measured by whether countries build capabilities, create decent jobs, safeguard resources, and advance shared prosperity.

The energy transition must, above all, serve people.

#EnergyForDevelopment #GreenHydrogen #JustEnergyTransition

caption:
Can AI in energy systems become a development opportunity, or will it deepen existing divides?

AI-enabled forecasting and optimization could unlock up to 175 GW of additional transmission capacity from existing power lines, without building a single new one. Improved forecasting has already increased wind power market value by up to 20% in some systems, while AI-driven fault detection can reduce outage durations by 30 to 50%.

But the stakes are equally high. Some of the largest AI data centres now consume as much electricity as around 2 million households, while more than 2,500 GW of renewable, storage, and large-load projects remain stuck in grid queues globally. The story can go one of two ways. If we are not careful, AI can push energy systems beyond what people and the planet can sustain. If we are deliberate, it can strengthen resilience and fairness.

This is what I will be exploring today at the University of Cambridge in a lecture titled "What Will Your Knowledge Make Possible?" with the next generation of energy leaders, looking at how energy, digital systems, and AI are converging into what I call planetary intelligence, and three priorities that stand out:

🔹 Treat energy data as public infrastructure to unlock investment at scale. Shared intelligence on demand, grid capacity, and system performance can reduce uncertainty and accelerate investment.
🔹 Govern AI and energy within land, water, and social limits. AI infrastructure cannot be planned outside ecological realities and resource constraints.
🔹 Measure success by access, resilience, and opportunity for people. The value of energy intelligence is ultimately measured through jobs, services, and human outcomes.

The future of energy is not something we simply predict. It is something we collectively build. Looking forward to today's conversation in #Cambridge University and to hearing perspectives from the next generation helping shape what comes next.

#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #AI

caption:
What kind of future do you envision in this new era of energy transition and digital revolution?
 
Today at the University of Cambridge, I had the pleasure of discussing how artificial intelligence, energy systems, and digital infrastructure are increasingly converging into the same transformation, reshaping economies, industrial systems, and development pathways simultaneously.
 
Throughout history, major energy transitions changed far more than how societies generated power.
 
And now we may be entering a new inflection point: planetary intelligence - the emergence of an intelligent layer across energy systems, digital infrastructure, finance, satellites, sensors, and public institutions.
 
Artificial intelligence is often described as something virtual. Yet it is becoming deeply physical. Some of the largest AI data centres now consume as much electricity as around 2 million households.
 
But perhaps the deeper question is this: Do we know yet whether AI will reduce inequality or deepen it?
 
The answer is, we do not know yet. What we do know is that behind every major technological shift lies a transformational opportunity.
 
Three opportunities particularly stood out during today’s discussion:
 
• Build AI infrastructure that strengthens energy systems rather than fragmenting them. Across Africa, data-centre demand could grow from around 0.4 GW today to between 1.5 and 2.2 GW by 2030, requiring an estimated $10–20 billion in investment. If planned strategically, this growth could help accelerate grid modernization, renewable integration, energy efficiency, and resilient infrastructure development.
 
• Turn renewable energy systems into intelligent systems. Renewable systems are becoming too large, decentralized, and dynamic to manage without advanced coordination. AI-enabled transmission management alone could unlock up to 175 GW of additional grid capacity from existing infrastructure.
 
• Build national digital-energy ecosystems and local value chains. Around $5.8 trillion is expected to flow into global grid infrastructure between 2026 and 2035, including roughly $700 billion in digital grid technologies. The deeper opportunity lies in building local industries, technical capabilities, services, software ecosystems, and new value chains around the transition itself.
 
Perhaps this is ultimately why the AI-energy transition matters for development.
 
Because energy innovation is never only about producing electricity differently. It is about reshaping how societies manage water, food systems, cities, industry, health, jobs, and resilience.
 
Many thanks to the University of Cambridge and all students for the engaging discussion today.
 
#EnergyforDevelopment

On Saturday, I joined the 2026 Oxford Africa Conference  Conference panel, “Powering Africa’s Energy Futures: From Resources to Markets.”
What stayed with me most was the urgency of reframing Africa’s energy transition as a development agenda, but, at the same time, the incredible opportunities the continent holds.
 
Around 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa still lack access to electricity, and more than 940 million people remain without clean cooking. The question is how energy systems can power homes, schools, hospitals, and businesses today, while also building the foundations for tomorrow’s industries, digital infrastructure, and AI economy.
 
This is where AI becomes central. Africa’s AI future will be shaped by its energy choices. Data centres, cloud systems, cooling infrastructure, and compute capacity all require reliable power. Africa’s data-centre capacity could grow from around 400 MW today to as much as 2.2 GW by 2030, yet the continent still receives only around 2% of global clean energy investment.
 
That gap is technical, financial, and political. Closing it will require affordable capital, stronger delivery systems, investable pipelines, and institutions capable of turning ambition into implementation.
 
But the opportunity goes far beyond electricity access. Africa holds around 30% of the world’s known mineral reserves and renewable energy potential estimated at 1,000 times projected electricity demand in 2040. The challenge is whether the continent remains a supplier of raw materials, or builds value chains in renewables, batteries, e-mobility, digital infrastructure, and AI-enabled systems.
Africa’s energy transition could create 26 million additional jobs by 2050, including more than 8 million in renewables. Reliable clean energy now underpins not only climate action, but also competitiveness, industrialisation, jobs, and economic sovereignty.
 
Many thanks to Haruna (Haroun) Inuwa for moderating the discussion, and to @Shaun Githiku, Rose M. Mutiso, Ph.D. , and Shakwa Nyambe for such thoughtful contributions.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #AfricaEnergyTransition #JustTransition #AI #GreenIndustrialisation #RenewableEnergy

caption:
I had a great conversation last week with students from the Cambridge African Studies and Energy Society on Africa’s energy future, green industrialization, and the role young people are already playing in shaping it. 
 
Three reflections stayed with me from today’s discussion: 

	1.	Africa’s energy transition is about far more than electricity generation. It is fundamentally about development, jobs, digital transformation, and expanding opportunity across the continent. Yet while Africa holds around 30% of the world’s critical mineral deposits, 565 million people still lack access to electricity. 
 
	2.	Young people are already driving change. In 2023, climate tech startups accounted for 36% of Africa’s startup market, attracting around $1.1 billion in investment. From AI-enabled energy systems to clean energy entrepreneurship, many of the systems of tomorrow are already being shaped today. 
 
	3.	The transition must also be equitable. Around 10–12 million young Africans enter the labor market each year, while only around 3 million formal jobs are created annually. Expanding local value creation, regional cooperation, and access to affordable finance will be essential to ensuring the energy transition translates into long-term economic opportunity. 

What gave me the most hope was hearing students speak openly about their goals, concerns, and visions for the future, and the deep desire many share to contribute meaningfully to their communities and countries. 
 
One thing I shared with them is something I continue reminding myself of as well: meaningful careers rarely follow a straight line. Real change is often built gradually, through persistence, curiosity, collaboration, and the willingness to keep moving forward despite uncertainty. 
 
Thank you again to everyone who made the discussion so thoughtful and inspiring.

caption:
Everyone is talking about the AI 'race'. But races aren't won in the first corner. They're won in the final sprint - and over the very last mile. And the last mile is something that the Global South knows very well.

Far from being left out or left behind, the Global South could set the pace for global AI direction. And we're working with governments around the world to prepare them for what we see as the crucial AI 'sprint' - in particular, how countries can position energy and AI as crucial catalysts for growth. With these two revolutions having the potential to become definitive inflection points for 21st century sustainable development. 

We've identified a 'Green Window of Opportunity' where decision-makers, policymakers, and innovators can leverage the combined potential of energy and AI to chart a new pathway. Some of the areas we're driving exploration around include:

🤝 How to build locally-owned and locally-relevant domestic AI–energy innovation ecosystems anchored in local talent, universities, businesses, and public institutions.

🏛️ The need to make 'Green AI' THE critical pathway through supportive regulation, infrastructure planning, and investment incentives - with the potential for this to become an area of national comparative advantage.

⬆️ Identifying how countries and communities can move up the clean energy, critical mineral, and digital value chains to retain greater economic value domestically - and how they can build crucial and cumulative energy, AI, and development gains.

⚡ How countries can shape and support AI and clean-energy entrepreneurs through targeted finance, incubation, market creation, and skills development.

We are not about abstract discussions of technology, status quo energy policy, or generic policy recommendations. We really do see an important moment for development in the coming months and years. Countries sitting at the intersection of renewable energy - many of which are in the Global South - and AI explorations (with countries across Latin America, Africa, and Asia-Pacific moving quickly) could reap an unprecedented digital development dividend. Get in touch if you want to explore what the AI and energy revolutions could mean for your country.

➡️ More in our recent UNDP  paper with the TIDE Centre, University of Oxford : The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries?

What does it take to make sure that the clean energy transition leaves no young person behind?
 
Today, I'm proud to launch the NextGen Energy Champions Initiative — a partnership between UNDP  and Goodwall  to connect young people across the Global South with the skills, knowledge, and opportunities of the clean energy transition.
 
The numbers tell a clear story. An accelerated energy transition could add up to 40 million jobs in the energy sector by 2050, with 18 million in renewables alone. But 67% of youth believe that they lack the technical skills to benefit from the digital and green economies that they are in the position to shape.
 
We can close that gap. And it starts by meeting young people where they are.
 
As a first step, through gamified learning on the Goodwall  platform, youth aged 16 to 30 from any country of the world are being invited to:
 
→ Watch curated videos on clean energy technology, policy, and careers
 
→ Complete knowledge quizzes
 
→ Record a 30-second video sharing their perspective on #CleanEnergy
 
Their voices will shape our work — including a major convening on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this September.
 
A just energy transition isn't built for young people. It is built with them.
 
If you're 16 to 30: download Goodwall and join the challenge.
 
If you work with youth: please share this post.

The AI race is arriving just as the energy transition enters its most consequential phase.
 
Countries are trying to decarbonize, expand access, strengthen resilience and meet rising electricity demand all at once. Now AI adds another layer: demand for compute, data centres, water, cooling and firm clean power.
 
But the AI-energy question is bigger than electricity consumption. It is about whether countries can use AI to strengthen both sides of the energy equation: cleaner, more reliable supply and energy use that is more efficient, flexible and productive for development.
 
The word intelligence comes from the Latin "inter-legere": to choose between, to discern, to make connections. That is the choice before us: will AI accelerate resilience, productivity and opportunity, or concentrate value in the hands of a few?
 
This is what we explore, together with Amir Lebdioui and Angel Melguizo, in our new UNDP -TIDE Centre, University of Oxford  Centre paper: "The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries?"

Today is World Environment Day.
 
It is a reminder that every transition we build must stay within planetary boundaries. And AI is no exception.
 
Artificial intelligence will be shaped less by algorithms alone than by access to sustainable energy. By 2030, data centres are projected to consume nearly 945 TWh of electricity, with demand from AI-focused data centres expected to triple.
 
For developing countries, this creates a defining choice. AI could deepen existing inequalities, strain fragile energy systems and create new forms of dependency. Or it could open a green window of opportunity: helping countries strengthen clean power systems, build local capabilities and capture more value from the digital economy.
 
This is why an energy-ready AI future must place People, Planet and Prosperity at the centre:
 
👥 People: building skills, inclusion and public-interest digital infrastructure
 
🌱 Planet: powering AI with clean energy while reducing pressure on water, land and minerals
 
📈 Prosperity: creating local value, strengthening energy systems and enabling inclusive growth
 
I believe AI can support a just energy transition, but only if it is powered, governed and shaped for sustainable development.

caption:
Can we move from Artificial Intelligence to Planetary Intelligence?

As we mark World Environment Day, this may be one of the most important questions of our time.
When World Environment Day was established in 1973, it carried the slogan "Only One Earth." More than 50 years later, that message feels more relevant than ever.

Today, the world is navigating profound transformations. Rising geopolitical tensions are reshaping energy security, while rapid advances in digitalization and artificial intelligence are accelerating demand for electricity and critical resources.
 
Yet amid these challenges, there are reasons for optimism. Despite the impacts of conflicts in the Middle East, global energy investment is expected to increase by 5%, reaching USD 3.4 trillion in 2026.
 
2025 also marked a historic milestone: for the first time, renewable energy generated more electricity globally than coal. Solar power expanded more rapidly in 2025 than any energy source in history.
 
The opportunity is significant. A just energy transition could reduce energy import bills by 38%, create 14 million green jobs, and lift 45 million people out of energy poverty by 2035.
 
At the same time, data centres already account for around 2% of global electricity demand and are projected to more than double their consumption by 2030. Yet the same technologies driving this growth can become part of the solution. AI-enabled grid management and digital twins are already improving renewable energy integration by 20–30%, helping build more flexible and efficient energy systems. More than half of critical mineral projects overlap with or are located near Indigenous Peoples' lands. 
 
But intelligence alone is not enough. The challenge is how we apply it.
 
Planetary Intelligence means using innovation not only to optimize economies, but also to better understand and manage the interconnected relationship between energy, nature, communities, and development. It means recognizing that healthy ecosystems, forests, wetlands, and oceans are as critical to our future as data centres, grids, and digital infrastructure. Nature-based solutions alone could provide up to one-third of the climate mitigation needed by 2030 while strengthening resilience and protecting livelihoods.
 
There is only one Earth. If we choose the right path, the journey from Artificial Intelligence to Planetary Intelligence may become one of the defining opportunities of our generation.

caption:
G7 leaders are gathering in Évian today to discuss energy security, AI, and critical minerals.
 
One question stays with me: Can countries make the right development choices before infrastructure is locked in?
 
I have come to see energy modelling not as a technical exercise, but as a way to inform decisions before they become irreversible. Without integrated planning, countries risk fuel import dependence, grid congestion, stranded assets, and missed jobs. With it, energy systems can be designed for industrialization, resilience, and inclusive growth from the start.
 
Three takeaways stand out:
 
🔹 Model demand and risk at subnational scale.
With more than 1,000 active Earth observation satellites, a tenfold rise in publicly available Earth observation data in a decade, and over 500 machine-learning-ready geospatial datasets, governments can now model demand growth, climate risk, and system constraints below the national level. That means infrastructure can go where it is most resilient, affordable, and impactful.
 
🔹 Link energy decisions to real development outcomes.
The transition is full of trade-offs: cost and resilience, speed and equity, access and industrial growth. Integrated models help countries test scenarios side by side, asking not only what is cheapest, but what is most robust under climate shocks, what reduces fuel imports, and what creates the most jobs per dollar invested. Complexity becomes a set of choices governments can act on.
 
🔹 Align governments and finance around one evidence base.
When planning ministries, utilities, finance ministries, and regulators work from the same models, coordination improves. Pipelines become clearer. Policy becomes more coherent. Finance becomes easier to mobilize. Modelling becomes a common language linking national plans, climate commitments, and investment decisions into one credible framework.
 
The conversations in Évian will shape the global energy agenda. But the deeper test is whether every country, not only the G7, can shape its own future with the same foresight. 
 
Energy modelling is no longer an add-on. It is strategic infrastructure. And it decides whether a country locks in vulnerability or builds lasting resilience.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #G7Summit #JustEnergyTransition

caption:
Ahead of next week's High-Level Political Forum, the latest Tracking SDG 7: The Energy Progress Report offers an important snapshot of where the global energy transition stands—and why this may be one of the greatest development opportunities of our time.
 
The numbers tell a story that goes well beyond the remaining challenges.
Since the SDGs were adopted in 2015, the number of people living without electricity has fallen from 958 million to 655 million. Renewable energy has grown by 79% since 2013, now accounting for 18% of global final energy consumption and more than 30% of global electricity generation. Installed renewable energy capacity has more than doubled—from 248 watts per person in 2015 to 544 watts per person in 2024—while international public finance supporting clean energy in developing countries has increased from USD 14.3 billion to USD 24.6 billion.
 
Yet if we look beyond the numbers, an even more important story is emerging.
 
The world is not facing the same energy transition we imagined in 2015. Geopolitical uncertainty, shifting supply chains, climate risks and the rapid rise of AI are fundamentally reshaping energy systems. But these changes are also creating unprecedented incentives to accelerate the transition.
Today, investing in clean energy is no longer driven only by climate ambition. It is increasingly about energy security, economic competitiveness, industrial development and resilience.
 
At the same time, digitalization and AI are creating new opportunities to build smarter grids, improve energy efficiency, integrate renewables and expand access to affordable and reliable energy.
 
Accelerating renewable energy deployment and energy efficiency strengthens energy security, reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels and enhances macroeconomic resilience, particularly in developing countries.
Important gaps remain. 645 million people are still projected to remain without electricity by 2030, nearly 2 billion people continue to rely on polluting cooking fuels, and globally only 22% of households without electricity can afford a basic electricity connection.
 
Universal access will require us to more than triple the current pace of progress.
 
As the final in-depth review of SDG 7 before 2030, this year's High-Level Political Forum is an opportunity not only to assess progress, but to redefine the just energy transition as one of the strongest drivers of development, resilience, prosperity and peace in an increasingly uncertain world.

In 2024, 655 million people were still living without access to electricity, and 645 million people are still projected to remain without electricity by 2030. Nearly 2 billion people continue to rely on polluting fuels for cooking, while globally only 22% of households without electricity can afford the monthly cost of a basic electricity service.
 
These figures, presented in the latest SDG 7 Tracking Report, remind us why a just energy transition matters. It is about far more than turning on the lights. Clean, affordable, and reliable energy has the power to transform societies—expanding opportunities for education, healthcare, jobs, and economic development, while strengthening resilience and turning today's uncertainties into tomorrow's opportunities.
 
At the same time, the global energy landscape is becoming increasingly complex. Rising geopolitical tensions are exposing vulnerabilities in energy systems and supply chains, while the rapid expansion of AI is driving an unprecedented surge in electricity demand, with data centres projected to consume more electricity by 2030 than all but the world's five largest electricity-consuming countries.
 
How do we accelerate progress towards SDG 7 in a world of rising energy demand, digital transformation, and widening financing gaps? More importantly, what practical solutions and emerging opportunities can help us get back on track?
 
On Thursday, 2 July, I will have the pleasure of moderating the high-level panel "Accelerating Progress Towards 2030 and Beyond" during the UN-Energy Webinar on the SDG 7 Review at the High-level Political Forum (HLPF) 2026.
 
Together with colleagues from across the UN system, we will discuss the latest SDG 7 findings, explore practical solutions and emerging opportunities, and examine how to accelerate implementation by advancing energy access, mobilising finance, and strengthening the links between energy, industrial development, and digital transformation.
I look forward to an engaging discussion with @Divya Kottadiel, @Luis Munuera, and @Isaac Elizondo Garcia.

caption:
What if SDG 7 is not only about closing the access gap, but about building clean, affordable energy systems that power the next generation of development?
 
That was the question I kept coming back to today while moderating Panel Discussion 3: Accelerating Progress Towards 2030 and Beyond during the webinar “Clean and Affordable Energy: Where do we stand? How to move forward?”, ahead of the SDG 7 review at the HLPF.
 
There is real momentum to build on. For the first time in history, universal electricity access is within reach. More than 90% of the global population now has access to basic electricity, and global investment in the energy transition reached a record US$2.3 trillion in 2025.
 
But the task ahead is changing. Geopolitical tensions are exposing the vulnerability of major energy routes, affecting around 20 million barrels of oil per day. AI and digitalisation are also increasing demand on energy systems. By 2030, data centres could consume more electricity than all but five countries, and enough water to meet the basic needs of 1.3 billion people in sub-Saharan Africa for a year.
 
The opportunity is to power digital transformation with clean, affordable and resilient energy systems while advancing a just energy transition for all.
 
I was joined by Divya Kottadiel from Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) , @Luis Manuera from UN Environment Programme , and Isaac Elizondo  from UNIDO  for a rich exchange on what acceleration must look like in practice.
 
For me, one message stood out clearly: access must move from connection alone to energy for development and opportunity. That means powering schools, hospitals, farms, digital services and livelihoods, while creating jobs, supporting local enterprises and closing the digital divide for the 2.2 billion people still offline.
 
Finance is central to making this possible. Global clean energy investment has reached around US$2 trillion annually, yet Africa attracts only US$30-40 billion, roughly 2% of global flows. Redirecting capital toward countries and communities with the greatest needs is one of the biggest opportunities for shared prosperity.
 
If we get SDG 7 right, we do more than expand access. We make energy cleaner, more affordable and more productive, strengthening resilience, enabling digital participation, jobs and a just transition.

caption:
Solar is one of the fastest ways to expand electricity access, particularly in hard-to-reach rural communities. But with many systems such as solar inverters having a lifespan of 15-20 years, how do we ensure that today's clean energy solutions don't become tomorrow's sustainability challenge?
 
That question is becoming increasingly urgent as Africa's clean energy transition gains pace.
Installed renewable energy capacity has doubled over the past decade, from around 35 GW in 2015 to 70 GW in 2024, while 2025 recorded a record 11.3 GW of new renewable capacity additions, led by Ethiopia, South Africa and Egypt. Today, eight African countries generate more than 80% of their electricity from renewable sources.
 
As this momentum continues, the next challenge is ensuring these gains are built to last. Embedding circularity across renewable energy value chains, from critical minerals and manufacturing to repurposing and second-life battery applications, can strengthen energy security, reduce waste, as well as create local industries and jobs.
 
Coming just days after the African Circular Economy Alliance Annual Meeting in Abidjan, I look forward to continuing this important conversation in New York at the UN High-level Political Forum side event, Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa.
 
Circular energy systems aren't a separate conversation from our global energy systems. They are how we make the clean energy transition more resilient, more sustainable, and more beneficial for communities across Africa, and across the world.

Solar is one of the fastest ways to expand electricity access, particularly in hard-to-reach rural communities. But with many systems such as solar inverters having a lifespan of 15-20 years, how do we ensure that today's clean energy solutions don't become tomorrow's sustainability challenge?
 
That question is becoming increasingly urgent as Africa's clean energy transition gains pace.
Installed renewable energy capacity has doubled over the past decade, from around 35 GW in 2015 to 70 GW in 2024, while 2025 recorded a record 11.3 GW of new renewable capacity additions, led by Ethiopia, South Africa and Egypt. Today, eight African countries generate more than 80% of their electricity from renewable sources.
 
As this momentum continues, the next challenge is ensuring these gains are built to last. Embedding circularity across renewable energy value chains, from critical minerals and manufacturing to repurposing and second-life battery applications, can strengthen energy security, reduce waste, as well as create local industries and jobs.
 
Coming just days after the African Circular Economy Alliance Annual Meeting in Abidjan, I look forward to continuing this important conversation in New York at the UN High-level Political Forum side event, Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa.
 
Circular energy systems aren't a separate conversation from our global energy systems. They are how we make the clean energy transition more resilient, more sustainable, and more beneficial for communities across Africa, and across the world.

caption:
What happens when the clean energy technologies we deploy today reach the end of their lives?
 
By 2050, the world could generate up to 78 million tonnes of retired solar panels. Recycling energy transition minerals could reduce the need for new mining by 25-40%, while creating a $200 billion global market. Yet circularity remains an overlooked—and key—part of the energy transition.
 
Today, I had the privilege of delivering the opening remarks and keynote at the UN High-level Political Forum side event, Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa, alongside colleagues and partners from across the public and private sectors.
 
Circularity isn't just about managing waste. It's about designing energy systems from the start to maximize the value of every clean energy investment.
 
Three takeaways stood out:
•⁠  ⁠Circularity is an industrial opportunity. Repair, remanufacturing, recycling, and second-life applications can create jobs, strengthen local industries, and capture more value from the energy transition.
•⁠  ⁠Digitalization is an enabler. From battery passports and AI-assisted mineral discovery to smart grids that could reduce the continent's estimated $5 billion in annual transmission and distribution losses, data is becoming the backbone of circular energy systems.
•⁠  ⁠Regional cooperation is essential. Integrated regional value chains, from critical minerals and manufacturing to repair, second-life use, and recycling, will be key to scaling circular industries.

As renewable and off-grid solar continue to expand across Africa, we have an opportunity to build energy systems that are circular, resilient, and designed to deliver long-term development benefits.
 
Thank you to all the organizers, speakers, and participants for an engaging discussion.

caption:
Honoured to be recognized by illuminem as one of the Top 10 Most Read Thought Leaders of the Year in AI.

This recognition feels especially meaningful at a moment when AI is reshaping how we think about energy, development, and sustainability. The question is no longer only how fast AI advances, but how responsibly it is powered, governed, and used to support a just energy transition.

At its foundation, the future of AI is a question of energy. Last year, AI consumed around 415 terawatt hours of electricity, more than 150 countries individually. By 2030, electricity demand from data centres is projected to more than double to around 945 terawatt hours, roughly equivalent to Japan’s entire electricity consumption today.

I have come to see this as less a story about technology than about people: whether the systems we build expand opportunity, strengthen resilience, and reach the communities that need them most. That question is not abstract when 655 million people still live without electricity and 2.0 billion people still lack access to clean cooking, even as AI places a vast new demand on the same energy systems.

The encouraging part is that AI also presents enormous opportunities to accelerate a just energy transition, from strengthening energy systems to expanding clean energy access. The challenge is ensuring these benefits are shared. Of the US$15.7 trillion AI is projected to contribute to the global economy by 2030, around 84% is expected to accrue to just three regions. A just transition means deliberately widening that circle, ensuring that the communities too often left behind are not left behind again.

At UNDP, we are working to ensure that emerging technologies accelerate clean energy access, strengthen resilience, and deliver real development outcomes for those who need them most.

Thank you to @illuminem and its global community of readers for this recognition. It is an honour to be recognised alongside Facundo Armas, Joe Romm, •Shep Hyken, Vincent Ruinet, Philipp Petry, Dr. Niladri Choudhuri, Aparna K., Monica Sanders, and Vilas Dhar. The future of AI will ultimately be defined not by how intelligent our systems become, but by whether they advance sustainable development for everyone, everywhere.

If you’re interested in these ideas, I invite you to explore two recent articles:

🔹 Can AI Help Power a Just Energy Future?

🔹 Digital, Data, and AI for the Future of Sustainable Energy

caption:
What if one of the defining energy challenges of this decade isn’t heating, but cooling?

In 2021, more than half a million people died from heat exposure, an increase of more than 60% since the 1990s. Every warming scenario tells us this is only the beginning.

Cooling is often seen as a household need, but it is essential across the entire development value chain. It keeps hospitals functioning, food systems running, and businesses productive. As temperatures rise and AI, digital infrastructure, and data centres drive growing electricity demand, cooling is becoming one of the defining pressures on energy systems. I have increasingly come to see cooling not as a matter of comfort, but as critical infrastructure for human development.

In this video, I share three reflections:

🔥 Heat is a justice issue. More than 1 billion people are already at high risk because they lack access to adequate cooling, with the greatest needs concentrated across the Global South, regions that have contributed the least to historical emissions. As temperatures rise, heat is amplifying existing inequalities and increasing risks for the most vulnerable communities.

📊 Cooling is a development multiplier. Cooling protects vaccines and medicines, keeps hospitals functioning, reduces food loss, and enables children to learn in safe classrooms. Today, around 13% of food is lost between harvest and retail, much of it because of inadequate cold chains.

⚡ The future of cooling depends on sustainable energy. Without action, global cooling demand could more than triple by 2050. Yet a sustainable cooling practices could cut cooling-related emissions by 64% while expanding access.

There is reason for optimism. Between 2015 and 2022, the number of countries with national cooling policies increased from 21 to 176. But policies alone are not the finish line. The next challenge is implementation at the speed and scale that today’s climate reality demands.

In a warming world, achieving SDG 7 is no longer only about expanding access to energy. It is about ensuring that energy protects lives, strengthens resilience, and enables development for everyone.

#EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7 #Cooling #JustEnergyTransition

caption:
The promise of green growth lies in turning the next wave of development investment into productive capacity, jobs and higher-value industries in developing countries. That opportunity is within reach, but the task is urgent: over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age, while current trajectories are expected to create only 400 million jobs and the sustainable development financing gap remains around $4 trillion a year.

Agro-value chains show what this can look like in practice. They connect production to higher-value activity after the farmgate, where reliable and affordable clean energy can reduce losses, strengthen SMEs, support local industry and help producer communities retain more value. Agrifood systems use about 30% of globally available energy, with around 70% of that energy used after the farmgate, making clean energy central to inclusive growth.

This week, I look forward to joining the HLPF 2026 side event “Powering Green Growth: Inclusive Solutions for Energy and Industry through Agro-Value Chains,” where we will explore how clean energy, sustainable industrialization and stronger partnerships can advance inclusive economic growth and progress on SDGs 7, 9 and 17.

📅 Wednesday, 8 July 2026 | 🕐 1:15–2:30 PM EDT | 📍 Conference Room 4, UN Headquarters, New York

Many thanks to the Permanent Mission of Malaysia to the United Nations and CPOPC for convening this timely discussion.

#HLPF2026 #SDG7 #SDG9 #SDG17 #GreenGrowth #SustainableEnergy #IndustrialDevelopment #AgroValueChains #DevelopmentFinance

The promise of green growth lies in turning the next wave of development investment into productive capacity, jobs and higher-value industries in developing countries. That opportunity is within reach, but the task is urgent: over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age, while current trajectories are expected to create only 400 million jobs and the sustainable development financing gap remains around $4 trillion a year.

Agro-value chains show what this can look like in practice. They connect production to higher-value activity after the farmgate, where reliable and affordable clean energy can reduce losses, strengthen SMEs, support local industry and help producer communities retain more value. Agrifood systems use about 30% of globally available energy, with around 70% of that energy used after the farmgate, making clean energy central to inclusive growth.

This week, I look forward to joining the HLPF 2026 side event “Powering Green Growth: Inclusive Solutions for Energy and Industry through Agro-Value Chains,” where we will explore how clean energy, sustainable industrialization and stronger partnerships can advance inclusive economic growth and progress on SDGs 7, 9 and 17.

caption:
What does it mean for the energy transition to reach the grid, the data centre and the electric vehicle, but still not reach the kitchen?
 
Today’s discussion brought that challenge into focus at the 2026 HLPF Regional Satellite Event, “From Commitment to Implementation: A Regional Dialogue on Coordinated UN-Energy Action for Clean Cooking.”
 
Clean cooking remains one of the most urgent and overlooked development challenges. While the world is investing over US$2.2 trillion in the energy transition, 2 billion people still cook with polluting fuels, and 1.8 billion are projected to remain without clean cooking in 2030.
 
The discussions made clear that clean cooking sits at the heart of health, gender equality, climate action and human dignity. Household air pollution caused 2.9 million deaths in 2021, including 309,000 children under five, while women and girls continue to carry the burden of smoke exposure and fuel collection.
 
Yet progress is possible: since 2010, India, China and Indonesia have driven 80% of the global reduction in the clean cooking access gap.
 
The conversation also reinforced the need for smarter, more targeted delivery. Of the 2 billion people without clean cooking access, 1.5 billion live in rural areas, and the top 20 access-deficit countries account for around three-quarters of the global gap. Using geospatial analytics and AI-driven tools such as the Clean Energy Equity Index, UNDP helps countries identify underserved communities and target clean energy investments where they are needed most.
 
But delivery also needs finance and systems that can turn commitments into results. Universal clean cooking access requires around US$8 billion annually, while the cost of inaction is estimated at US$2.4 trillion each year. Examples from Ghana, Rwanda and Morocco show how clear targets, public finance and delivery systems can move clean cooking from pledge to practice.
 
I left the discussion with one clear reflection: the energy transition cannot be judged only by how much power we generate, but by whether it reaches the kitchens, classrooms, clinics and communities still being left behind.
 
#HLPF2026 #SDG7 #CleanCooking #CleanEnergy #JustEnergyTransition #UNEnergy #UNDP

caption:
The world is proving that clean energy can scale at record speed. For me, the real test now is whether it can reach the countries and communities still being left behind.
 
I was pleased to participate today in the HLPF 2026 Special Event: “Implementing the Global Plan of Action for the Decade of Sustainable Energy for All to 2030,” which also marked the launch of the UN-Energy Work Programme 2026–2030.
 
The launch comes at a decisive moment for SDG 7. Clean energy is scaling faster than ever: in 2025, the world added 692 GW of new renewable electricity capacity, the largest annual increase on record, with renewables accounting for almost 97% of all new power capacity installed globally.
 
Yet progress remains too uneven. Around 655 million people still lack electricity, nearly 2 billion still rely on polluting cooking fuels, and installed renewable capacity stands at 544 watts per person globally, compared with just 33.6 watts in low-income countries.
 
This is the challenge of the final stretch to 2030.
 
The Global Plan of Action provides the roadmap. The UN-Energy Work Programme provides the coordination platform to help turn that roadmap into delivery through foresight, acceleration, partnerships, data, convening and communications.
 
What stood out to me is how deeply connected these issues have become: energy access, clean cooking, AI and digitalisation, critical minerals, green jobs, finance, gender equality and industrial development. Fragmented action will not deliver the speed or scale required.
 
SDG 7 must also move beyond access to become an engine of opportunity. The global energy sector now employs 76 million people, including at least 16.6 million in renewable energy, but many of these opportunities remain concentrated in economies with established clean-energy value chains.
 
Finance must also reach those furthest behind. International public finance for clean energy in developing countries reached US$24.6 billion in 2024, yet LDCs, LLDCs and SIDS received less than 30% of these flows.
 
At UNDP, we see this through our work supporting 398 energy projects in 131 countries: helping countries turn policy into investment, and investment into development outcomes.
 
The years to 2030 must be about delivery with speed, scale and equity.
 
#SDG7 #HLPF2026 #JustEnergyTransition #RenewableEnergy #UNEnergy #UNDP

caption:
Every year, inadequate cold chains waste 526 million tonnes of food, enough to feed 950 million people. Farmers lose around 15% of their income because they cannot access higher-value markets.
 
How much value are we leaving on the table?
 
The answer depends on one critical factor: energy.
 
It was a pleasure to join the Permanent Mission of Malaysia and CPOPC at the HLPF 2026 side event on Powering Green Growth: Inclusive Solutions for Energy and Industry through Agro-Value Chains.
 
Nearly 30% of global energy is used by agri-food systems, and more than 70% of that energy is consumed after food leaves the farm in cooling, processing, transport, and logistics. This is where countries capture value, build competitive industries, and create better jobs.
 
The real opportunity is not producing more. It is producing more value. Clean energy enables higher-value processing, stronger cold chains, digital and AI-enabled services, and the next generation of green jobs. Already 375 million people work in off-farm agri-food activities, and as agricultural production grows by 14% over the next decade, geospatial intelligence can help direct investment where renewable energy creates the greatest economic impact.
 
At UNDP, we are helping make that happen. In Nepal, our first agrovoltaic farming system supports more than 450 households with renewable energy, irrigation, and higher-value agriculture. In Kenya, our partnership with UNCDF is expected to mobilize US$31 million for solar cold storage, strengthening local value chains and reducing post-harvest losses.
 
Green growth is ultimately about turning clean energy into productive capital, connecting renewable energy with agriculture, finance and local enterprise so countries create more value at home rather than exporting it abroad.
 
Thank you to the Permanent Missions of Malaysia and Indonesia, CPOPC and fellow panelists for an excellent discussion.
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #SDG7 #SDG9

caption:
As clean energy technologies advance at record speed, can our institutions, financing models and energy systems keep pace?

Over the next five years, global electricity demand is expected to grow around 50% faster than it did over the previous decade, driven by electrification, industry, AI and digitalization. Yet financing costs for renewable energy projects remain two to three times higher in many developing economies than in advanced economies. The opportunity to accelerate development through clean energy has never been greater. Delivering on that promise requires faster implementation, stronger institutions and financing that reaches the countries where demand is growing fastest.

Join us today at the 2026 High-level Political Forum on Sustainable Development for a high-level discussion on Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition for Equity and Resilience to Advance Global Sustainable Development.

🗓️ 10 July 2026
🕒 3:00–5:30 p.m. (EDT)
📍 ECOSOC Chamber, United Nations Headquarters, New York

Organized by GEIDCO and co-organized by the Permanent Mission of China to the United Nations, UNDP, UNESCAP, UNESCWA, Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL), and the Sustainable Development Solutions Network (SDSN), the event will bring together senior leaders from across the UN system, governments and international organizations to discuss how innovation, finance, digitalization and partnerships can accelerate progress towards SDG 7.

I look forward to moderating the panel discussion with distinguished speakers from the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL), UNEP, and the WRI Polsky Energy Center, as we explore practical solutions for accelerating equitable and resilient energy transitions.

If you are in New York, we would be delighted to welcome you in person. The event will also be streamed live on UN Web TV.

🎥 Watch live: https://lnkd.in/g4FHs_kQ

caption:
US$2 trillion was invested in clean energy globally last year, yet international public clean energy finance for developing countries amounted to just US$24.6 billion.
 
At today's Building Investment Plans to Unlock Climate Finance for Vulnerable Nations dialogue at #HLPF2026, I posed a simple question: Are SIDS and LDCs truly lacking bankable projects, or are we failing to recognize where value is being created?
 
The economics of the energy transition are increasingly compelling. Renewable electricity costs are projected to fall 30% by 2030, while electricity demand over the next five years is expected to grow 50% faster than over the previous decade. Capital is available. Demand is growing.
 
The opportunity is to connect the two.
 
That starts with better data. UNDP's satellite analysis identified 1.18 billion people living in energy poverty, around 60% more than those captured by conventional electricity access metrics. Better intelligence helps reveal hidden demand, reduce investment risk, and direct finance where it can deliver the greatest development impact.
 
It also means financing economic value creation. Clean energy should power industries, transport, agriculture, and digital economies that create jobs and strengthen resilience. This matters because manufacturing value added per capita in LDCs has increased by more than 40% since 2015, yet it remains far below the global average.
 
It also requires the right conditions for private investment. With around 80% of public clean energy finance coming as debt and only 5% supporting risk mitigation, countries need policy reform, blended finance, and tools like UNDP’s Energy Finance Innovation Labs to build investable pipelines and reduce risk.
 
Investment plans become bankable pipelines when we stop financing energy as a standalone asset and start financing the economic value it unlocks.
 
That is UNDP 's role: helping countries build the institutions, markets, and investment ecosystems that turn clean energy into jobs, industries, resilience, and long-term development.
 
My thanks to SEforALL and the Governments of Australia, Barbados, Fiji, and Tuvalu for convening this timely dialogue ahead of Pre-COP31 and for advancing the broader conversation on unlocking climate finance for vulnerable countries in the lead-up to COP31.
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #PreCOP31 #RisingUpForSIDS

It also means financing economic value creation. Clean energy should power industries, transport, agriculture, and digital economies that create jobs and strengthen resilience. This matters because manufacturing value added per capita in LDCs has increased by more than 40% since 2015, yet it remains far below the global average.
 
It also requires the right conditions for private investment. With around 80% of public clean energy finance coming as debt and only 5% supporting risk mitigation, countries need policy reform, blended finance, and tools like UNDP’s Energy Finance Innovation Labs to build investable pipelines and reduce risk.
 
Investment plans become bankable pipelines when we stop financing energy as a standalone asset and start financing the economic value it unlocks.
 
That is UNDP 's role: helping countries build the institutions, markets, and investment ecosystems that turn clean energy into jobs, industries, resilience, and long-term development.
 
My thanks to SEforALL and the Governments of Australia, Barbados, Fiji, and Tuvalu for convening this timely dialogue ahead of Pre-COP31 and for advancing the broader conversation on unlocking climate finance for vulnerable countries in the lead-up to COP31.

caption:
The question I kept coming back to while moderating the discussion at the #HLPF2026 High-level Thematic Event on Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition for Equity and Resilience was a simple one:
 
Can our institutions evolve as quickly as our technologies?
 
The numbers tell an interesting story. 92% of the world's population now has access to electricity, yet the pace of electrification has slowed: Reaching universal access by 2030 will require progress at more than three times today's rate.
 
Meanwhile, the transition itself is accelerating. Renewables now generate over 30% of global electricity, solar and wind consumption has increased fivefold in the past decade, and AI could save the power sector up to USD 110 billion every year through smarter planning and operations.
 
If we have technology, innovation, what is the real bottleneck? Are we still treating electricity as the end goal, when it should be the beginning of economic transformation? 
 
I was pleased to moderate the panel discussion at today's #HLPF2026 High-level Thematic Event on Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition for Equity and Resilience, bringing together experts from the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC), Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the World Resources Institute (WRI).
 
The discussion reinforced that stronger institutions, better planning, bankable investment pipelines and financing models that reduce risk are what will determine whether innovation reaches the countries and communities that need it most. Unlocking nearly USD 1 trillion in annual private investment in emerging and developing economies will require around USD 80–100 billion of concessional finance each year.
 
My thanks to GEIDCO(Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization)  and all the partners for convening this timely dialogue, to our excellent panelists, and to everyone who contributed to such a thoughtful exchange.
 
What innovation - technological, financial or institutional - will have the greatest impact on accelerating SDG 7?
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #SDG7

caption:
The next big opportunity for sustainable cities may not be only how much clean power we generate, but how well we move it, manage it and deliver it.

The scale of opportunity is enormous. Global energy investment is set to reach US$3.3 trillion in 2025, with US$2.2 trillion flowing to clean energy technologies, including renewables, grids, storage and electrification. But that investment only delivers its full value if clean power reaches people, businesses and growing cities.

Cities are already home to 3.69 billion people, around 45% of the world's population, and account for 75% of global energy use and 70% of CO₂ emissions. As cities grow, demand from cooling, buildings, electric mobility, digital services and public infrastructure will make grids central to sustainable urban planning.

This is where grids become development infrastructure.

Modern, flexible and digital grids can connect more renewable energy, reduce outages, support electric mobility, power efficient buildings, enable cooling, strengthen water and sanitation systems, improve services in underserved communities, reduce reliance on diesel backup and unlock cleaner, more productive urban economies.

Around 3,000 GW of renewable energy projects were stuck in grid connection queues in 2023. Unlocking that power through better planning, digital systems, storage and grid investment could turn stranded clean energy into jobs, services and resilience.

By 2040, around 80 million kilometres of grids may need to be added or replaced, roughly equivalent to the entire existing global grid. This is one of the largest infrastructure opportunities of the energy transition.

For rapidly growing cities in Africa and Asia, grid investment can help avoid high-carbon lock-in and support a different urban future: cleaner air, reliable services, productive enterprises, safer streets, better cooling and more resilient communities.

As HLPF continues, the message is clear: SDG 7 and SDG 11 must be planned through the grid. Modern grids can turn clean energy ambition into sustainable urban transformation.

#SDG7 #SDG11 #JustEnergyTransition #HLPF2026 #UNDP

caption:
Africa’s energy story is not only about closing an access gap. It is about what access makes possible.
 
As we look towards 2030, this is one of the questions I believe deserves far greater attention. More than 560 million people across Sub-Saharan Africa still live without electricity, while around 970 million lack access to clean cooking. Yet Africa also holds immense potential: 60 per cent of the world’s best solar resources, over 30 per cent of known critical mineral reserves, growing digital capabilities and a new generation of entrepreneurs ready to build.
 
The challenge is to connect these strengths to delivery.
 
On Wednesday, 15 July, I will be speaking at the High-level Political Forum side event, From Evidence to Action: Accelerating Energy Access and Just Transitions in Africa, at the Permanent Representation of Nigeria to the United Nations in New York.
 
I look forward to discussing how we can accelerate a just energy transition that expands access, powers businesses, strengthens essential services and creates jobs, while using evidence, AI, geospatial analytics and real-time data to target finance, track progress and scale solutions faster.
 
Africa does not lack energy potential. What is needed now is the ability to translate that potential into results that people can see and feel in their daily lives.
 
📅Date: Wednesday, 15 July 2026

🕘Time: 9:00–10:30 AM EDT

📍Venue: Permanent Representation of Nigeria to the United Nations, 828 Second Avenue, 21st Floor, New York
 
I look forward to contributing to this timely conversation and reflecting on how we can turn evidence into action, and energy access into opportunity.

caption:
"The clean energy transition is unstoppable. The question is whether the development transition will keep pace."
 
That was the defining message emerging from the UN High-Level Meeting on Critical Energy Transition Minerals and the thematic roundtables at #HLPF2026.
 
Demand for critical energy transition minerals is expected to almost triple by 2030, while around US$500 billion in new mining investment will be needed by 2040. Yet between 2020 and 2024, nearly 90 percent of new refining capacity for key critical minerals was added by a single leading producer for each mineral. The challenge is no longer only securing supply. It is creating more diversified, resilient and equitable value chains that also deliver development.
 
Throughout yesterday’s  discussions, one message resonated across governments, industry, international organizations, Indigenous Peoples and civil society:
The energy transition cannot repeat yesterday's extractive model.
 
Resource-rich countries should not remain exporters of raw materials while higher-value industries, technology and jobs are created elsewhere. Critical minerals must become a catalyst for industrialization, economic diversification, decent work and long-term prosperity.
 
The conversation has moved beyond principles. It is now about implementation. 
 
The Secretary-General's Guiding Principles provide the roadmap. The task now is to translate them into country-level action through stronger institutions, financing, technology transfer, local value creation and trusted international partnerships.
 
As co-chair of the UN Joint Task Force on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, together with UNCTAD and UNEP, and with UNDP leading the Country Support Mechanism, we are working with countries to turn these principles into practical support that strengthens governance, mobilizes investment and helps countries move up mineral value chains.
 
Critical minerals can power the energy transition if we ensure they also power development.
 
#EnergyforDevelopment #HLPF2026 #UNDP

caption:
Digital technologies, including AI and Digital Public Infrastructure, are becoming central to sustainable development. They can strengthen energy systems, improve public services and build resilience, but their rapid growth is also increasing demand for electricity, water, critical minerals and computing capacity.
 
As we approach 2030, this tension deserves greater attention. Around US$7 trillion could be invested in data centres and computing infrastructure, including more than US$5 trillion linked to AI. Yet developing economies may capture only around 10 per cent of AI’s projected US$15.7 trillion in global value.
 
The challenge is to ensure the digital transition advances sustainable development without adding new environmental pressures or widening inequality.
 
On Thursday, 16 July, I will be speaking at the High-level Political Forum side event, Advancing Digital Environmental Sustainability for SDG Implementation: Aligning the Global Digital Compact with the HLPF, at UN Headquarters in New York.
 
I will also be sharing insights from UNDP’s latest publication, The Energy Sprint of the AI Race, which explores how countries can align AI, energy, infrastructure, skills and natural resources to capture the opportunities of the digital transition.
 
We will discuss how AI, Digital Public Infrastructure and other innovations can accelerate the SDGs while managing their environmental footprint, and how the Global Digital Compact can support a more sustainable Beyond 2030 agenda.
 
Digital transformation and sustainable development must move together so that technology creates jobs, strengthens resilience and improves lives.
 
📅Date: Thursday, 16 July 2026
🕐Time: 13:15–14:30 ET
📍Venue: UN Headquarters, Conference Room 4, New York

caption:
What if Africa’s energy challenge is not only about who gets connected, but what those connections make possible?

That was the reflection I took from yesterday’s discussion on “From Evidence to Action: Accelerating Energy Access and Just Transitions in Africa,” hosted at the Permanent Representation of Nigeria.

Electricity access in sub-Saharan Africa rose from 51% in 2017 to 61% in 2023, with more than 120 million people gaining access in six years. Yet the scale of the challenge remains stark: the region still accounts for 86% of the global electricity access deficit, with 563 million people without power, while around 970 million people lack clean cooking.

The message from today was clear: energy access must become a platform for jobs, resilience, industry and a just transition.

Africa has the resources to lead this shift. The continent holds around 60% of the world’s best solar resources and more than 30% of known critical mineral reserves, yet imports over 80% of the technologies needed for renewable energy deployment. The opportunity is to turn this potential into cheaper power, local value chains, clean industries and decent jobs.

Decentralized energy systems are central to this agenda, especially in hard-to-reach communities.

Through initiatives Africa Minigrids Programme, Energy for Grwoth and Solar for Healts, and collaborating with Mission 300 partners, UNDP is helping African countries move beyond isolated pilot projects by creating the enabling environment for renewable energy system to scale through commercial investment, rural electrification and productive energy use.

Delivery must also become smarter. AI-enabled grid management can improve renewable integration by 20–30%, while geospatial planning, as seen in Rwanda, Zambia and Nigeria, can target grid, mini-grid and off-grid solutions where they best support rural electrification, agriculture, healthcare and local enterprise.

Africa’s energy future is not defined by a lack of potential, but by how quickly we can turn evidence into investment, and investment into delivery that creates jobs, strengthens local enterprise and expands shared prosperity.

#SDG7 #Africa #EnergyAccess #JustEnergyTransition #UNDP
