caption:
Can AI become a catalyst for sustainable development without becoming a growing burden on the planet?

That was the central question from today’s 2026 HLPF side event on Advancing Digital Environmental Sustainability for SDG Implementation. As the HLPF draws to a close, the discussion reinforced that digital transformation must be integrated into the sustainable development agenda.

AI is reshaping development, but behind every algorithm lies a physical system powered by electricity, water, minerals and infrastructure. By 2030, data centres could use 945 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent of the current electricity consumption of Africa.

By 2030, AI is expected to add US$15.7 trillion to the global economy, while developing countries may capture only 10% of that value.

I shared insights from UNDP ’s report, The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries, which shows that AI’s next frontier will depend as much on energy systems as computing power. It calls for Green AI that advances people, protects the planet and expands prosperity by aligning digital investment with clean energy and national priorities.

I shared three key priorities: directing AI towards practical development challenges, building skills and innovation ecosystems that create domestic value, and embedding sustainability and accountability into investment from the outset.

Examples are emerging. In Kenya, AI-enabled energy systems are improving affordability and resilience. In Moldova, UNDP is supporting 500,000 smart meters by 2030. UNDP tools, such as the Clean Energy Equity Index and the Electricity Access Forecasting Model, are helping countries improve AI and digital planning and resilience.

My takeaway is that the Global Digital Compact must move from ambition to implementation. Beyond 2030, digital progress should be defined not by technological scale alone, but by its contribution to inclusion, resilience and sustainable development.

#UNDP #HLPF2026 #GreenAI #DigitalSustainability

caption:
What does mineral security mean if mineral-rich countries remain at the lowest-value end of the supply chain?

Following last week's first UN High-Level Meeting on Critical Energy Transition Minerals, attention is rightly focused on building more resilient and diversified supply chains.

But I have increasingly come to see mineral security as more than securing supply. It must also be about where value is created, who develops the technology and skills, and whether communities share in the benefits of the transition. This is particularly important for many countries across the Global South that supply critical minerals for renewable energy, battery storage and e-mobility.

Critical minerals have moved from being solely an energy issue to becoming an energy, economic and national security issue. As demand for clean energy technologies continues to grow, the opportunity for producing countries extends far beyond mining. If Latin America refined its lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths domestically—and processed two-thirds of its copper—the economic value generated could increase by nearly 50%, reaching approximately USD 220 billion by 2035.

This points to a broader shift: from exporting raw materials to building regional value chains, developing manufacturing capacity, creating skilled jobs and strengthening economic resilience. It also requires investment, technology, workforce development, international cooperation and traceability to build transparent, trusted and resilient value chains that attract investment while ensuring producing countries capture a greater share of the benefits.

South-South cooperation can help make this transformation possible by connecting mineral resources with shared infrastructure, knowledge, investment and markets.

Critical minerals must power development, not reproduce dependency.

The measure of mineral security is not only supply. It is shared prosperity.

It must also be about where value is created, who develops the technology and skills, and whether communities share in the benefits of the transition. This is particularly important for many countries across the Global South that supply critical minerals for renewable energy, battery storage and e-mobility.

Critical minerals have moved from being solely an energy issue to becoming an energy, economic and national security issue. As demand for clean energy technologies continues to grow, the opportunity for producing countries extends far beyond mining. If Latin America refined its lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths domestically—and processed two-thirds of its copper—the economic value generated could increase by nearly 50%, reaching approximately USD 220 billion by 2035.

This points to a broader shift: from exporting raw materials to building regional value chains, developing manufacturing capacity, creating skilled jobs and strengthening economic resilience. It also requires investment, technology, workforce development, international cooperation and traceability to build transparent, trusted and resilient value chains that attract investment while ensuring producing countries capture a greater share of the benefits.

South-South cooperation can help make this transformation possible by connecting mineral resources with shared infrastructure, knowledge, investment and markets.

Critical minerals must power development, not reproduce dependency.

The measure of mineral security is not only supply. It is shared prosperity.

caption:
⚡ Renewables can do more than generate clean power. Combined with modern grids, storage and digital intelligence, they can deliver reliable energy for people.
 
In 2025, the world added a record 692 GW of renewable power capacity, alongside 108 GW of new battery storage, 40% more than the year before.  
 
Together, these investments create a major opportunity. Grids can move electricity where it is needed, storage can make it available beyond the hours when the sun shines or the wind blows, and digital tools can help systems respond to changing supply and demand.
 
For people, that means health facilities that keep operating, schools that stay connected, businesses that can grow and communities that are better prepared for disruption.
 
Uruguay shows what coordinated investment can achieve. Through long-term policy, public investment and power-system planning, the country reached a 98% share of renewables in its electricity mix in 2019.
 
For me, this is how energy progress should be measured: not only by how much clean power a system can produce, but by how reliably it improves people’s lives.
 
For close to 1 billion people served by health facilities with unreliable electricity or none at all, reliability determines whether vaccines stay cold, medical equipment works and essential care continues.  
 
Three investments can unlock this opportunity:
 
🌍 Modern and decentralized grids bring clean energy closer to people, connecting generation, storage and demand while helping essential services withstand disruptions.
 
🔋 Storage makes variable power dependable, capturing electricity when supply is abundant and releasing it when demand rises.
 
📊 Digital management adds flexibility. Better forecasting and digitally enabled demand response could reduce renewable curtailment by more than 25% by 2030.
 
Across the Global South, this is an opportunity to build renewable capacity and the infrastructure that makes it reliable at the same time.
 
Renewable capacity shows what we can generate. Integrated energy systems show what we can deliver.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #EnergyStorage #EnergyResilience

I recently went hiking in #California, and my family were * thrilled * when I started talking about California geological history and want it means for my day job in #energy.

Some of the oldest rocks in California are over 1.5 billion years old. (The world 'billion' also makes sense outside of the state's Silicon Valley too!). Layered up over time, they've formed sediments of mud, fossils, stones, and dirt. And what else has this kind of layering I hear you ask? (I'm pretty sure you asked...?).

Our Digital Energy Stack!

As the AI 'race' reaffirms how energy is both a key driver of sustainable development and #21stCentury industrial policy, energy needs to be much more intertwined with how we develop and deploy digital. This is the thinking behind our stack. Identifying - and supporting countries and communities to implement - the tech (and non-tech) elements needed to unlock the combined power and potential of digital and energy.

We'd love your reflections on this. The seven layers we've identified are:

1️⃣ Data - crucial for energy planning, optimisation, and measuring energy inclusion.

2️⃣ Connectivity - including the potential of shared business models, such as PAYG solar.

3️⃣ Compute - processing power to shape energy inclusion planning, but also a resource that needs to be carefully shaped alongside domestic energy supply.

4️⃣ Digital Public Infrastructure - our digital roads and railways, which can improve energy access through better credit scoring and improved data exchange.

5️⃣ Cybersecurity - protecting energy assets which are critical national infrastructure. 

6️⃣ AI - already improving grid planning, and also providing opportunities to better connect under-served communities.

And(!), 7️⃣ governance. Digital is just a tool in our energy toolkit. We need to build the skills, expertise, and institutions to make this strategic thinking happen.

Read more at @Illuminem: https://lnkd.in/erzAG8Fg

caption:
This #InternationalYouthDay is a reflective one for me. The theme of the day - Different Contexts, Common Aspirations - is particularly centred around young people living, working, and growing in #LeastDevelopedCountries, #LandlockedDevelopingCountries and #SmallIslandDeveloping States (SIDS). Settings where I've spent the majority of my UN career. And, our recent collaboration with @Goodwall has highlighted what these three different contexts have in common: energy.
 
From the urgent needs of last-mile energy infrastructure in least developed settings, to the crucial collaborations driving cross-border energy infrastructure in landlocked countries - as well as the phenomenal renewable energy potential of SIDS - the common aspiration we need to be talking about this International Youth Day is that of a just energy transition that works for all people. Everywhere. And where young people are the drivers of this transition.
 
So, to empower young people at this crucial juncture we're meeting them where they are. Through the NextGen Energy Champions Initiative — a partnership between UNDP  and Goodwall  — youth aged 16 to 30, anywhere in the world, can use gamified learning on the Goodwall platform to:

→ Watch curated videos on clean energy technology, policy, and careers

→ Complete knowledge quizzes

→ Record a 30-second video sharing their perspective on #CleanEnergy

Because a just energy transition isn’t built for young people. It’s built with them.

Aged 16 to 30? Download Goodwall and take on the challenge.

caption:
⚡ Can the AI and energy revolutions grow without deepening water stress?
 
As World Water Week 2026 continues in Stockholm under the theme "Water for People and Progress," this is the question I keep coming back to: AI is no longer only an energy story.
 
By 2027, AI is projected to withdraw 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic metres of water annually, up to six times Denmark's total annual water withdrawal. Cooling is a major part of the equation. Data centres generate enormous amounts of heat, and removing that heat can require significant volumes of water, especially in hot climates.
 
I have come to see this as a siting and governance question rather than a technology one. Where digital infrastructure is built, and under what rules, will determine whether it strengthens or strains local water systems.
Three approaches are worth watching:
 
📐 Set measurable standards. Singapore's Green Data Center Roadmap prioritises energy efficiency and cooling technologies suited to tropical climates, and steers new development toward areas with cleaner grids and more abundant resources.
 
💧 Make water conditions part of approval. Malaysia, South-East Asia's most water-stressed country, has more than 100 proposed data centres that could consume over 808 million litres a day. Regulators now require all new facilities to use only recycled, reclaimed or rainwater as a condition of approval.
 
🌍 Plan for local conditions, not imported models. In Asia and the Pacific, water-use effectiveness averages 1.65 litres per kilowatt-hour, more than three times the global average of 0.5. Cooling strategies that work in Stockholm will not work in Kuala Lumpur.
 
For countries across the Global South, the opportunity is not simply to host the next generation of digital infrastructure, but to shape how it is powered, cooled and governed.
 
The AI revolution will be judged not only by what it computes, but by what it consumes.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #WorldWaterWeek

caption:
⚡ What if the path to universal energy access is not about choosing between grid and off-grid solutions, but planning them together?
 
That question is becoming more urgent. Electricity demand from data centres is set to more than double by 2030, reaching around 945 TWh. In several emerging data-centre hubs, AI infrastructure already accounts for 5 to 20 percent of total electricity demand.
For developing countries, digital growth can crowd in investment and modernise power systems, or compete with households, clinics and small businesses for limited electricity. The outcome depends on how power systems are planned today.
 
New analysis across Burkina Faso, Mali, Nigeria and Senegal shows why this matters. Where grid expansion is constrained, mini-grids can serve between 47 million and 110 million people out of 171 million needing access, accounting for more than half of new connections in some scenarios.
 
Battery storage can strengthen that pathway. Across the scenarios assessed, fuel savings average around US$2 for every US$1 of additional storage investment. Under optimistic mini-grid costs at Tier 2–3 demand levels, savings can reach up to US$4 for every US$1 invested by reducing diesel generation.
 
For me, the lesson is that grid extension, mini-grids, storage and digital infrastructure cannot be planned in isolation. Digital demand is reshaping power-system needs, while grids and storage determine how that growth can be served.
 
For countries still closing their access gaps, the opportunity is to plan grids, storage and digital growth together, so that rising demand expands access and opportunity rather than competing for scarce power.
 
🔗 Further reading: IRENA, Unlocking battery storage potential for sustainable mini-grid electrification in West Africa
https://bit.ly/4ynideG

caption:
⚡ What does development look like in an age when electricity is becoming more important to the global economy, but 655 million people still live without it?
 
As the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opens today, the world is entering what the IEA calls the “Age of Electricity.”
 
🌍 92% of the world now has access to electricity. Yet 655 million people remain without it — and 86% of them live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
🍳 2 billion people still rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, including 970 million in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
⚡ Meanwhile, global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6% annually through 2030, adding around 1,100 TWh each year.
 
💻 Data centres alone could consume around 945 TWh by 2030, more than double today’s level.
 
☀️ Renewables now provide over 30% of global electricity. But renewable generating capacity averages just 33.6 watts per person in low-income countries, compared with 1,224 watts in high-income countries — a gap of more than 36 times.
 
For me, these numbers point to a fundamental development challenge: we are building an increasingly electrified global economy, but we are not yet building it equally.
 
AI, data centres, advanced manufacturing, electric mobility and cooling are increasing the value of reliable power. Yet where energy could unlock some of the greatest development gains, hundreds of millions still lack basic access.
 
The energy transition therefore cannot be measured only in gigawatts installed or emissions avoided. We also need to ask where new capacity is built, who can access it, and what opportunities it creates.

caption:
⚡The energy transition is about Jobs. But where and for who ?
 
Renewable energy employment reached a record 16.6 million jobs globally in 2024.
 
Yet more than 85% of those jobs are concentrated in just five countries and regions.
 
That raises a bigger question: the energy transition is creating enormous economic value — but who will have the opportunity to create, own and benefit from it?
 
A just transition is not only about creating more green jobs.
 
🏭 It is about socio-economic development, where new industries and supply chains are built. Between 2018 and 2024, China accounted for around 80% of global investment in manufacturing facilities for solar, wind, batteries and hydrogen technologies.
 
💰 It is about where investment flows. Low- and lower-middle-income countries are home to more than 40% of the world’s population, yet account for only 7% of global clean energy spending. In emerging and developing economies, the cost of capital for renewable energy projects can be two to three times higher than in advanced economies.
 
👷 It is about whether workers can access the opportunities being created. Around 60% of energy companies report labour shortages, and the number of graduates entering the energy sector would need to increase by around 40% by 2030 just to prevent today’s skills mismatch from worsening.
 
⚡ And it is about whether the transition ultimately delivers for people and planet. Even as clean energy investment and employment reach record levels, 655 million people worldwide still live without electricity.
 
These numbers are connected.
 
Where investment and manufacturing concentrate, jobs and economic value tend to follow.
 
For developing economies, a just transition must therefore be about more than replacing one energy source with another. It must help create decent jobs, build local industries and skills, expand affordable and reliable energy access, mobilize investment and support economic diversification.
 
As #UNGA81 gathers momentum, the question is not only how fast we can move. It is how we ensure more countries, communities and people can participate in creating the value generated by the transition — and share in its benefits.
 
Speed matters. But so does where the transition takes us — and who gets there with us.
 
#JustEnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

caption:
🌍 YOUNG PEOPLE ARE NOT WAITING FOR THE ENERGY TRANSITION. THEY ARE ALREADY SHAPING IT.
 
As #UNGA81 gathers momentum, young people should not be discussed only as the generation that will inherit the energy transition.
 
They are already part of it.
 
👥 Over the next decade, 1.2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age. Yet only around 420 million jobs are projected to be created.
 
⚡ At the same time, the energy transition is opening new economic opportunities. Renewable energy already supports 16.6 million jobs worldwide.
 
🎓 But there is a skills gap. Globally, only 1 in 20 Gen Z workers has the green skills needed for the changing economy, compared with 1 in 8 workers overall.
 
💡 This is not simply a jobs challenge. It is a youth opportunity challenge.
 
Young people are already developing ideas, building businesses, learning new technologies and creating solutions in their communities.
 
But meaningful participation requires more than asking for their views.
 
It means giving young people the skills and practical experience to turn ideas into action. Access to mentors, networks and finance. Opportunities to build businesses and careers. And a real voice in the decisions shaping the energy systems they will live with for decades.
 
Young people should not simply inherit the energy transition.
 
They should have the opportunity to build it.
 
As UNGA81’s High-Level Week approaches, we will continue bringing young people’s perspectives into the energy conversation in New York — and exploring how we can better connect their ambition and ideas with real opportunities.
 
The next generation is ready.
 
The question is whether the opportunities will be ready for them.
 
#UNGA81 #YouthInEnergy #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

caption:
Could clean cooking be one of the most powerful opportunities to advance health, gender equality and sustainable development?
 
On the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies, I keep coming back to clean cooking.
 
Nearly 2 billion people still lack access to clean cooking. In rural Sub-Saharan Africa, only 7% of the population has access to clean cooking fuels.
 
The consequences reach far beyond the kitchen. Household air pollution caused an estimated 2.9 million deaths in 2021, while polluting cooking also affects productivity, gender equality and economic opportunity.
 
Yet the investment gap remains striking.
 
Around US$2.5 billion is invested in clean cooking solutions each year, less than a third of the US$8 billion needed annually to achieve universal access. Meanwhile, the health, environmental and productivity costs associated with polluting cooking are estimated at US$2.4–4 trillion every year.
 
For me, this makes clean cooking not simply an energy technology, but a development priority across the Global South.
 
Three shifts can help accelerate progress:
🔌 Integrate clean cooking into national energy planning. Nepal aims for 25% of households to adopt electric cooking by 2030, linking clean cooking directly to wider electrification efforts.
💰 Make finance reach the households most often left behind. Grants, subsidies and blended finance can help reduce upfront costs for rural and low-income communities.
🗺️ Use data and digital tools to target solutions better. Mapping grid reliability, consumer demand and e-cooking potential can help direct investment where it can deliver the greatest impact.
 
Clean air, energy access and development should not be treated as separate agendas.
 
Clean cooking can improve health, expand opportunity and make a just energy transition more inclusive at the same time.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustEnergyTransition #CleanCooking #CleanAir

caption:
On Sept. 23, at #UNGA81, UNDP will bring more than 58,000 young voices into the conversation at “Sparking the Next Generation of Energy Talent.”

Working with Goodwall, we heard directly from young people around the world on how they see their roles in the energy transition. And their engagement was encouraging:
- "Give us the skills, give us the affordable tools, and we will be powering Kenya's digital future."
- "Every hour of darkness is an hour of lost potential... In Nigeria, we have some of the most abundant sunshine on earth. We just need the will to use it."
By 2030, 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce. Fewer than 40% are projected to have the skills needed for the green economy.

Demand for green talent is already accelerating:
☀️ Solar PV supported 7.2 million jobs globally in 2024.
💼 Workers with green skills are hired at a rate 46.6% above the workforce average.
🎓 Only 1 in 20 Gen Z workers has the green skills needed to access these opportunities.

We have listened to more than 58,000 young people about their ambitions, the opportunities they want to pursue and the barriers they face. We are bringing their voices to #UNGA81.

Creating green jobs must be matched by access to relevant skills, work experience, mentorship, networks and finance.

We need stronger links between learning and employment, skills and jobs, ideas and capital, and young talent and the industries emerging through the energy transition.
Young people are the workforce needed to deliver the transition now.

#YouthInEnergy #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

caption:
What if the strongest case for greening our operations is what clean energy enables beyond carbon?

UNDP’s new Greening Moonshot report offers a useful answer.

Halfway to 2030, we have reduced operational emissions by 25 percent compared with 2018. More than 200 projects now reduce over 4,000 tonnes of CO₂e each year while saving nearly $2 million annually in energy costs. Every $1 invested in green energy solutions now delivers around $8.5 in lifetime energy savings.

But the development story goes further.

⚡ Reliable energy enables delivery. In Afghanistan, more than 370 kWp of solar capacity is reducing dependence on diesel where the national grid is unreliable. In Haiti, renewable energy supplies around two-thirds of office power through chronic blackouts and fuel shortages.

💰 Efficiency creates development resources. Greening investments have enabled more than $21 million to be reprogrammed to country priorities.

📊 Data makes the transition smarter. Different energy systems require different solutions. Solar and batteries make sense for generator-dependent offices. E-mobility can deliver greater gains where electricity is already clean.

This is why I increasingly see clean energy as development infrastructure.

It keeps teams working, reduces exposure to energy shocks and frees resources for the communities we serve.

The energy transition succeeds when it improves how development is delivered.

#EnergyForDevelopment #CleanEnergy #ClimateAction #GreeningMoonshot

caption:
AI is creating a global race for power. Governments are moving quickly to build generation, grids and dedicated capacity for data centres. That urgency should extend to the energy needed by schools, hospitals, farms and businesses.

On 23 September, I will join the IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit during New York Climate Week to discuss The Role of AI in Accelerating Energy System Innovation and Transition.

The numbers show how quickly the energy landscape is changing:

Data-centre electricity consumption could almost double between 2025 and 2030, rising from around 485 TWh to 950 TWh.

More than 100 GW of new gas capacity is planned as dedicated onsite supply for data centres. Almost all of it is in the United States, with around 13 GW announced or under development elsewhere.

Middle-income countries generate around half of ChatGPT traffic, while low- and middle-income countries host only about one-quarter of global data-centre capacity.

AI is a double-edged sword for energy systems. It can improve renewable forecasting, grid management, efficiency and investment planning. It can also drive major new electricity demand, make fossil-fuel extraction cheaper and more productive, and extend dependence on existing fuels. Policies, safeguards and financing decisions will determine which effects dominate.

I look forward to discussing how countries can shape this expansion around their own development priorities: building additional clean power, strengthening grids, protecting people and ecosystems, and ensuring that the infrastructure and value created are more widely shared.

#ClimateWeekNYC #ArtificialIntelligence #EnergyTransition #EnergyForDevelopment #SustainableAI

caption:
On Sept. 23, at #UNGA81, UNDP  will bring more than 58,000 young voices into the conversation at “Sparking the Next Generation of Energy Talent.”

Working with Goodwall , we heard directly from young people around the world on how they see their roles in the energy transition. And their engagement was encouraging:
- "Give us the skills, give us the affordable tools, and we will be powering Kenya's digital future."
- "Every hour of darkness is an hour of lost potential... In Nigeria, we have some of the most abundant sunshine on earth. We just need the will to use it."
By 2030, 1.2 billion young people are expected to enter the global workforce. Fewer than 40% are projected to have the skills needed for the green economy.

Demand for green talent is already accelerating:
☀️ Solar PV supported 7.2 million jobs globally in 2024.
💼 Workers with green skills are hired at a rate 46.6% above the workforce average.
🎓 Only 1 in 20 Gen Z workers has the green skills needed to access these opportunities.

We have listened to more than 58,000 young people about their ambitions, the opportunities they want to pursue and the barriers they face. We are bringing their voices to #UNGA81.

Creating green jobs must be matched by access to relevant skills, work experience, mentorship, networks and finance.

We need stronger links between learning and employment, skills and jobs, ideas and capital, and young talent and the industries emerging through the energy transition.
Young people are the workforce needed to deliver the transition now.

#YouthInEnergy #EnergyForDevelopment #SDG7

caption:
Before I led UNDP's work on decarbonization and sustainable energy, I served as Senior Principal Advisor for Small Island Developing States.
 
That work taught me something: in SIDS, energy is never just infrastructure. It's sovereignty. It's fiscal space. And after a storm, it's survival.
 
On Sept. 22, I'll be joining the AEG Caribbean Energy Roundtable during Climate Week. Here's what's on my mind:
 
Over 90% of energy across SIDS is imported oil. Caribbean households pay up to 3x more for electricity than in the US.
 
In Dominica, two primary schools destroyed by Hurricane Maria were rebuilt to survive Category 5 winds, with solar microgrids that now double as hurricane shelters. In Haiti, a 120-bed hospital in Bonne Fin with no grid connection ran straight through Hurricane Matthew on solar and batteries. 
 
Decentralization isn't the second-best option for small islands. It's the resilient one.
 
The region needs roughly $1.25B a year to transition.
But actual investment has been closer to $50M.
 
The technology isn't the gap. It's capital not showing up: 
- It's aging grids that can't absorb distributed generation. 
- It's projects stalling between preparation and financing. 
- And it's fiscal space: six of the world's ten most indebted small island economies are Caribbean, while fuel imports alone consume between 7 and 12% of GDP across much of the region, and over 20% in some.

Which is why I'm looking forward to this conversation. Not another round of pledges, but a room built to move money: leaders of Caribbean heritage alongside regional public, private, and civic partners, committed to catalytic impact within 12 months.
See you there. 
 
#ClimateWeekNYC #SIDS #EnergyTransition

caption:
With the start of UNGA, electrification is moving to the centre of the development agenda. 

Are we able to move from ambition to implementation?


“35 by 35” captures the scale of the challenge: increasing electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from just over 20% today to 35% by 2035.

Tomorrow, at #UNGA81, on September 22, the COP31 Presidency, the International Energy Agency (IEA)  and the United Nations will convene the third High-Level Energy Transitions Solutions Dialogue during UNGA High-Level Week.

The discussion will focus on the systems needed to support electrification across transport, buildings and industry, including stronger grids, storage and flexibility:

* Global grid investment is expected to reach around US$550 billion in 2026, up 17% in one year, although higher equipment costs account for part of this growth.
* Battery storage investment is expected to exceed US$100 billion.
* More than 2,500 GW of renewable generation, storage and large-load projects are waiting in grid connection queues worldwide.

The dialogue will also address energy efficiency, clean cooking and energy security, with a focus on moving these priorities into national plans, investment pipelines and implementation.

UNDP  is supporting countries to translate global energy ambitions into country-level delivery and impact at scale.

I look forward to the discussion around advancing the systems, financing and partnerships required to deliver 35 by 35.

#UNGA81 #COP31 #EnergyTransition #Electrification #EnergySecurity

caption:
What is the development return on a clean cookstove?

Yesterday, UNDP  joined the first High-Level Event on Clean Cooking at the UN General Assembly, convened by Kenya and Norway with support from the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Africa is expanding clean cooking access faster than ever. In 2024, progress was three times faster than in 2010. Yet population growth meant that, by year’s end, 14 million more people were relying on wood and charcoal.

Polluting cooking costs the world more than US$2.4 trillion each year. Universal access would require around US$8 billion annually through 2030.
We are paying trillions to avoid investing billions.

Clean cooking requires more than distributing stoves. It needs fuels, finance, infrastructure, local businesses and services that households can depend on every day.

More than 120 clean cooking policies have been introduced across Africa over the past two years. Through Mission 300, its partnership with UNCDF and a portfolio reaching more than 2.5 million people, UNDP is helping turn that momentum into functioning markets and investable programmes.

The return is cleaner air, time returned to women and girls, stronger local businesses and more resilient economies.

The return is measured in lives saved, hours reclaimed by women and girls, businesses built and forests protected. At US$8 billion a year, the question is why we continue to pay US$2.4 trillion instead.

#CleanCooking #EnergyAccess #SustainableDevelopment #GenderEquality #Mission300

What is the development return on a clean cookstove?

Yesterday, UNDP  joined the first High-Level Event on Clean Cooking at the UN General Assembly, convened by Kenya and Norway with support from the International Energy Agency (IEA).

Africa is expanding clean cooking access faster than ever. In 2024, progress was three times faster than in 2010. Yet population growth meant that, by year’s end, 14 million more people were relying on wood and charcoal.

Polluting cooking costs the world more than US$2.4 trillion each year. Universal access would require around US$8 billion annually through 2030.
We are paying trillions to avoid investing billions.

Clean cooking requires more than distributing stoves. It needs fuels, finance, infrastructure, local businesses and services that households can depend on every day.

More than 120 clean cooking policies have been introduced across Africa over the past two years. Through Mission 300, its partnership with UNCDF and a portfolio reaching more than 2.5 million people, UNDP is helping turn that momentum into functioning markets and investable programmes.

The return is cleaner air, time returned to women and girls, stronger local businesses and more resilient economies.

The return is measured in lives saved, hours reclaimed by women and girls, businesses built and forests protected. At US$8 billion a year, the question is why we continue to pay US$2.4 trillion instead.

#CleanCooking #EnergyAccess #SustainableDevelopment #GenderEquality #Mission300

caption:
74% of participants wanted to explore clean energy careers. 56% asked how to start.

These are findings from UNDP and Goodwall’s conversations with more than 58,000 young people across over 180 countries. One participant described people travelling long distances just to charge their devices. With 655 million people still without electricity, that journey says a great deal about who can access the digital economy.

Today, we brought public and private sector partners together to discuss how to close the skills gap and bring clean energy jobs to places that need them most.

Renewable energy already employs 16.6 million people, but more than 85% of those jobs are concentrated in five countries and regions. The talent is far more widely distributed.

Young people proposed businesses ranging from solar-powered kitchens to sustainable energy consultancies. They also asked for practical ways to learn the skills those ideas require. UNDP’s upcoming Sustainable Energy Academy will offer more than 40 hours of modules spanning energy finance and governance, access and efficiency, data and technology, and the climate-energy nexus.

As a young man from the Philippines told us: “Invest not only in clean energy technologies, but also in the young people who build them. Because when we power communities with clean energy, we don't just light homes, we ignite opportunities.”

Every year of delay leaves communities without reliable power and holds back the people ready to build a cleaner energy future.

Tomorrow, UNDP  and Goodwall  will release "Powering the Future," our full report on the careers young people want to pursue, the businesses they want to build, and what they need to get started.

#CleanEnergyJobs #YouthEmployment #EnergyAccess #JustEnergyTransition #SDG7

caption:
The world is planning for a surge in electricity demand. 

How can this be turned into an opportunity for energy security and socio-economic resilience?

Yesterday, UNDP  joined the COP31 Türkiye –IEA–UN High-Level Energy Transition Solutions Dialogue at UN Headquarters. The IEA also released new analysis prepared for the COP31 discussions.

Its findings point to the scale of the opportunity. Electricity could cost-effectively meet 33% of global final energy use by 2035, up from 23% today, putting the proposed 35% goal within reach. In a faster electrification scenario, fuel-importing countries could cut their energy import bills by more than US$400 billion by 2035—reducing exposure to volatile fossil-fuel markets and strengthening energy security.

Accelerating electrification can create a broader development dividend. Investment in renewable energy, grids, storage and clean technologies can support green jobs, build domestic value chains and drive green industrialization, to power that businesses and communities need to grow.

But realizing this opportunity will require investment in generation and grids, while addressing the upfront costs that can prevent households and businesses from benefiting. Around 1.18 billion people still experience energy poverty, while Africa receives only 2% of global clean energy investment.

UNDP is supporting this effort alongside around 30 UN entities, with the aim of helping at least 100 countries build the policies and project pipelines needed to put finance to work.

The opportunity is not simply to electrify more of the global economy, but to use electrification to build more secure, resilient and inclusive economies. By 2035, can we ensure that growing electricity demand translates into new industries and green jobs, while also delivering reliable and affordable energy to hospitals, businesses and households?

Read the International Energy Agency (IEA)  analysis here: https://lnkd.in/geS9jit6

#UNGA #COP31 #EnergyTransition #SDG7

caption:
Everyone is asking who will win the AI race. During yesterday’s IEEE Tech for Sustainability Summit in New York, I posed a different question: what does winning actually mean?

For me, the answer starts with energy.

AI could help unlock up to 175 GW of capacity from existing transmission lines. Across the Global South, companies are already using it for grid optimisation, smart metering, forecasting and industrial efficiency.

But the same technology can push in the opposite direction. AI is also making oil and gas exploration faster and cheaper, with recent modelling suggesting the resulting emissions could be 3.3 to 13.3 times larger than estimated 2025 data-centre emissions.

So the question is not whether AI is efficient. It is what AI is making more efficient.

This matters when 91% of new utility-scale renewable projects are already cheaper than the cheapest new fossil alternative. In Pakistan, low-cost solar imports helped avoid more than $12 billion in fuel imports. In Chile, financing for the 151 MW Calama wind farm was linked to emissions avoided through early coal retirement.

AI will add another major source of electricity demand. Whether that extends the age of energy addition or accelerates the transition will depend on choices around grids, finance, standards and public policy.

And who captures the value?

Middle-income countries generate more than 40% of ChatGPT traffic, yet middle- and low-income countries host only around 27% of shared data-centre facilities.

A sustainable AI framework must therefore ask what AI enables across the economy, where infrastructure is built, who owns the capabilities, and what countries gain in return.

Human intelligence created this wave. The task now is to decide where we direct it.

We explore these questions further in UNDP’s The Energy Sprint of the AI Race: A Green Window of Opportunity for Developing Countries?

caption:
Which country, after Norway, had the highest share of electric cars in new car sales last year? Nepal, at 68%.

I opened with that question at today’s SDG7 Action Forum in New York. We often describe SDG7 through its gaps: 655 million people without electricity and two billion without clean cooking. But that account misses how quickly energy markets are changing.

Solar’s share of global electricity has risen from 1% to around 9% in a decade. Developing and emerging economies will account for 85% of electricity demand growth through 2035. Three priorities follow:

Build the systems around the power. Africa is heading for around 17 GW of new solar this year. Grids and storage must keep pace. In Mauritius, UNDP  has supported smart-grid technology and 18 MW of battery storage.

Lower financing costs. The same solar project can face two to three times the cost of capital in many emerging economies. A one percentage point reduction could save US$150 billion a year.

Keep more value locally. Electricity should power farms, businesses, and industry. Yet of 16.6 million renewable energy jobs worldwide, only 344,000 are in Africa.

By 2030, how much of the transition’s value will stay in the countries producing its power?

#SDG7 #EnergyforDevelopment #UNGA81
